**Constitutional Amendment #1 (applied and re-validated):** Chapter 6's self-review surfaced a genuine inconsistency between Chapter 1 §1.8 (ownership stays with the Examiner until a turn's audio is *fully delivered*) and Chapter 4 §4.10 (originally: `confirmAdvance` fires once delivery *begins*, inherited from Chapter 3 §3.6's original closing-turn-ordering fix). User-approved resolution: Chapters 1 and 2 stay untouched; Chapter 3 §3.6 (the original source of the "begins delivery" framing) and Chapter 4 §4.10 (which inherited it) were both amended so the ownership-transfer/state-advance point is **delivery fully completes**, not delivery begins — matching Chapter 1's stronger, unchanged invariant. Chapter 3 §3.16 and Chapter 5 §5.6 were refreshed to match (wording only, no rule change in either). Re-validated across all four affected chapters (3, 4, 5, and the paused Chapter 6) with no further issue found — see each chapter's own forward-reference index for the amendment entry.

**Constitutional Amendment #2 (applied and re-validated):** the fresh, independent document-wide audit found a genuine contradiction between two frozen chapters over whether the Prompt Library category list is closed. Chapter 10 §10.9 stated "§1.11 fixes the library list as closed" and that the "six-library list has no room for" a seventh — using that (overbroad) phrasing to make the narrower, correct point that no *Decision-Engine-triggered* intervention needs its own new category. Chapter 23 §23.6 later, legitimately, added a seventh category (Fallback) triggered by a Safety/Validation Layer outcome, not a Decision Engine trigger — and its own compatibility pass had checked §7.5–§7.8 but never §10.9, so the tension went undetected (Chapter 24's cross-check chapter missed it too). Resolution: §1.11's own text only enumerates six libraries and never states closure, so §10.9's "closed" was the overreach; §10.9's wording was narrowed to its actual scope (Decision-Engine-triggered categories need no new entry) with an amendment note, and §23.6 gained an explicit reconciliation clause. No mechanism changed in either chapter; §23.6's seventh category and §10.9's topic-drift reasoning both stand, now consistently. Re-validated: no other passage in the document relies on the Prompt Library list being a globally closed set of exactly six (Chapters 7, 15, 24, 25 all treat it as extensible or cite the seventh category without asserting closure).

**Freeze rule (governs every future chapter):** Once frozen, a chapter is the constitutional foundation of this architecture. No later chapter may redefine or contradict a frozen chapter. Later chapters may only extend it. If a later chapter's design appears to require modifying a frozen chapter, work stops immediately and the conflict is explained before any change is made — a frozen chapter is never silently adjusted to fit a later chapter's convenience.

**Constitutional amendment procedure:** the one exception to the freeze rule. If, while writing a later chapter, a genuine defect in a frozen chapter is discovered (not a preference, not something merely inconvenient to work around, but an actual contradiction, missing invariant, or gap that cannot be closed by extension alone), the defect is reported explicitly — which frozen chapter, which exact text, why it's a real defect and not a workaround-able gap — and work stops on the current chapter until the user explicitly approves the amendment. Only then is the frozen chapter edited, and the edit is logged in that chapter's own forward-reference index (the existing `§N.NN Forward-Reference Index` pattern already used throughout) under an explicit "Constitutional Amendment" entry, dated and reasoned, never folded silently into the original text as if it had always read that way.

**Validation discipline (governs every chapter from Chapter 2 onward):** no chapter is considered complete until it has passed, in order, and had every discovered issue fixed before proceeding: (1) adversarial review — attempting genuinely to reject the chapter, not confirm it; (2) constitutional-compatibility review — verified against every previously frozen chapter, with the amendment procedure above as the only path to touching one; (3) implementation review — mentally building the chapter's content end-to-end, module by module; (4) five-engineer validation — would independent senior engineers, given only the frozen chapters plus this one, converge on one implementation; (5) production-readiness validation — read start-to-finish as new, simulate real failure/concurrency/scale scenarios; (6) a quantitative scorecard, scored honestly against a 95-is-production-ready / 98+-is-exceptional / 100-is-reserved bar, with every category's score defended, not asserted; (7) a closing **Traceability Matrix** — every requirement the chapter introduces, mapped to the future chapter(s) that own its full implementation (or marked self-contained), with an explicit orphan count that must read zero before the chapter can be considered done. **As of Chapter 8, this discipline is no longer documentation-internal only:** every design decision is actively checked against the real, deployed codebase — schema, migrations, runtime behavior — wherever the chapter's content touches something that already exists, not assumed to match; own assumptions are actively attacked, not just reviewed; simplification opportunities are actively sought, not only defects. A chapter is only frozen once it has been through every pass above with no surviving defect — the same discipline already applied to Chapters 1–8, now standing policy for the rest of this document.

**Scope:** This document defines the system architecture for DeutschMaster's AI Speaking Examination Engine (Mündlich AI examiner). It does not define examiner behavior — that is a separate Behavior Specification document, written after this one is fully approved.

**Fixed technology stack** (given, not re-litigated here): **Gemini Flash** (reasoning), **Deepgram** (speech-to-text), **Gradium** (text-to-speech) — every vendor swappable behind a provider-adapter layer (§1.5, fully designed Chapter 22).

---

## Chapter 1 — Overall AI Architecture

### 1.0 Grounding: what already exists

DeutschMaster already has a working, deployed speaking-exam system (Fly.io relay service, `muendlich-relay/`, Node + WebSocket, live in production, currently one process handling multiple concurrent rooms). A factual survey of that system informs everything below.

**What stays:** the room/participant state machine in Postgres, WebSocket transport and client-side audio pipeline, server-authoritative timing with clock-offset sync, atomic dual-participant credit deduction, append-only transcript persistence, post-exam evaluation generation, room creation/matchmaking/room-codes, access control gating.

**What is being replaced:** the AI core — today, one opaque Gemini Live Audio session per room handles recognition, reasoning, and synthesis together, with "control" exercised by injecting text hints and trusting compliance.

**A durability distinction that matters for §1.10 below:** the existing transcript system (`muendlich_transcript_nodes`, an append-only write-ahead log, plus the evaluation reports generated from it) is retained *by design* — it is what post-exam scoring and reports read from, today and in any future scoring module. This is a different thing from the AI's *working memory* during a live exam, and the two must never be conflated (§1.10 makes this precise).

### 1.1 Purpose

Establish the definitive architectural foundation for the AI Speaking Examination Engine: the governing philosophy, the component shape, the state/event/ownership model, and the structural guarantees every later chapter must honor — verified in this revision against a start-to-finish read, a full implementation walkthrough of every module, and simulated cross-module interaction.

### 1.2 Core Philosophy

> **This is not an AI chatbot. This is a real-time TELC Speaking Examination Engine that happens to use AI — specifically, a language model — as one of its components.**

Throughout the entire examination, a student should genuinely feel they are speaking with an experienced human TELC examiner. Every decision — every response, every silence, every interruption, every transition — should reinforce that illusion, never break it. This is the test every other principle in this document is measured against.

> **The AI must never own examination logic.**

The language model never decides: when a section starts or ends; who speaks, or who speaks next; when to interrupt; when to ask a follow-up; when to transition; how many questions remain; when the exam finishes. Every one of those decisions belongs exclusively to the Orchestrator.

> **The AI executes. The Orchestrator controls.**

The language model is invoked, exactly once per turn, to produce a natural-sounding examiner *utterance* given a context the Orchestrator constructs. There is no code path by which its output can change the state machine, advance a timer, deduct a credit, or transition a stage.

### 1.3 Behavior/Architecture Separation

A second law, as fundamental as §1.2:

> **The examiner may behave differently in every single examination. The architecture itself never changes.**

Personality, tone, phrasing, questioning style, intervention timing, encouragement frequency, examiner gender/voice, even the exam format itself — all of it is **behavior**, and behavior always flows from exactly three places: the Prompt Builder's selection from its Prompt Libraries (§1.11), the Personality & Variation Config (§1.5), and the Decision Engine's policy rules (Chapter 10). None of those three things are the architecture — they are configuration and content the architecture *hosts*.

> **If implementing a new examiner style, personality, exam format, or intervention pattern ever requires touching the State Machine's shape, the Event Bus's event types, or the pipeline's stages, that is not a new behavior — it is evidence this document was incomplete, and it must be revised before that implementation proceeds.**

Two concrete corollaries, verified explicitly in this revision:

- The State Machine constrains **structure** (which stage is active, how long it lasts) — never **content** (what is actually said or asked). Any given stage has many valid conversational realizations.
- Personality and style variation changes **how** something is said. It never changes **whether** the Fairness Engine's rules, the Safety/Validation Layer's checks, or the Ownership Model's reclaiming rule apply.

### 1.4 Design Rationale

Four forces, in priority order: (1) §1.2 and §1.3 are constraints every decision must satisfy; (2) human realism requires low, predictable latency and natural turn-taking; (3) production-grade values (reliability, maintainability, vendor independence, cost control) favor independently-tunable, decomposed stages; (4) the system must remain operable without touching source code or the model's prompt — durations, thresholds, personality, question limits all live in the Configuration System (Chapter 16).

### 1.5 High-Level Components

**Terminology:** "Orchestrator" and "Orchestration Server" name the same thing — the whole server-side system below, encompassing every module in this section — and are used interchangeably throughout this document. "Prompt Builder" (§1.11) and "Context/Prompt Builder" (this section, §1.10) likewise name one module, not two: context-assembly and prompt-assembly are one responsibility, never split across collaborating modules.

**Process topology:** one long-lived process capable of handling many concurrent rooms, matching today's relay — not one process per exam. Horizontal scaling (multiple instances, each owning a disjoint, sticky set of rooms) is the assumed strategy for production-scale concurrency (capability: thousands of concurrent exams); full design is Chapter 20's, but every module below is scoped to one room's data at a time specifically so that assumption holds without rework.

**Sole source of truth for state and ownership:** the **State Machine** holds both current examination state and current conversational ownership — there is exactly one place either fact lives. The **Decision Engine** only ever *proposes* a transition or an ownership change; it never holds either as its own authoritative copy (§1.7, §1.8).

**Orchestration Server — named internal modules:**

| Module | Responsibility (one line) | Fully designed in |
|---|---|---|
| **State Machine** | Sole source of truth for current state and current ownership; guarantees transitions are idempotent (§1.7) | Chapter 4 |
| **Event Bus** | Routes events between modules with an ordered, per-room stream (§1.9); delivery semantics (at-least-once vs. exactly-once) an open question for Ch.13 | Chapter 13 |
| **Decision Engine** | Proposes transitions/ownership changes; gates LLM invocation; monitors topic relevance and conversation quality. **Flagged risk:** this module's responsibility list has grown broad — Chapter 10 must explicitly decide whether it stays one cohesive module or decomposes (e.g. a Relevance Monitor, a Quality Monitor, an Ownership Arbiter under a thin coordinator), and must define a **priority/conflict-resolution rule** for when its inputs (Silence Management, Fairness, topic-drift) disagree in the same turn | Chapter 10 |
| **Timing Engine** | Owns all durations/deadlines; remaining time shapes question-strategy, not just display | Chapter 11 |
| **Silence Management Engine** | Escalating response to raw silence *duration* — distinct from natural-completion detection (§1.9) | Chapter 12 / 15 |
| **Fairness Engine** | Tracks per-participant speaking time/question count; drives who's addressed next, independent of personality (§1.3) | Chapter 12 / 15 |
| **Context / Prompt Builder** | Assembles the stateless per-turn payload; selects from Prompt Libraries; includes active persona and language | Chapter 7 |
| **Personality & Variation Config** | Parametrizes rhythm, sentence structure, transition style, encouragement style, questioning style, formality, voice/gender identity, and language — selected at room-creation/configuration time, never hardcoded | Chapter 15 / 16 |
| **Cost Controller** | Filters/batches so the LLM is invoked only when genuinely needed | Chapter 21 |
| **Safety / Validation Layer** | Checks LLM output — against role/content boundaries and against leaking internal orchestration metadata (§1.13) — using both the generated text and the context payload that produced it; owns the bounded fallback path when output is rejected | Chapter 23 |
| **Logging / Observability Layer** | Records every decision made, not just every utterance spoken | Chapter 17 / 18 |

**Component responsibilities** (full detail Chapter 6):

| Component | Responsibility | Explicitly NOT its responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Client** | Capture/stream mic audio; play back synthesized audio; render exam state, transcript, and visual presentation driven by the same state/event/ownership signals the Orchestrator emits | Any business decision |
| **Orchestration Server** | Everything today's relay does, plus every module above | Does not generate text itself — delegates generation, retains every decision about when/whether/under what constraints |
| **Deepgram (STT, initial)** | Convert audio to text, streaming, with both interim and final results | Does not decide utterance completeness or response-worthiness (§1.10) |
| **Gemini Flash (LLM, initial)** | Given a context payload, return the examiner's next utterance as text | Knows nothing not explicitly supplied; holds no memory between calls |
| **Gradium (TTS, initial)** | Convert approved text to audio, executing given pacing/emphasis/pause cues and the selected voice/gender identity | Does not decide *how* something should sound or *which voice* to use beyond executing given instructions |
| **Database** | Persistent source of truth for durable data, including the transcript/evaluation record — distinct from AI working memory (§1.10) | Not queried live by AI vendors |

### 1.6 The Examination State Machine (Overview)

```
Waiting for Exam Start
  ↓
Greeting
  ↓
Teil 1 — Präsentation
  ↓
Teil 1 — Follow-up Questions
  ↓
Transition
  ↓
Teil 2 — Discussion
  ↓
Teil 2 — Follow-up Questions
  ↓
Transition
  ↓
Teil 3 — Discussion
  ↓
Teil 3 — Follow-up Questions
  ↓
Exam Closing
  ↓
Finished
```

**Naming:** "Waiting for Exam Start" is deliberately distinct from the existing production system's room-level `waiting_for_partner` state (which means waiting for a second participant, before prep or AI conversation begins). This state machine's first state begins only once both participants are present, ready, and prep is complete.

**"Transition" is a stage type, not a uniquely-named node.** The diagram shows two stages both labeled "Transition" — intentional, and it must not be implemented as one shared graph node that two different paths pass through. Each is a distinct entry in the ordered stage list below, carrying its own destination (the first entry's next stage is Teil 2 — Discussion, the second's is Teil 3 — Discussion). Two stages sharing a display label is a presentation-layer detail; the underlying data structure must identify stages positionally/by-id, never by display label alone — otherwise two engineers building this could easily converge on a single reused "Transition" node and lose track of which transition is currently active.

**This diagram is the TELC B2 instantiation of a general shape, not the shape itself.** A state-machine definition is data, not code: an ordered list of stage specifications, each carrying a name, a duration (or duration rule), and a full state contract (below) — loaded from the Configuration System per exam type. Chapter 4 must design the State Machine engine to consume that data structure generically; this exact diagram is the TELC B2 configuration's *value*, never a hardcoded structure the engine itself assumes.

**Chapter 4 versus Chapter 5.** Chapter 4 (State Machine) designs this state graph's transition mechanics — storage, idempotency, the stage-list data structure itself. Chapter 5 (Conversation Lifecycle) designs the room's life *around* this state machine — Preparation leading in, post-exam finalization leading out, and resumability after a full process restart. That is a distinct, broader scope this chapter deliberately leaves to Chapter 5 rather than silently assuming Chapter 4 covers everything lifecycle-related.

Every AI-generation call must include the current state as a mandatory field. **Every state's specification must define a full state contract, not merely an ownership contract:** entry conditions (what must be true to enter this state), exit conditions (what ends it), the ownership contract (who currently owns the conversation, who is expected to speak next, the conditions under which ownership changes, and when the Examiner observes, intervenes, interrupts, or remains silent), the set of valid events for this state, explicit handling for invalid events (an event that is structurally possible but semantically nonsensical here — e.g. a `TOPICS_SELECTED` event arriving during Teil 3 — must be defined as ignored, logged, or erred, never left to fall through undefined), recovery behavior (what happens if this state is re-entered after a crash or reconnect mid-state), and its invariant guarantees (facts that must remain true for the whole duration of the state). Chapter 4 may not define a state without answering all seven of those questions for it.

As an illustration of the *shape* such a contract takes (not a real design — that's Chapter 4's job): *"Teil 1 — Präsentation — entry: both participants ready and prior state = Greeting; exit: natural completion signal or timeout; owner = the presenting student; expected next speaker = same student, unless silence/confusion triggers reclaim; ownership returns to Examiner on completion or timeout; Examiner observes by default, intervenes only on a named trigger; valid events = {SILENCE_DETECTED, VOICE_STARTED/STOPPED, TIME_WARNING, TIME_LIMIT_REACHED, STUDENT_DISCONNECTED}; invalid events such as TOPICS_SELECTED are logged and dropped; on reconnect mid-state, resume with elapsed time preserved rather than restarting the stage; invariant: exactly one participant is the presenter for the state's duration."* This is the minimum shape every state must specify — Chapter 4 owns the actual content.

**Structure versus content:** this state machine fixes *when* Teil 2 happens and *how long* it lasts. It says nothing about what specific questions get asked or how the conversation unfolds — that is generated dynamically (§1.11) and differs, correctly, every time the same state is reached.

### 1.7 System-Driven Transitions

```
Timer expires
  ↓
Orchestrator emits END_TEIL1 event
  ↓
AI receives, via its next context payload, that this section is ending
  ↓
AI naturally closes Teil 1 (its one turn of output reflects the closing instruction)
  ↓
Orchestrator advances the State Machine to Transition → Teil 2
```

The timer expiring is a fact the Orchestrator observes and acts on directly. If the AI's response were somehow inconsistent with the transition, the state machine advances anyway. This generalizes to any system-detected condition (silence breached, fairness imbalance, all questions asked, unresolved topic drift): Orchestrator decides → AI is informed → AI executes narratively → Orchestrator's state is authoritative regardless of what the AI said.

> **Invariant: state transitions must be idempotent.** If a transition-triggering event is delivered more than once (duplicate delivery — a real possibility per §1.9's still-open delivery-semantics question), processing it a second time must never advance the state machine a second time for that same logical event. The State Machine must be able to recognize "this transition has already happened" and no-op safely. This is a hard requirement on Chapter 4's design, not an implementation detail — without it, a duplicated `END_TEIL1` event could silently skip an entire Teil.

### 1.8 The Conversation Ownership Model

> **At every moment during the examination, exactly one of three actors — Person A, Person B, or the Examiner — owns the conversation.** The owner is the party currently responsible for what happens next. There is never a moment where ownership is undefined.

**Precise definition of "the Examiner" as an ownership-holder:** when the Examiner owns the conversation, this always and only means *the Orchestrator has determined, via its deterministic State Machine and Decision Engine, that it is the Examiner's turn to act.* What the Examiner then actually says is generated by the AI, under constraints the Orchestrator set for that one turn — but the ownership decision itself, like every decision in §1.2's list, is never made by the AI. It is invoked *because* the Orchestrator has already decided the Examiner currently owns the conversation.

**Distinct from "who is currently speaking."** Ownership is a responsibility, not an audio state — the Examiner can own the conversation while producing no sound at all (silently deciding what happens next, or awaiting a generation in flight). `SPEAKER_CHANGED` (§1.9) reports who is making sound right now; `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` reports who is responsible for what happens next. These are related but never interchangeable, and no later chapter may conflate them.

Ownership moves naturally, and not always through the Examiner: a question is asked → ownership transfers to the student expected to answer; an answer concludes → ownership returns to the Examiner. But TELC B2 Teil 2 and Teil 3 are, by exam format, peer-to-peer discussions — the architecture must equally support ownership transferring directly between Person A and Person B without passing back through the Examiner between every exchange, with the Examiner still observing per §1.12 and still remaining owner of last resort exactly as below. Which discussion states permit direct peer transfer versus Examiner-mediated turn-taking is a per-state ownership-contract detail (§1.6) — Chapter 4's job to set — but the architecture must make direct peer-to-peer ownership transfer a representable case, not an impossible one. The critical rule:

> **Whenever ownership is lost or ambiguous — silence, hesitation, confusion, interruption, disagreement, technical delay, an answer that trails off unfinished, or an AI-generated response failing the Safety/Validation Layer's check — the Examiner automatically reclaims ownership (following whatever detection thresholds Chapter 12 defines; this section fixes that reclaiming is automatic and system-driven, not the exact timing) and restores the flow. The Examiner is the owner of last resort.**

A rejected AI response is deliberately included in that trigger list: if the Safety/Validation Layer rejects generated text, the exam must never simply go silent while the Orchestrator figures out what to do — that is exactly the kind of dead air the Ownership Model exists to prevent. The Safety/Validation Layer (§1.5) therefore owns a defined fallback path (retry with tightened constraints, or fall back to a neutral pre-approved Prompt Library utterance) — never silent pass-through of unvalidated text, and never a turn with no examiner action at all. That fallback path is bounded, not open-ended: retry is attempted up to a small, fixed maximum (the exact count is a Configuration System parameter, Chapter 16), and exhausting it always resolves deterministically to the neutral pre-approved utterance — an unbounded retry loop would itself violate the §1.10 latency budget and recreate the dead-air failure this rule exists to close.

**Turn overlap — a race condition made explicit.** While the Examiner owns the conversation and a generation/synthesis is in flight (the STT→LLM→TTS round-trip triggered by that ownership grant), new student audio may arrive — a student who mistook a processing pause for their cue, or who is genuinely trying to interrupt. The architecture fixes the rule now, precisely because two engineers could otherwise build this two incompatible ways: **ownership remains with the Examiner for the duration of an in-flight turn.** New audio arriving during that window is captured and buffered, never silently discarded, but it does not itself change ownership mid-flight. Once the in-flight turn completes (audio delivered to clients), that buffered audio becomes input to the *next* decision cycle — unless the Decision Engine's interruption-handling logic (a genuine behavior decision, Chapter 12/15) explicitly permits real-time barge-in for a given state, in which case that is expressed as configuration/policy on top of this rule, not an exception to it. What is fixed here, non-negotiably, is that ownership itself is never ambiguous during the overlap window, however the barge-in policy is eventually tuned.

This connects, rather than competes with, the modules in §1.5: the **State Machine** holds current ownership as authoritative state; the **Event Bus** carries ownership changes as first-class, ordered events (`OWNERSHIP_CHANGED`, new owner + reason, §1.9); the **Decision Engine** detects lost ownership and proposes reclaiming it.

**Interruption as an ownership mechanism, not rudeness.** Whenever time allows, the Examiner should wait for a natural stopping point before asserting ownership, rather than cutting off an important sentence mid-thought. Full trade-off design is Chapter 12/15.

**Scope.** Formal ownership applies from Greeting through Exam Closing. The existing Preparation room-state precedes this model.

**Open questions, named rather than left silent, for Chapter 19:** (a) what happens to a three-actor Ownership Model when one student *permanently* disconnects mid-exam — unresolved in both this document and the existing system; (b) how ownership is preserved across a *transient* disconnect/reconnect (a few seconds of dropped connection) during an in-flight turn — a distinct, narrower scenario from (a) that still needs an explicit answer, not an assumption that it's the same problem.

### 1.9 Event-Driven Backbone and Signal Precision

The Orchestrator is architected around an internal event bus, decoupling timing, silence, fairness, ownership, connection health, and vendor health from one another while all of them influence the same shared state.

Representative event categories (not exhaustive — Chapter 13's job):

- **Lifecycle:** `ROOM_CREATED`, `ROOM_JOINED`, `ROOM_READY`, `TOPICS_SELECTED`, `ROOM_FINISHED`
- **Audio / conversation:** `VOICE_STARTED`, `VOICE_STOPPED`, `SILENCE_DETECTED`, `QUESTION_COMPLETED`, `SPEAKER_CHANGED`
- **Ownership:** `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` (§1.8) — new owner, reason
- **Understanding / relevance:** `STUDENT_CONFUSION_DETECTED`, `TOPIC_DRIFT_DETECTED`
- **Timing:** `TIME_LIMIT_REACHED`, `TIME_WARNING`, `TRANSITION_STARTED`
- **Reliability:** `STUDENT_DISCONNECTED`, `STUDENT_RECONNECTED`, `STT_FAILURE`, `TTS_FAILURE`, `LLM_FAILURE`

**Two signals that must not be conflated:** `SILENCE_DETECTED` measures raw *absence of audio* for a duration — timer-driven. Whether a student has *actually finished their thought* is a separate, semantic/prosodic judgment (a thoughtful mid-sentence pause looks identical to silence in duration but means something different) — the Decision Engine's "is this utterance actually complete?" check (§1.14 step 3), informed by STT endpointing signals, never merely duration. Treating "quiet for N seconds" as equivalent to "finished speaking" would make interruptions feel mechanical — precisely the failure mode this document exists to avoid.

**Event ordering, not just delivery.** Two further guarantees, beyond at-least-once/exactly-once delivery (still an open Chapter 13 question), are fixed here because correctness depends on them: events for a single room must be processed in a strict, deterministic order (so, for example, two near-simultaneous `VOICE_STARTED` events from both participants resolve to one deterministic outcome, not a race); and where an ownership change is a direct *consequence* of a state transition (as in §1.7's example — Teil 1 closing hands ownership back to the Examiner), that ownership change must be processed atomically with the transition, never as an independently-racing event that could theoretically be observed out of order relative to the transition that caused it. A direct implementation corollary: this ordering guarantee means per-room event processing is effectively serialized — two engineers building this must not independently let two Decision Engine evaluations for the same room run concurrently against stale state; the ordering guarantee is what rules that out, not an unstated assumption of single-threading.

**Every event type — not only transition-triggering ones — needs a producer, a consumer set, an idempotency rule, and a failure/retry behavior; Chapter 13 must specify all four for each event in the list above, not just delivery semantics.** Two are worth fixing at the definitional level now, since they touch modules this chapter already commits to: `STUDENT_CONFUSION_DETECTED` and `TOPIC_DRIFT_DETECTED` are produced by the Decision Engine's own analysis (via whatever heuristic or auxiliary model call Chapter 10 specifies) — never by treating an LLM's incidental phrasing as a self-executing signal. Whatever computes them, the output is advisory input to a Decision Engine determination, exactly like every other signal in this document, never an action in itself (§1.2).

The governing principle: **the system reacts to events, not to AI decisions.** The AI is never a producer of events.

### 1.10 Statelessness and Context Discipline

Gemini Flash — and any future LLM provider — is a pure, stateless function: the system must never rely on the model "remembering" anything not explicitly re-supplied.

**Session memory — what the AI is allowed to know, and what must never persist.** Within a single, currently-running exam, the Context/Prompt Builder maintains rich session memory: who spoke first; who has spoken more/less; previous follow-up questions asked; previously discussed and previously unanswered ideas; full conversation history for the room; running speaking-balance figures; the Examiner's own previous interventions. (The concrete data structure holding this memory — the Session Object — is formalized in Chapter 14; this chapter only fixes its content and destruction rule, not its shape.)

> **This working memory is destroyed completely when the examination ends. No AI-facing information persists from one examination to the next. Every examination begins with a completely clean memory.**

This is distinct from the **durable transcript and evaluation record** (§1.0) — intentionally retained for evaluations and future scoring, but never fed back into a *future* exam's AI context. "Nothing persists" means nothing persists into the AI's working memory of a *different* examination; it does not mean the durable record is deleted.

**Mandatory per-call context fields:**

- Person A and Person B identity, and who's currently addressed
- Current examination state (§1.6) and current ownership (§1.8)
- Current turn's objective
- Selected topics for this room
- Relevant prior questions already asked
- Remaining time in the current section — shapes strategy, not just display
- Recent speaking history
- Current silence/confusion/topic-drift status, if relevant
- **The active persona configuration** — personality parameters, voice/gender identity, language — so the LLM's generated text stays consistent with what Gradium renders it as (without this, a "female examiner" configuration could select the correct TTS voice while the generated text stayed persona-agnostic — an inconsistency a real student would notice)
- **A student-progress signal.** This field is **always present** in the context schema — never conditionally omitted — with an explicit, defined "not yet assessed" default value for turns where the Decision Engine hasn't computed a real signal yet. This avoids the ambiguity of an optional field that different engineers might implement as present-when-available versus always-present-with-a-default; the schema fixes the latter. The exact signal computation is Behavior Specification / Chapter 10 territory; the field's presence and default are fixed here.

**Latency budget, defined precisely enough to be measured consistently.** The provisional target is **sub-second time from the Decision Engine's completeness determination to the first audio byte of the Examiner's response reaching the client** — a streaming pipeline, so the *first* byte is the meaningful bar, not the full utterance's total generation+synthesis time. This is a placeholder Chapter 11 must refine with real numbers, but the measurement point is fixed now so two engineers can't legitimately claim compliance against two different definitions of "latency."

**STT interim vs. final results:** the Decision Engine's completeness check evaluates finalized or high-confidence-interim results only — the exact confidence threshold is a Configuration System parameter (Chapter 16), not a fixed value baked into this document. It does not run full decision logic on every interim STT fragment.

**Language as configuration, not assumption:** the target language is a parameter supplied by the Configuration System and carried through context, the same way exam-type and persona are.

### 1.11 The Prompt Builder and Prompt Library Architecture

The Prompt Builder assembles the context (§1.10) plus a state-derived task instruction into one request per turn.

**Dynamic, context-derived generation — never a static list.** Every follow-up must be generated from what has actually happened in the conversation — the student's previous answers, ideas raised but not explored, natural next angles — never selected from a fixed tree. This is why the same state, reached in two different rooms, can and should produce different, equally valid conversations.

**Multiple specialized Prompt Libraries:** Greeting, Encouragement, Transition, Follow-up, Silence-recovery, Closing — each holding many natural variations, selected and assembled by the Prompt Builder rather than filled from one canonical template per category.

### 1.12 The Human Examiner Philosophy

A technically correct but emotionally robotic examiner fails the project's actual goal (§1.2). **Every item below describes the observable behavior the Decision Engine's rules and the Prompt Builder's generation are designed to produce — none of it describes the AI itself deciding anything; the AI never "decides" to observe or intervene, it generates the utterance that makes the Decision Engine's already-made determination sound natural.** With that read firmly in mind, the target examiner:

- leads naturally, remains professional, gives students genuine room to speak
- observes by default (the Decision Engine's default state produces no intervention), intervening only when a specific trigger fires — excessive silence, topic deviation, one student dominating, time management, needed clarification, or discussion recovery
- adapts to student performance (calmer guidance, more challenge, simplified wording, additional probing rather than correction) while remaining an examiner, never a teacher (§1.13)
- detects misunderstanding and rephrases before abandoning a thread
- uses natural, sparse backchannel acknowledgement, never repetitive, never substituting for a substantive response
- keeps praise controlled and rare, professional rather than effusive

This is a philosophy the architecture must enable, not define. What belongs here is confirming the named modules (Silence Management, Fairness, Decision Engine, Personality Config, Prompt Libraries, the student-progress context field) collectively give the Behavior Specification enough surface area to express this fully.

### 1.13 Fairness, Safety, and Variation as Architectural Guarantees

**Fairness and participation balance, independent of personality.** The Fairness Engine tracks per-participant speaking time and question count, and this data — not the AI's impression — determines who's addressed next. This guarantee holds identically regardless of which examiner personality is configured — style changes *how* the invitation to participate is phrased, never *whether* it happens. The same tracked data feeds conversation-quality monitoring as an extended responsibility of the Fairness Engine and Decision Engine together, not a new module.

**Topic relevance.** Monitored via `TOPIC_DRIFT_DETECTED`; guidance back to topic happens as part of the Examiner's normal turn.

**Safety and examiner role protection.** The AI must never leave the examiner role and must never become a teacher: no grammar correction, no vocabulary explanation, no model answers, no coaching, no revealing expected answers. Questions must never contain hidden hints; ideas must be the student's own. No casual chat, political/religious debate, answering unrelated questions, or renegotiating exam rules.

**Metadata and prompt leakage prevention — an explicit, named check, not an implied one.** The context payload the Prompt Builder assembles (§1.10) legitimately includes internal orchestration signals — the student-progress field, silence/confusion status, fairness data — that must inform *how* the AI generates text but must never appear *in* that text. The Safety/Validation Layer's inspection explicitly includes a check that no such internal signal, instruction, or system-level metadata has leaked into the spoken output (e.g., the examiner must never audibly say anything resembling "I notice your confidence score is low" or otherwise reveal that it is being fed structured internal state). This is enforced at the same two structural points already established: the Prompt Builder frames instructions so the model has no natural reason to describe its own inputs, and the Safety/Validation Layer inspects output before Gradium ever receives it. Mechanically, this requires the Safety/Validation Layer's input to be the generated text *and* the context payload that produced it — not the text alone; without the context payload to compare against, there is nothing to check the text for leaking against. Chapter 23 owns the exact comparison mechanism, but this chapter fixes that both inputs are available to it.

**Variation and anti-repetition.** Greetings, transitions, encouragements, and closings each vary naturally, drawn from the Prompt Libraries rather than one canonical formulation per category.

### 1.14 Data Flow — One Conversational Turn

1. Student speaks; client streams audio to the Orchestrator over the existing WebSocket transport.
2. Orchestrator forwards audio to **Deepgram**, receiving interim and final transcripts.
3. The **Decision Engine** evaluates finalized/high-confidence results — is this utterance complete (distinct from mere silence, §1.9)? does current state/ownership call for a response? A signal that doesn't meet the bar produces no LLM call.
4. If warranted, the **Fairness Engine**, **Silence Management Engine**, and topic/confusion signals contribute input; the **Prompt Builder** assembles context plus a task instruction from the right **Prompt Library**.
5. **Gemini Flash** returns text. The **Safety/Validation Layer** inspects it — using both the text and the context payload that produced it — for role adherence, teaching/coaching boundaries, metadata-leakage (§1.13), and content boundaries — before it can become the examiner's voice. **On rejection, the bounded fallback path defined in §1.8 applies — the turn never simply goes silent, and retries never loop unbounded.**
6. Approved text, with Orchestrator-decided behavior cues (pacing, emphasis, pauses, voice/gender identity), is sent to **Gradium**, returning synthesized audio, streamed to minimize time-to-first-byte against the §1.10 budget. **Ownership remains with the Examiner for the duration of this in-flight turn (§1.8) — new student audio arriving now is buffered, not discarded, and does not itself reassign ownership.**
7. Audio forwarded to both clients and played back.
8. In parallel: transcript nodes, timers, state/ownership, credits update as today; the **Logging/Observability Layer** records the Decision Engine's decision and inputs, not just the final utterance.

This eight-step walkthrough sketches the turn-level shape only. Streaming mechanics — backpressure if Deepgram's or Gradium's stream stalls, partial-result buffering, what happens to an in-flight TTS stream if the state transitions mid-utterance — are pipeline-internals Chapter 3 (AI Pipeline) must fully design; nothing here should be read as already deciding them.

### 1.15 Advantages of This Architecture

The core philosophy (§1.2), the behavior/architecture separation (§1.3), and the Ownership Model (§1.8) — including its turn-overlap, peer-to-peer, and bounded rejection-fallback rules — are enforced structurally, not by convention. Independent observability and control per pipeline stage. Vendor independence (Chapter 22). A genuine safety/business-logic insertion point twice per turn. Builds on proven, already-deployed infrastructure.

### 1.16 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Keep the current unified Gemini Live Audio approach.** Simpler, but preview-model risk, ambient LLM access at odds with §1.2, single-vendor lock-in. Rejected.

**(b) Client calls vendors directly.** Rejected outright.

**(c) Decomposed pipeline, Orchestrator as sole director (recommended).** The only option that satisfies §1.2 by construction.

### 1.17 Recommended Approach

Option (c), under a single Orchestration Server evolving the existing `muendlich-relay`. All vendor calls through thin provider adapters (Chapter 22); all durations/thresholds/personality/language parameters and Prompt Library contents from the Configuration System (Chapter 16), never hard-coded.

### 1.18 Possible Risks

Latency stacking against the §1.10 provisional budget. Three independent failure surfaces (Chapter 19), including the open permanent- and transient-disconnect questions (§1.8). Context/prompt assembly as a genuinely new responsibility (Chapters 7–9). Migration risk against a live system. Decision Engine responsibility growth (§1.5, flagged for Chapter 10). Event delivery semantics undecided (§1.9, Chapter 13). Scope/complexity discipline required going forward.

## Answering the governing question directly

**"If we implement the remaining 24 chapters exactly as planned, will Chapter 1 ever force us to redesign the architecture?"**

**No.** Four full review passes — an adversarial architecture review, a future-capability audit, a constitutional review with explicit session simulation, and this production-readiness validation with a full mental implementation walkthrough of every module — have now been applied. Every finding across all four was resolved by naming a rule, an invariant, a terminology reconciliation, or a cross-reference explicitly, never by changing the pipeline shape, the module list, or the Ownership Model itself. This round's findings were qualitatively different from Revision 5's: no race conditions, no missing invariants — only places where the *wording* still allowed two competent engineers to diverge (an ambiguous diagram label, an under-specified state contract, an implicit assumption about peer-to-peer discussion ownership, an unbounded retry, two modules referred to by three names). That shift — from correctness gaps to precision gaps — is itself the signal that the architecture has converged.

§1.3 remains the standing test for every future chapter. Having now read Chapter 1 start-to-finish as a new engineer would, mentally implemented all eight core modules and their interactions, verified every state transition and event against the seven-part/four-part checklists in §1.6 and §1.9, and confirmed Chapters 2–24 each have a clear, non-overlapping, non-contradicting scope pointer rather than an unstated assumption — I genuinely believe this document is production-ready. A new engineering team, handed this chapter alone, could build the intended system without needing to guess at any of the points this round tested.

## Chapter 2 — AI Orchestrator

### 2.0 Compatibility with Chapter 1 (frozen)

Before any new content: this chapter was checked against every relevant Chapter 1 fact, and **no point below required modifying Chapter 1.** Where this chapter needed something Chapter 1 hadn't fully specified, it extends — never edits — the frozen text. Specifically, this chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- The **State Machine is the sole source of truth** for state and ownership (§1.5, §1.8) — Chapter 2 introduces no second authority.
- The **Decision Engine only proposes**, never holds state (§1.5) — unchanged.
- The **11 named modules** in §1.5's table are the complete module list — Chapter 2 adds no 12th decision-making module (§2.3 explains why).
- **"The AI executes, the Orchestrator controls"** (§1.2) and **"the AI is never a producer of events"** (§1.9) — Chapter 2's entire purpose is making these literally true at the wiring level, not just stated intentions (§2.7).
- The **process topology** (one long-lived Orchestration Server process, many concurrent rooms, horizontal scaling via sticky room ownership, §1.5) — Chapter 2's Room Runtime (§2.3) is the per-room composition unit that process *hosts*, never a replacement for it; "Orchestrator" continues to mean the whole process, exactly as §1.5 fixed.
- The **event-ordering and per-room serialization guarantees** (§1.9) — Chapter 2 treats the Event Bus as the only inter-module communication path, never bypassed by a direct call.

If a future chapter (3 onward) surfaces a genuine conflict with Chapter 1, the same rule applies: stop, explain, do not silently edit the frozen chapter.

### 2.1 Purpose

Chapter 1 establishes *that* an Orchestrator exists, governs, and never lets the AI own logic, and fixes "Orchestrator" as a synonym for "Orchestration Server" — the whole process (§1.5's terminology note). What it deliberately leaves open is what runs *inside* that process for each active room. Chapter 2 closes that gap: it defines the per-room composition unit the Orchestration Server hosts — how Chapter 1's 11 named modules are composed, instantiated, connected, and torn down for a single exam room — and precisely how the chain of authority Chapter 1 mandates is *enforced*, not merely followed by convention.

### 2.2 Design Rationale

Without an explicit answer to "what wires the 11 modules together," two engineers implementing Chapter 1 could converge on very different systems — one might have each module reach out and call its neighbors directly (ad hoc coupling, silently reintroducing exactly the "two engineers, two implementations" risk Chapter 1 exists to prevent); another might centralize everything into one large coordinating class that quietly starts making decisions itself, becoming a second, undeclared authority competing with the State Machine. Chapter 2 forecloses both failure modes by naming the composition mechanism explicitly and constraining what it is and is not allowed to do.

### 2.3 The Orchestrator Is a Composition Root, Not a Module

> **The Orchestrator (the Orchestration Server, §1.5) does not itself decide anything, and no single module within it acting alone decides anything either. What runs inside the process for each active room is a composition, not a 12th authority.**

This per-room composition unit is the **Room Runtime**: one instantiated per active exam room, hosted inside the single Orchestration Server process (§1.5, §2.0) alongside every other concurrently active room's own Room Runtime. It holds references to that room's own instances of the State Machine, Event Bus, Decision Engine, Timing Engine, Silence Management Engine, Fairness Engine, Context/Prompt Builder, Cost Controller, Safety/Validation Layer, and Logging/Observability Layer — ten per-room module instances, drawn from §1.5's table (unchanged). Personality & Variation Config is deliberately not in this list: §2.4 below fixes it as a process-wide *source* the Room Runtime reads from, once, to parametrize those per-room instances (most directly the Context/Prompt Builder) — never a per-room instance the Room Runtime itself holds a reference to. The Room Runtime is not a rename of "the Orchestrator" — it is the concrete, per-room thing the Orchestrator (still the whole process, per §1.5) creates and hosts.

The Room Runtime's own code is limited to exactly three things: **instantiate** the room's module set at room start, **wire** their communication through the Event Bus (never through direct module-to-module calls that bypass it), and **release** them at room end. It contains no `if` statement that inspects exam content, student behavior, or AI output to decide what happens next — every such decision already belongs to the Decision Engine and State Machine per Chapter 1. A Room Runtime that accumulates business logic over time has stopped being a composition root and has become the very undeclared second authority §2.2 warns against — this is named explicitly as an ongoing discipline risk in §2.13, not something solved once and forgotten.

**"Communication through the Event Bus" governs proposals and notifications, not read access to authoritative state.** A module reading the State Machine's *current* value (e.g. the Prompt Builder reading current state/ownership to assemble context, per §1.10) is a direct, synchronous query against the single authoritative holder of that data — this is not "bypassing" the Event Bus, because nothing is being decided or mutated by the read. What must never happen as a direct call is any *proposal* (a transition, an ownership change) or any *cross-module notification* (a signal one module wants another to react to) — those exist only as Event Bus events, exactly as the diagram in §1.5 shows the Decision Engine's arrows running through ownership tracking rather than a direct write. This distinction — read access permitted directly from the sole authoritative source, all decisions and notifications event-mediated — is fixed here so two engineers don't diverge on whether a `getCurrentState()`-style call constitutes forbidden coupling.

Why not option (b) — an Orchestrator that *does* supervise and decide? Because Chapter 1 already fixed the State Machine as sole source of truth (§1.5) and the Decision Engine as the sole proposer (§1.5, §1.8); a supervising Orchestrator would have to either duplicate that authority (a consistency hazard) or defer to it completely (in which case it isn't actually supervising anything, and calling it a "supervisor" is misleading). The composition-root framing is the only one that doesn't quietly contradict the frozen chapter.

### 2.4 Module Composition & Dependency Graph

Instantiation is ordered, not simultaneous, because several modules depend on others already existing to subscribe to them:

1. **State Machine** and **Event Bus** first — the substrate. Every other module depends on one or both.
2. **Decision Engine** next — subscribes to the Event Bus, reads State Machine state, and registers itself as the (sole) proposer of transitions and ownership changes.
3. **Timing Engine, Silence Management Engine, Fairness Engine** — each subscribes to the Event Bus independently and feeds signals toward the Decision Engine; they do not depend on each other (this is what makes them independently replaceable per §1.9's decoupling rationale).
4. **Context/Prompt Builder** — instantiated once the above exist, since it reads State Machine state, Decision Engine output, and (per Chapter 14, forward reference) the room's Session Object.
5. **Safety/Validation Layer** — instantiated last among the decision-adjacent modules, since its only inputs are the Prompt Builder's context payload and the LLM's output (§1.13); it has no dependency on Timing/Silence/Fairness directly.
6. **Logging/Observability Layer** — attached last, as a pure subscriber to the Event Bus and to every other module's decision points (§1.5: "records every decision made, not just every utterance spoken"); nothing depends on it, which is what makes it safe to attach last and remove without affecting exam behavior.

**Instantiation order is acyclic; runtime event flow is not, and must not be forced to be.** The ordering above governs only construction time — which module must already exist before another can be wired to it. Once running, data flows in loops by design: e.g. the Fairness Engine observes `SPEAKER_CHANGED`/`OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` events (§1.9) that are themselves consequences of State-Machine transitions the Decision Engine proposed using, in part, earlier Fairness Engine signal. This is a normal event-driven feedback loop, not a circular *dependency* — no module's constructor requires another module that in turn requires it back, which is the only kind of cycle this section forbids. Chapter 13 must not attempt to eliminate this feedback loop while satisfying this section's acyclic-instantiation requirement; the two are compatible by construction, and conflating them would be a design error.

**Per-room versus process-wide.** State Machine, Event Bus, Decision Engine, Timing/Silence/Fairness Engines, Context/Prompt Builder, Safety/Validation Layer, and **Cost Controller** are all **per-room instances** — this is what §1.5's "every module is scoped to one room's data at a time" already committed to, made concrete, with no exception. **Personality & Variation Config** and the **Configuration System** (Chapter 16) are process-wide *sources* the Room Runtime reads from once at room-start to parametrize its per-room instances — the config data is shared and read-only per room; the resulting instances are not. A process-wide aggregate spend cap across all concurrent rooms is a real future need, but it is explicitly **not** designed here: a shared, mutable, cross-room counter would itself violate the no-exception rule just stated and reintroduce the cross-room coupling §2.6 exists to prevent. Chapter 21 owns finding a way to achieve aggregate budget control — e.g. an out-of-band aggregator each Room Runtime reports to asynchronously, never a shared in-process counter — without breaking that guarantee. Named here as an open, real, non-trivial constraint on Chapter 21, not resolved.

### 2.5 Room Runtime Lifecycle

**Birth.** Triggered by the existing room becoming ready (§1.6: prep complete, both participants present) — the Room Runtime instantiates its per-room module set per §2.4's order, loads Personality & Variation Config and exam-type state-machine configuration (§1.6) from the Configuration System, and transitions the State Machine into "Waiting for Exam Start."

**Birth is atomic and fail-closed.** If instantiating or wiring any module in §2.4's order fails partway — including a process refusing the room outright because it is at capacity (an admission-control policy fully designed in Chapter 20, but whose failure mode is fixed here) — the Room Runtime must never be left half-built. Every module instance already created during the failed attempt is released immediately, the room is reported as failed to create rather than silently left sitting in "Waiting for Exam Start" with modules missing, and no Run phase ever begins against a partially initialized Room Runtime. There is no code path that lets an exam start with, for example, a Safety/Validation Layer that failed to instantiate.

**Fresh birth versus resumed birth are two distinct entry paths, not one.** Everything above describes *fresh* birth: a room with no prior state, starting at "Waiting for Exam Start." A room whose hosting process died mid-exam and is being picked up by a different process instance is a second, distinct path — *resumed* birth — which Chapter 5 (Conversation Lifecycle) already owns under "resumability after a full process restart" (§1.6). Chapter 2 fixes only that these are two different cases the Room Runtime's Birth logic must distinguish (by checking persisted room state before assuming a fresh start); what a resumed birth actually reconstructs — and what, if anything, is unrecoverable about the destroyed session memory (§1.10) of a room that died mid-exam — is Chapter 5's and Chapter 19's question, not silently assumed to be identical to fresh birth.

**Run.** The Room Runtime itself does nothing during this phase beyond having wired the Event Bus — all behavior is the modules reacting to events, exactly as Chapter 1 describes (§1.7, §1.9, §1.14).

**Teardown.** Triggered by the State Machine reaching "Finished" (§1.6). Two things happen, in this order, and must not be conflated: (1) the durable record — transcript nodes, evaluation inputs, timing/credit records — is **not** batch-written at teardown; per §1.0 it has been persisted incrementally throughout the exam, so teardown does not risk losing it. (2) The room's **session memory is destroyed** (§1.10's hard rule) by releasing the Room Runtime's per-room module instances and their held Session Object (Chapter 14, forward reference) — this is the literal mechanism behind §1.10's "completely clean memory" guarantee, not a separate promise Chapter 2 has to re-justify. A Room Runtime that somehow kept a per-room instance alive or pooled it for reuse after teardown would silently violate §1.10 — this is flagged as an implementation hazard for Chapter 14/19 to guard against explicitly, not assumed away.

**Teardown is best-effort-complete, not all-or-nothing.** Unlike Birth, Teardown must not abort partway because a single module fails to release — if releasing one module instance throws, the remaining instances are still released, and the failure is recorded via the Logging/Observability Layer (§2.4 item 6 — released last, specifically so it can still capture a teardown-time failure) rather than silently swallowed or left to leak the rest. Aborting Teardown early on the first failure would leak every resource held by whatever hadn't been released yet — exactly the leaked-resource failure mode this chapter must rule out.

**Client-facing finalization sequencing is explicitly out of scope here.** Exactly when the client WebSocket connection closes relative to Teardown's two steps — e.g. whether a final "exam finished" notification and any closing summary are sent before the connection drops — is part of "post-exam finalization leading out," which §1.6 already assigns to Chapter 5. Chapter 2 fixes only the internal module-release sequence above; it does not assume the WebSocket closes at any particular point in that sequence, so Chapter 5 is free to specify it without contradicting anything fixed here.

### 2.6 Concurrency & Isolation Model

One Room Runtime instance per room; a fault inside one Room Runtime (a module throwing, a vendor adapter hanging) must not be observable by any other room's Room Runtime — each is its own failure boundary. This is what makes a Room Runtime the natural unit of the horizontal-scaling and sticky-room-ownership strategy §1.5 already assumed: an instance of the process owns a disjoint set of Room Runtimes, and losing a process loses only that process's rooms, never the whole fleet. Chapter 20 owns the full scaling design (how Room Runtimes are assigned to processes, rebalancing, etc.); Chapter 2 fixes only that the Room Runtime — not the room's raw data, not an individual module — is the unit that gets assigned.

**This is also the architecture's cross-room and cross-session containment guarantee, stated explicitly rather than left as an implicit consequence:** because per-room module instances (§2.4) share no mutable state with any other room's instances — the sole process-wide component is the read-only Configuration System (§2.4, §2.9) — there is no wiring path by which one room's session memory, transcript, or in-flight turn can leak into or influence another room's. This holds by construction, because no shared mutable state exists to leak through — not by a runtime check that could be bypassed or forgotten.

### 2.7 Enforcing the Chain of Authority

This section makes Chapter 1's philosophical laws structurally true, not just stated, by naming every gate a turn's data must pass through and confirming none is skippable.

> **Five gates, all wiring-enforced, none bypassable: the Event Bus (the only channel connecting modules, §2.3), the Decision Engine (the only gate before generation is invoked, §1.14 step 3), the Prompt Builder (the only assembler of what the LLM receives, §1.14 step 4), the Safety/Validation Layer (the only gate before synthesized output can reach a client, §1.14 step 5), and the Ownership Model / State Machine (the only authority that can confirm a turn is still valid before it is delivered, below).**

**Inbound path.** Client audio reaches Deepgram only through the Room Runtime's fixed pipeline entry point. Deepgram's output reaches Gemini Flash only after passing through the Decision Engine's gate and the Prompt Builder's assembly — there is no shorter wiring path that skips them.

**Outbound path.** Gemini Flash's output reaches Gradium only after passing through the Safety/Validation Layer — there is no shorter wiring path that skips it either.

**Delivery gate — the stale-turn discard rule.** A gate at generation time is not sufficient by itself: a turn can be correctly generated and approved, and still be *wrong to deliver* if enough time passed during generation that the State Machine has since moved on — the timer fired, a transition occurred, the room reached Teardown — a real possibility under load or vendor latency spikes (§1.18; Phase 6/8-class scenarios). To close this, every in-flight turn is tagged, at the moment the Decision Engine gates it, with the State Machine state and ownership grant it was generated under. Before the Room Runtime *begins* delivering synthesized audio to any client, it checks that tag against current State Machine state. A mismatch means the turn is **stale**: it is discarded, never delivered, logged via the Logging/Observability Layer, and — if the Examiner's turn is still needed — a fresh turn is generated against the *current* state rather than a client ever hearing a response that no longer matches reality. This makes ownership (§1.8) a delivery-time guarantee, not merely a generation-time one, and composes directly with §1.7's transition-idempotency invariant and §1.8's turn-overlap rule rather than adding a competing mechanism alongside them.

**This gate fires once, before streaming starts — what happens if the state changes *during* an already-started stream is deliberately not decided here.** §1.14 already reserves "what happens to an in-flight TTS stream if the state transitions mid-utterance" as pipeline-internals Chapter 3 (AI Pipeline) must fully design. Chapter 2 fixes the gate that decides whether a delivery is allowed to *begin*; whether an already-*started* stream can be truncated, must play out, or is handled some third way is intentionally left to Chapter 3, and nothing in this section should be read as having silently assumed an answer to that narrower question.

**Adapter-binding exclusivity — closing the last possible bypass.** §2.8 establishes that AI vendors are reached only through adapter interfaces, but does not by itself say *which* module may hold *which* adapter binding — and that gap would otherwise reopen exactly the bypass this section exists to close. Fixed here: **the Gemini Flash (LLM) adapter binding used to generate examiner utterances, and the Gradium (TTS) adapter binding used to synthesize them, are held exclusively by the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer-to-Gradium pathway.** No other module — including the Decision Engine, even though §1.9 allows it a private, auxiliary model call for confusion/topic-drift analysis (via whatever mechanism Chapter 10 specifies) — holds or uses that same generation-pathway binding. Whatever internal analysis mechanism Chapter 10 gives the Decision Engine is a separate, distinctly-bound capability whose output is advisory data on the Event Bus (§1.9), never text that can reach Gradium or a client directly, and it does not depend on the Context/Prompt Builder existing (§2.4's instantiation order is unaffected). This is what makes "no shorter wiring path" in this section a binding-level guarantee, not merely a description of the intended call graph.

This is the concrete meaning of §1.2's "there is no code path by which its output can change the state machine": it is not achieved by the LLM choosing to behave, it is achieved by the Room Runtime never wiring a path that would let it do otherwise, and never delivering output the State Machine can no longer vouch for. The same applies in reverse — the Decision Engine, Timing Engine, Silence Management Engine, and Fairness Engine all communicate their findings *to* the State Machine (proposing) via the Event Bus, never by mutating State Machine data directly; the State Machine remains the only writer of its own state, which is what makes "sole source of truth" (§1.5) enforceable rather than aspirational.

**Logging must never sit on this critical path.** The Logging/Observability Layer's writes are non-blocking with respect to all five gates above — a slow or failing log write must never delay a state transition, an event's delivery, or a turn's progress through the pipeline. A logging failure is itself just logged-best-effort and counted, never a reason to stall the exam — this closes a concrete starvation risk: a synchronous, blocking logging call sitting on the Event Bus's path would be a single point where many concurrent rooms could all stall on one slow disk write.

### 2.8 External Interfaces (Boundary Contracts)

Chapter 1's component table (§1.5) already names four boundaries; Chapter 2 fixes the *shape* of each contract (full schemas remain Chapter 7/8/22 territory):

- **Client ↔ Room Runtime:** the existing WebSocket transport (§1.0, unchanged) carries three message families — audio frames inbound; state/ownership/event notifications and synthesized audio outbound; and control acknowledgements. The Room Runtime is the only thing on the server side that terminates this connection; no individual module (Decision Engine, Safety Layer, etc.) ever holds a client connection directly. WebSocket is today's transport, reached only through a transport adapter the Room Runtime depends on — the same pattern applied to AI vendors below, so a future transport is an adapter swap, not a Room Runtime rewrite.
- **Room Runtime ↔ Database:** writes are incremental and continuous during Run (transcript nodes, state transitions, timing checkpoints, credit deductions — §1.0's existing mechanisms, unchanged); reads happen once at Birth (room config, participant identity, credit balance, exam-type state-machine configuration). No module queries the database mid-turn on the latency-critical path (§1.10's budget) except where §1.0's existing credit-deduction mechanism already does so. Database access is likewise reached only through a persistence adapter, never a direct dependency on today's specific database technology.
- **Room Runtime ↔ AI vendors:** exclusively through the provider-adapter layer (§1.5, fully designed Chapter 22) — the Room Runtime and every module import only an adapter interface (an STT adapter, an LLM adapter, a TTS adapter), never a vendor SDK directly. Swapping Deepgram, Gemini Flash, or Gradium is an adapter swap; it does not touch Room Runtime wiring, which is what makes §1.15's "vendor independence" claim actually hold at the code level.

**One pattern, four boundaries.** Transport, database, and the three AI vendors are all reached exclusively through an adapter interface, never a direct technology dependency inside the Room Runtime or any module — a single, consistently-applied pattern, not four separate decisions. This is what makes the extensibility claim (new languages, new exam formats, new providers, new databases, new transport layers, all addable without touching a frozen chapter) hold everywhere it's claimed, not only for AI vendors.

### 2.9 Startup, Shutdown, and Multi-Instance Coordination

At the process level (not the per-room level): the Configuration System (Chapter 16) loads once when a process instance starts, before any Room Runtime can be born. Sticky routing of a given room to a given process instance (§1.5, §2.6) is assumed but not designed here — Chapter 20's job. Graceful shutdown of a process instance mid-exam (deploys, scaling events) is named as an open concern for Chapter 19/20 rather than silently assumed away: an in-flight Room Runtime cannot simply vanish without either completing its current turn or handing off state cleanly, and Chapter 1 already commits (§1.8) to naming disconnect-adjacent failure modes explicitly rather than assuming they don't happen.

**Two failure modes worth naming explicitly.** If the Configuration System fails to load at process startup, the process fails closed — it refuses to birth any Room Runtime — rather than falling back to defaults that could silently misconfigure an exam; a wrong exam-type state machine or a wrong retry parameter is worse than refusing to start. And: **this architecture has no Redis or other distributed cache/broker dependency.** The Event Bus (§1.9) is an in-process, per-Room-Runtime construct, not a shared distributed system — a Room Runtime's Event Bus failing is a fault inside that Room Runtime, already covered by §2.6's isolation guarantee (it tears down that one room, never the process). If a future chapter (13 or 20) introduces a distributed broker for cross-instance coordination, that is a new dependency to be evaluated then, not one assumed to already exist now.

### 2.10 Advantages

A single, named composition mechanism means every future chapter that touches a module's *internals* (Chapters 4, 7–13, 15–18, 21, 23) can do so without ever having to re-answer "how does this get wired into the room" — that question is answered once, here. The chain-of-authority wiring guarantees in §2.7 turn Chapter 1's laws into things a code reviewer can verify by reading import statements, not just trusting good intentions. Per-room failure isolation (§2.6) is a direct, load-bearing consequence of choosing the Room Runtime as the composition unit, not a bolted-on afterthought.

### 2.11 Alternatives Considered

**(a) No explicit composition root — modules wire themselves ad hoc, via shared global state or direct references to each other.** Rejected: this is exactly the "two engineers, two implementations" failure mode Chapter 1's entire discipline exists to close, and it risks modules bypassing the Event Bus's ordering guarantees (§1.9) by calling each other synchronously and directly.

**(b) An Orchestrator that actively supervises and decides — a 12th module with real authority.** Rejected: directly conflicts with the frozen §1.5 fact that the State Machine is the sole source of truth and the Decision Engine the sole proposer; a supervising Orchestrator would be an undeclared second authority.

**(c) Room Runtime as a pure composition root, Event Bus as the only enforced inter-module communication path (recommended).** The only option that is a strict extension of Chapter 1 rather than a competing interpretation of it.

**(d) Stateless per-turn reconstruction — no persistent Room Runtime; rebuild session memory from the database on every turn.** Rejected: this would place a database round-trip inside the latency-critical path (§1.10's sub-second, time-to-first-byte budget) for *every single turn*, at the "thousands of concurrent rooms" scale §1.5 already targets — a direct, quantifiable conflict with an already-fixed Chapter 1 constraint, not a style preference. It also buys nothing the Room Runtime's per-room isolation (§2.6) doesn't already provide.

### 2.12 Recommended Approach

Option (c): one Room Runtime per active room, instantiating and wiring the 10 per-room modules per §2.4's dependency order (Personality & Variation Config remains the process-wide source §2.4 already fixes, not an 11th per-room instance), communicating exclusively over the Event Bus, holding zero business logic of its own, and torn down per §2.5's two-step teardown the moment the State Machine reaches "Finished."

### 2.13 Possible Risks

**Composition-root erosion.** The single largest risk to this chapter's design is social, not technical: over time, "just add one small check here, it's easier than going through the Decision Engine" is how a composition root quietly becomes an undeclared 12th module. This must be treated as a defect the moment it's found, not a pragmatic shortcut — flagged here explicitly so later chapters (and code review, once implementation starts) treat it as a standing invariant to defend, not a one-time design decision.

**Per-room memory footprint at scale.** Many concurrent Room Runtimes, each holding 10 per-room module instances plus a Session Object, has real memory cost at the "thousands of concurrent exams" scale §1.5 already targets — a genuine input to Chapter 20's scaling design and Chapter 21's cost design, not solved here.

**Teardown ordering bugs.** §2.5's two-step teardown (durable data already safe → then destroy session memory) is easy to get backwards during implementation; getting it backwards in the *other* direction (destroying session memory before confirming the durable record is complete) would silently violate §1.0's durability guarantee. Named here as a specific thing Chapter 14/19's design and any future test plan must verify directly, not merely assume from the ordering stated here.

**Stale-turn tagging overhead.** §2.7's delivery-gate check adds a small, constant-time comparison (tagged generation-state vs. current state) to every turn — negligible against the §1.10 latency budget, but worth naming so it isn't rediscovered as a mystery cost during Chapter 3/11's detailed pipeline timing work.

### 2.14 Future Improvements

The strict adapter-only boundary (§2.8), now extended to all four external boundaries rather than only AI vendors, is what would let a future chapter introduce a second concurrent LLM/STT/TTS vendor (for A/B cost or quality comparison), a new database, or a new transport as a configuration choice rather than a wiring change. The per-room isolation model (§2.6) is what would let a future chapter support exam types with different concurrency needs (e.g., a group exam with more than two students) without redesigning the composition mechanism — only the module set and state-machine configuration loaded at Birth would change.

## Chapter 2 — Freeze Assessment

Sixteen findings total have now surfaced across two full adversarial passes (eleven under the constitutional validation, five under this five-engineer implementation validation) — all sixteen fixed above, none requiring a change to frozen Chapter 1. The five found in this pass were of a different character than the first eleven: not contradictions or missing invariants, but *unstated boundaries* — points where Chapter 2 was correct as far as it went but hadn't yet said where its own jurisdiction ends and another chapter's begins (the read/event distinction, adapter-binding exclusivity, the stream-truncation boundary, fresh-vs-resumed birth, WebSocket-close timing). Closing boundary ambiguity rather than finding new contradictions is itself a signal of convergence, consistent with what happened between Chapter 1's Revision 5 and Revision 6.

One explicit note on Phase 11's per-module completeness checklist (purpose, responsibility, owner, inputs, outputs, dependencies, lifecycle, failure behavior, recovery behavior, boundaries, invariants, for every module): Chapters 1 and 2 together fix each module's name, one-line responsibility, position in the composition/dependency graph, and lifecycle phase membership — but deliberately do not fully specify per-module failure/recovery/invariant detail, because that is explicitly the job of each module's own dedicated chapter (4, 7, 9–13, 15–18, 21, 23), a boundary this document has held consistently since Chapter 1's first draft and re-confirmed by the user across six revisions. Treating that deferral as a defect would mean pre-writing two-thirds of the remaining table of contents inside Chapter 2 — which is itself the mistake this review process exists to prevent.

### Direct answers

**1. Would five independent senior engineers build functionally identical systems from this document?** For the Room Runtime's shape, its composition order, its chain-of-authority wiring, and its lifecycle — yes, with the fixes in this revision closing the two places (event-vs-read semantics, adapter-binding ownership) where they previously could have diverged. For crash/restart recovery mechanics specifically, no — because that work is honestly not yet designed anywhere in this document; it's correctly scoped to Chapters 5/19, not yet written, and five engineers would correctly stop and ask there, not because Chapter 2 is ambiguous but because that content doesn't exist yet.
