## Chapter 6 — Component Responsibilities

### 6.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–5

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–5. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§1.5's six-row component table** (Client, Orchestration Server, Deepgram, Gemini Flash, Gradium, Database) — this chapter expands each row's one-line treatment into a full boundary, never changes what any row already said.
- **Everything Chapters 2–5 already specified about the Orchestration Server** — this chapter cross-references it (§6.3) rather than restating it.
- **Chapter 3's pipeline mechanics for the three AI vendors** (streaming model, backpressure, failure handling) — this chapter states each vendor's *contract boundary*; it does not touch how the pipeline calls them.
- **Chapter 2 §2.8's four-boundary adapter-only access rule** — this chapter's per-component boundaries are stated consistently with it, not as a redesign.
- **Chapter 3 §3.7's UI/audio-desync risk**, explicitly left unresolved and pointed at this chapter and Chapter 13 — this chapter resolves *whose* responsibility it is; Chapter 13 still owns the event mechanics that responsibility depends on.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 6.1 Purpose

Give five of §1.5's six components — everything except the Orchestration Server, whose responsibilities Chapters 2–5 already exhaustively specify — a complete responsibility boundary: what each does, what it explicitly does not do, and where its contract ends. Resolve, along the way, the one real open question Chapter 3 left for this chapter: whose job it is to keep the Client's visual state in step with what the student is actually hearing.

### 6.2 Design Rationale

Two forces: (1) §1.5's one-line "Explicitly NOT its responsibility" column was enough to establish the *shape* of each boundary but not enough to build against — five components still only have a sentence each; (2) re-describing the Orchestration Server here, after four chapters already went deep on it, would create two descriptions of the same thing that could silently drift apart from each other — the discipline this whole document has held is to say something once, in the chapter that owns it, and point everywhere else.

### 6.3 The Orchestration Server's Responsibility Is Already Fully Specified

This section exists to state a scope boundary explicitly, not to add content. The Orchestration Server's responsibilities — composition (Ch.2), pipeline mechanics (Ch.3), state and ownership (Ch.4), and the room's life around the exam (Ch.5) — are already complete, frozen, and internally cross-referenced. Restating any of it here would not add precision; it would create a second copy of the same facts with no mechanism keeping the two in sync as later chapters extend either one. This chapter's actual content is the five components that have never received this treatment.

### 6.4 Client — Full Responsibility Boundary

§1.5 already fixed the shape: capture/stream mic audio, play back synthesized audio, render exam state and presentation driven by the Orchestrator's signals — and, explicitly, no business decision of any kind. This section adds the detail that shape didn't yet carry:

- **The Client never decides *whether* something happens** — every state, ownership, and event signal it renders originates from the Orchestrator (§1.5, §4.11); the Client's only judgment calls are about *how* to present an already-decided fact, never about the fact itself.
- **The Client owns reconnection attempts on its own side of a transient disconnect** — initiating a new WebSocket connection is a Client responsibility; what the *server* does once reconnected (§1.8's open Chapter 19 question) is not.
- **The Client is responsible for keeping its own visual state in step with what the student is actually hearing — resolving §3.7's UI/audio-desync risk.**

> **The Client defers its own visual state-transition rendering until its local audio-playback-complete signal fires — never the instant the server-emitted state event arrives.** The server emits state-transition events immediately and unconditionally, exactly as it already does for every other event in this document (§1.7) — this section does not ask the server to change that, or to predict when a given client's audio will finish playing over a real, jittery network. Instead, the Client — which already reliably knows the moment its own audio stream stops, via the ordinary playback-ended signal any audio-rendering client has — is the one responsible for waiting on that local signal before updating what it shows. This single rule covers both of §3.7's transition classes without the Client ever needing to know which one occurred: an **ordinary** transition's audio plays to its natural end before the local signal fires, so the UI updates right as the old content finishes; an **emergency** transition's audio is truncated server-side (§3.7), so the client's stream stops almost immediately and the local signal fires almost immediately too — the UI catches up just as fast as the abrupt truncation the emergency case already calls for, with no separate code path required. This chapter fixes that this is the Client's responsibility and this is the rule; the exact signal/event shape the Client listens for is Chapter 13's to fully design.

### 6.5 Deepgram / Gemini Flash / Gradium — Contract-Level Responsibility Boundaries

§1.5 already gave each vendor a one-line contract; this section confirms and tightens each at the responsibility level, deliberately not re-describing Chapter 3's pipeline mechanics:

- **Deepgram's contract is audio in, transcripts out — nothing else.** It does not decide utterance completeness (§1.10) and it does not decide response-worthiness; both are Decision Engine judgments made *from* its output, never delegated to it. Its failure modes (connection drop, degraded throughput) are Chapter 3's to handle; its contract boundary is simply that it is never asked to do more than transcribe.
- **Gemini Flash's contract is a context payload in, one complete text response out — nothing else.** It holds no memory between calls (§1.10) and is never asked to decide anything on §1.2's list; if its output ever *resembles* a decision (an instruction, a state reference, a claim about what should happen next), that output has exceeded its contract and the Safety/Validation Layer's job (§1.13) is to catch it, exactly as already specified — this chapter does not add a new check, only confirms the contract that check is measured against.
- **Gradium's contract is approved text plus behavior cues in, audio out — nothing else.** It does not decide pacing, emphasis, or which voice to use beyond executing instructions already given to it (§1.5); any apparent "creative" variation in delivery that wasn't explicitly cued is outside its contract, not a feature of it.

None of the three vendors' contracts include awareness of exam state, ownership, or any other participant — each is invoked with exactly the payload its contract requires and returns exactly what its contract promises, never more.

### 6.6 Database — Role Boundary

The Database is a **passive persistence layer** — §1.5's "not queried live by AI vendors" stands unchanged, and this chapter adds: it is not queried live by the Client either, and it is never the authoritative copy read during Run (§4.4 already fixed that the in-memory State Machine instance is). It is reached exclusively through the Room Runtime's persistence adapter (§2.8) — no component holds a direct database connection outside that boundary. This chapter does not redescribe what gets persisted or when (Ch.4, Ch.5 already did that in full); it fixes only the Database's passive, adapter-mediated role relative to every other component.

### 6.7 The Full Component Responsibility Table

| Component | Responsibility | Explicitly NOT its responsibility | Boundary contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Client** | Capture/stream mic audio; play back synthesized audio; render exam state, transcript, and presentation from Orchestrator signals; own its own reconnection attempts; defer visual state updates to its local audio-playback-complete signal (§6.4) | Any business decision; predicting server-side state ahead of what it's actually rendering audio for | Reached only via the transport adapter (§2.8) |
| **Orchestration Server** | Everything Chapters 2–5 already specify in full | Does not generate text itself | See §6.3 — fully specified elsewhere, not restated here |
| **Deepgram (STT)** | Convert audio to text, streaming, interim and final | Deciding completeness or response-worthiness | Reached only via the STT adapter (§2.8, §2.7's binding exclusivity) |
| **Gemini Flash (LLM)** | Given a context payload, return one complete examiner utterance as text | Any decision on §1.2's list; holding memory between calls | Reached only via the LLM adapter, exclusively by the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer pathway (§2.7) |
| **Gradium (TTS)** | Convert approved text + cues to audio | Deciding pacing/emphasis/voice beyond given instructions | Reached only via the TTS adapter, same exclusivity as above (§2.7) |
| **Database** | Persistent, passive source of truth for durable data | Not queried live by AI vendors or the Client; never the in-Run authoritative copy | Reached only via the persistence adapter (§2.8) |

### 6.8 Advantages

Five components that previously had only a sentence each now have a complete, buildable boundary. The Client's UI/audio-desync resolution closes a real risk Chapter 3 correctly declined to solve outside its own scope, using a signal (local playback-complete) the Client already has rather than asking the server to predict something it structurally cannot know precisely. Explicitly declining to re-describe the Orchestration Server keeps this document's single-source-of-truth discipline intact rather than creating a second description that could drift.

### 6.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Have the server delay state-event emission until it estimates client-side playback will have finished.** Rejected: the server cannot know a given client's actual playback timing under real network jitter and buffering variance; this would trade a well-understood problem (client-local playback timing) for an unsolvable one (server-side prediction of client-side timing).

**(b) Give the Client two different code paths for ordinary vs. emergency transitions.** Rejected: unnecessary — waiting on the local playback-complete signal produces the correct behavior for both cases without the Client ever needing to know which class occurred, per §6.4's reasoning.

**(c) Fully re-describe the Orchestration Server's responsibilities in this chapter for completeness.** Rejected: pure duplication of Chapters 2–5, with no mechanism to keep two descriptions in sync as those chapters are extended later.

**(d) The responsibility boundaries in §6.4–6.7, with the Client-side local-signal resolution for the UI/audio-desync risk (recommended).** The only option that closes Chapter 3's open question without asking the server to solve an unsolvable prediction problem.

### 6.10 Recommended Approach

Option (d): five components fully specified (§6.4–6.6), the Orchestration Server cross-referenced rather than duplicated (§6.3), and the Client resolved as the owner of UI/audio synchronization via its own local playback-complete signal, with the exact event shape that depends on left to Chapter 13.

### 6.11 Possible Risks

**The Client-side local-signal resolution assumes every client implementation reliably exposes a playback-complete signal.** This is true of standard audio-rendering APIs, but if a future client platform's audio stack doesn't expose one cleanly, this chapter's resolution would need a fallback — named here as a dependency on Chapter 13's eventual event design, not assumed away.

**Vendor contract boundaries (§6.5) describe intent, not enforcement.** Nothing in this chapter *prevents* Gemini Flash from returning decision-shaped text — that enforcement is the Safety/Validation Layer's job (§1.13), already specified. This chapter's contribution is naming the boundary that enforcement is measured against, not a second enforcement mechanism; conflating the two would be a real risk for a future chapter to avoid.

### 6.12 Future Improvements

The Client-side local-signal pattern (§6.4) generalizes cleanly to any future client platform this architecture supports (§2.8's transport-adapter extensibility) — any platform with a reliable local playback-complete signal gets correct UI/audio synchronization for free, without this chapter's rule changing. The vendor contract boundaries (§6.5) are what make the provider-adapter layer's future vendor swaps (Ch.22) verifiable against a fixed, named contract rather than an implicit one.

### 6.13 Forward-Reference Index — Pre-Validation Self-Review

Attacked genuinely before any formal pass, same discipline as Chapters 3–5. One finding escalated beyond this chapter's own scope; everything else held.

| Finding | Resolution |
|---|---|
| **The most significant finding of this chapter's entire development: stress-testing §6.4's assumption that "at most one turn's audio delivery is ever in-flight" always holds surfaced a genuine contradiction between Chapter 1 §1.8 and Chapter 4 §4.10** — `confirmAdvance` originally fired once delivery *began*, meaning ownership (and state) could advance to a new stage's contract while the previous turn's audio was still streaming, contradicting §1.8's invariant that ownership stays with the Examiner for a turn's whole in-flight duration. Concretely: the Greeting → Teil 1 Präsentation handoff could flip ownership to the student before the greeting finished playing. | Escalated to the user rather than resolved inside this chapter, since it required amending frozen Chapters 3 and 4. **Constitutional Amendment #1** applied and re-validated (see the amendment note at the top of the document and each affected chapter's own closing amendment entry) — Chapters 3 and 4 corrected so `confirmAdvance` fires only once a turn's audio *fully finishes delivering*, matching Chapter 1 §1.8 exactly. Chapters 1 and 2 were not touched. |

## Chapter 7 — Prompt Architecture

### 7.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–6

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–6. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **The Prompt Builder's one-line contract** (§1.5) — this chapter is that design.
- **Context (§1.10) plus a state-derived task instruction, assembled into one request per turn** (§1.11) — this chapter fixes exactly how, never changes what's assembled.
- **Dynamic, context-derived generation; multiple specialized Prompt Libraries** (§1.11) — unchanged; this chapter mechanizes the selection process those libraries require.
- **Anti-repetition drawn from the Prompt Libraries** (§1.13) — this chapter gives that a concrete, and — per this revision's added requirement — deterministic mechanism.
- **The Prompt Builder as one of the five wiring-enforced gates, the only assembler of what the LLM receives** (§2.7) — unchanged; this chapter designs what happens inside that gate.
- **The LLM as a single-shot, non-streamed call per turn** (§3.4) — this chapter produces the request Stage 2 consumes; it does not redesign Stage 2 itself.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 7.1 Purpose

Give the Prompt Builder an actual design: the concrete request structure it assembles, the mechanism mapping the current exam stage to a Prompt Library category, what a task instruction structurally is, and — the chapter's central new contribution — a fully deterministic mechanism for selecting a variation within a Prompt Library, satisfying anti-repetition without ever relying on randomness.

### 7.2 Design Rationale

Four forces: (1) §1.11 already committed to Prompt Libraries holding "many natural variations" without ever specifying how one gets chosen — an unmechanized requirement is exactly the kind of orphaned capability this document's discipline forbids; (2) §2.7 already fixed the Prompt Builder as one of five wiring-enforced gates, which only means something if what happens *inside* the gate is itself fully specified; (3) **this revision's governing constraint: the Prompt Builder must be deterministic.** Given the same state, the same context payload, the same Prompt Library version, and the same configuration, it must always assemble the exact same prompt. This is a hard requirement on everything in this chapter, not a preference — the variation-selection mechanism (§7.7) is designed around it from first principles, not retrofitted onto a random-selection design; (4) three later chapters (8, 9, Behavior Specification) each plausibly overlap this one's territory, and the boundary between them needs to be drawn explicitly now rather than discovered as a conflict later (§7.9).

> **Why determinism, and why it doesn't conflict with anything already frozen.** §1.11's "dynamic, context-derived generation" describes Gemini Flash's own output variety — an inherent property of the LLM call itself (Ch.3, Stage 2), governed by the vendor, not something this architecture controls or needs to replicate at the Prompt Builder layer. Nothing in Chapters 1–6 requires the Prompt Builder's *own* selection logic to be random; §1.13's "variation" requirement is about what a real listener experiences, and a well-designed deterministic mechanism (§7.7) produces exactly that — different rooms and different turns naturally select different variations — without sacrificing reproducibility. A deterministic Prompt Builder is testable, debuggable, and replayable in a way a randomized one structurally cannot be; that engineering value, combined with the absence of any existing requirement for randomness, is why this chapter treats determinism as the default and unrandomized selection as the only option it designs.

### 7.3 The Prompt Builder as a Realized Module

The Prompt Builder is instantiated in §2.4's dependency order (item 4 — after the State Machine, Event Bus, Decision Engine, and the Timing/Silence/Fairness Engines exist, since it reads all of their output). Its inputs, at the module-boundary level: the current state+ownership snapshot (§4.11's atomic read), the Decision Engine's determination that a turn is warranted, the active Fairness/Silence/topic-drift signals, the room's Personality & Variation Config (§1.5), and its own session memory (§1.10 content, Chapter 14's Session Object). Its output: one complete, structured request, handed to Stage 2 (Gemini Flash, §3.3) and to nothing else — per §2.7's binding exclusivity, no other module holds this same generation-pathway output path.

### 7.4 The Request Structure

A request assembled by the Prompt Builder has exactly two parts, matching §1.11's original commitment precisely:

1. **The context payload** — the ten mandatory fields §1.10 fixed and §8.4 schematizes as exactly ten (identity/addressee; state and ownership together; the turn's objective; topics; prior questions; remaining time; speaking history; silence/confusion/topic-drift status; active persona; and the student-progress signal — the last already counted among the ten, not an eleventh). This chapter treats the payload as a fixed input it consumes; its full field-level schema is Chapter 8's job, not redesigned here.
2. **The task instruction** — a compact, state-derived directive (§7.6) selected via the deterministic mechanism this chapter defines (§7.5, §7.7).

These two parts are assembled into **one** request and sent to Gemini Flash **once** per turn, which returns **one** complete text response — this chapter does not touch that contract, already fixed by §1.2 and realized in pipeline terms by §3.4; it only fixes what goes into the request before that call is made.

### 7.5 Stage-to-Library Mapping

Two different kinds of mapping exist, and conflating them was an early draft's mistake this section corrects: **structural** categories, tied to exactly one specific stage's default turn, and **cross-cutting** categories, available from any in-scope stage whenever the Decision Engine's own trigger conditions fire, independent of that stage's structural default.

**Structural mapping** — each stage's own default turn, per §4.7's contracts:

| Stage (§4.7) | Prompt Library category |
|---|---|
| 2 — Greeting | Greeting |
| 3, 6, 9 — Präsentation / Discussion | *(no Examiner-initiated turn by default — observation only, per §4.7's contract)* |
| 4, 7, 10 — Follow-up Questions | Follow-up |
| 5, 8 — Transition | Transition |
| 11 — Exam Closing | Closing |

**Cross-cutting mapping** — available from **any** in-scope stage (2 through 11), whenever a Decision Engine trigger fires, regardless of that stage's structural default above:

| Category | Fires on |
|---|---|
| Encouragement | §1.12's named intervention triggers — dominance, topic deviation, time management, needed clarification, discussion recovery — none of which are limited to the discussion stages specifically |
| Silence-recovery | §1.8's ownership-reclaim triggers (silence, hesitation, technical delay, etc.) — scoped exactly as broadly as §1.8 itself already scopes ownership: Greeting through Exam Closing, not a narrower subset |

This table fixes *which category* a stage draws from — never which specific variation, and never the variation's wording. A stage with no structural default (3, 6, 9) is not a gap: per §4.7, the Examiner observes by default there, and only reaches for a library — structural or cross-cutting — when a trigger condition fires, at which point the tables above still apply exactly as they do for every other stage.

### 7.6 The Task Instruction

Structurally, a task instruction is a single, compact directive layered on top of the context payload — never a second copy of context, never a restatement of state. It incorporates: the *content* of the specific variation selected within the mapped Prompt Library category (§7.5, §7.7) — the actual Behavior-Specification-authored text/instruction that variation holds — plus any Decision-Engine-supplied parameters it needs filled in (e.g., which follow-up thread to continue). **It never includes the variation's own identity as visible instruction text** — no "category=Greeting, variant=7" label is ever sent to the model; the model receives the chosen content, never a meta-reference to the fact that a choice was made or which one it was. This is the same structural discipline §7.8 fixes for context-payload signals, applied here to the selection mechanism's own bookkeeping. The task instruction is *derived from* state (§1.11) — it is never itself a source of state, and nothing about assembling it writes back to the State Machine, Decision Engine, or any other module; the Prompt Builder remains a pure assembler, never a decision-maker, consistent with §1.2 throughout.

### 7.7 Variation Selection Within a Prompt Library — Deterministic by Design

This is the mechanism §1.13 named ("anti-repetition... drawn from the Prompt Libraries") but never specified. It is designed from the determinism requirement (§7.2) outward, not adapted from a random one:

> **Selection is a pure function of stable inputs — never a random draw.** Given the room's identifier, the current transition sequence number (§4.8), the selected Prompt Library category (§7.5), and the current stage id, a deterministic hash produces a candidate index into that category's ordered list of variations (the list's content and order are Behavior Specification's, but the list itself is part of "Prompt Library version," §7.2's determinism inputs). This is the same candidate every time, for the same inputs — no call to a random-number source anywhere in this mechanism.

**Why these four inputs, and not the whole context payload.** All four are either directly part of the context payload's mandatory state/ownership field (§4.11's atomic read already carries stage id and, via the transition sequence number, a stable position within the room) or trivially derived from it (the room identifier is implicit in any per-room payload; the category is a structural function of stage id, §7.5) — so "the same context payload" already implies "the same four hash inputs," keeping this mechanism consistent with, not an addition to, the determinism requirement's own terms (§7.2). These four are deliberately *not* the full context payload: several of its other fields (remaining time, recent speaking history) are expected to differ, sometimes at fine granularity, between two calls that are otherwise "the same turn" in every way that matters to selection. Hashing the full payload would make the same logical turn select differently on nearly every real invocation, defeating the purpose — the four chosen inputs are exactly the subset that changes only at the granularity an actual, distinct turn does.

**Anti-repetition, without breaking determinism.** Session memory (§1.10) already tracks the Examiner's own previous interventions for this room — this chapter reuses that existing record rather than inventing a second one. Before a candidate is accepted, it is checked against a recently-used set drawn from that session memory (e.g., variations used in this category within the last *N* turns, *N* a Configuration System parameter, Chapter 16). If the candidate is excluded, selection deterministically advances — walking the ordered list from the hashed index, wrapping at most once around the full list (a bounded walk of at most one pass through every variation in the category, never an unbounded search), never re-rolling anything — until a non-excluded variation is found. If every variation in the category is currently excluded after that full pass (a small library, a long session), the mechanism deterministically falls back to the least-recently-used one, computed from the same session-memory record; **if more than one variation ties for least-recently-used (including the common case of a fresh session where several have never been used at all), the tie is broken by the same hashed index used above — the tied candidate closest to it in list order, wrapping the same way, wins.** No step in this fallback is a random pick, and no step leaves a tie unresolved. The selected variation is then recorded into session memory's tracking, which is what makes the *next* selection's exclusion set correct.

**This runs entirely inside the Prompt Builder, before Gemini Flash is ever called — it does not conflict with §6.5's "Gemini Flash holds no memory between calls."** The vendor still receives one stateless context-plus-instruction payload per turn, exactly as §6.5 fixes; the history this mechanism reads and updates is the Prompt Builder's own bookkeeping in session memory, not anything the model is aware of or asked to track itself.

**Retries and regeneration behave correctly under this mechanism by construction, not by special-casing.** A bounded retry of a failed call (§1.8, §3.8's `LLM_FAILURE`/`TTS_FAILURE` paths) re-invokes with the same room, sequence number, category, and stage — so it deterministically reselects the *same* variation, which is correct: a network timeout is not a reason to change which greeting the Examiner is partway through delivering. A turn regenerated after a stale-turn-gate discard (§3.6) is, by definition, tagged against a *new* current state — a different stage id, and often a different sequence number — so it naturally selects independently, with no special-case code needed to distinguish "retry" from "regeneration" at the selection layer.

**Why this satisfies real-world variety despite being fully deterministic.** Two rooms with different room identifiers, or the same room at two different transition sequence numbers, hash to different candidates — variation is a natural, structural consequence of the inputs already being different in practice, not something a random draw needs to manufacture. Replaying the exact same room at the exact same point, with the exact same session history, is the only condition under which the same selection recurs — which is precisely the reproducibility this chapter's determinism requirement asks for, not a defect of it.

**If controlled randomness is ever wanted**, that is explicitly out of this chapter's scope to introduce: per this revision's governing constraint (§7.2), it would require a future chapter to add it as a deliberate, documented deviation — never a default this chapter assumes.

### 7.8 The Metadata-Leakage-Prevention Structure

§1.13 already asserted that "the Prompt Builder frames instructions so the model has no natural reason to describe its own inputs" — this section gives that a concrete structural form: **every internal-only signal in the context payload (student-progress, silence/confusion status, fairness data) is carried as a clearly-demarcated data field, addressed only by the task instruction's logic (§7.6) — never interpolated into instruction text phrased as prose the model might plausibly echo back.** A task instruction that says "the student's confidence signal is low; ask a simplifying follow-up" is structurally wrong under this rule, because "confidence signal is low" is phrased as sayable content; a task instruction that says "use simplification-tier-2 phrasing for the next follow-up" — where "simplification-tier-2" is a category selected *because of* the internal signal, never a restatement of the signal itself — satisfies it. This is the structural half of the leakage prevention §1.13 already promised; the Safety/Validation Layer's inspection (§1.13, §2.7) remains the enforcement backstop, unchanged, in case this structural discipline is ever violated in a future implementation.

### 7.9 Explicit Scope Boundaries

Stated once, directly, so no later chapter has to re-derive it:

- **Chapter 7 (this chapter)** owns the Prompt Builder's assembly mechanics — request structure, stage-to-library mapping, task instruction shape, and deterministic variation selection.
- **Chapter 8 (Context Architecture)** owns the context payload's full field-level schema — this chapter treats that payload as a fixed input, never redesigns its shape.
- **Chapter 9 (Memory Architecture) and Chapter 14 (Session Object)** own the memory model and the concrete structure holding it — this chapter reuses the existing "previous interventions" record (§7.7) without redesigning how or where it's stored.
- **Behavior Specification** owns every Prompt Library's actual content — the variations' wording, tone, and phrasing — this chapter designs only how one gets *selected*, never what it *says*.

### 7.10 Advantages

Anti-repetition now has a real, testable mechanism instead of an unmechanized requirement. Determinism makes the Prompt Builder replayable and debuggable — a specific prompt assembled for a specific room at a specific turn can be reproduced exactly from the same recorded inputs, valuable for both debugging and any future audit/compliance need. The explicit four-way scope boundary (§7.9) closes a real ambiguity between this chapter and three others before any of them are written, rather than after a conflict is discovered.

### 7.11 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Random variation selection (e.g., a random-number draw per turn).** Rejected outright by this revision's governing constraint: the Prompt Builder must be deterministic, and a random draw is definitionally not reproducible from the same inputs.

**(b) One canonical template per Prompt Library category, no variation at all.** Rejected: directly contradicts §1.11's "many natural variations" requirement and would make every Examiner sound mechanically identical across rooms.

**(c) Track repetition globally across all rooms, not per-room session memory.** Rejected: session memory is explicitly destroyed at exam end (§1.10) and never shared across exams; a cross-room tracking mechanism would either violate that isolation or require inventing a new, unauthorized persistent store — out of this chapter's scope and unnecessary, since per-room variety is what actually matters to a student who only ever experiences one room.

**(d) Deterministic, hash-based selection keyed to stable per-room/per-turn inputs, with exclusion drawn from existing session memory (recommended).** The only option that satisfies both §1.11's variety requirement and this revision's determinism requirement simultaneously.

### 7.12 Recommended Approach

Option (d): the two-part request structure (§7.4), the structural stage-to-library mapping (§7.5), a task instruction that only ever derives from state and never writes to it (§7.6), and deterministic, session-memory-aware variation selection (§7.7) as the concrete mechanism behind anti-repetition — with metadata-leakage prevention enforced structurally (§7.8) and the four-way scope boundary (§7.9) stated explicitly rather than left implicit.

### 7.13 Possible Risks

**A small Prompt Library, combined with a long session, could exhaust the non-excluded variation set often**, falling back to least-recently-used more frequently than truly ideal variety would prefer. This is a content/sizing concern for the Behavior Specification (how many variations each library actually holds), not a mechanism defect — named here so it isn't mistaken for one.

**Determinism is only as strong as the inputs it's keyed to.** If a future chapter changes what counts as "the same context payload" (e.g., a field that should be state-derived but drifts into being wall-clock-derived), the reproducibility this chapter promises would quietly break without this chapter's own text changing. Named as a standing constraint future chapters touching the context payload (Ch.8 especially) must respect.

**The hash function's exact choice is unspecified here.** Any pure, well-distributed hash satisfies this chapter's requirements; the exact algorithm is an implementation detail this document doesn't need to fix, but it is named so a future engineer doesn't mistake "unspecified" for "unimportant" — a poorly-distributed hash could cluster selections in ways that look like reduced variety even though the mechanism is technically correct.

### 7.14 Future Improvements

If controlled randomness is ever deliberately wanted (§7.7's closing note), the deterministic hash-based mechanism here is what a future chapter would replace one specific step of — not redesign from scratch — since the exclusion/tracking logic around it is independent of whether the candidate-selection step is a hash or a seeded random draw. The stage-to-library mapping (§7.5) is a plain data table, making a future new exam format's mapping a configuration change, not an engine change, consistent with Chapter 4's generic Stage Specification engine.

### Direct answers

## Chapter 8 — Context Architecture

### 8.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–7

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–7. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **The ten mandatory context fields** (§1.10) — this chapter is their full schema; it adds no eleventh field and removes none of the ten.
- **The context payload as a fixed input the Prompt Builder consumes, never redesigns** (§7.4, §7.9) — this chapter supplies exactly that payload.
- **State and ownership read via §4.11's atomic four-field snapshot** — this chapter reuses that read interface directly for field 2, never opening a second read path to the State Machine.
- **§7.7's determinism mechanism and §7.13's standing request** that this chapter classify field volatility explicitly — this chapter's central contribution.
- **The existing, unchanged Preparation-phase data** (§1.0, §5.4) — topic selection and participant identity are read from what Preparation already produces, never redesigned here.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 8.1 Purpose

Give the context payload a complete, field-by-field schema: what each of the ten mandatory fields actually contains, which module sources it, and — closing the standing request Chapter 7 left open — an explicit classification of whether each field is stable within a single turn or continuously changing, since Chapter 7's entire determinism guarantee depends on that distinction being drawn correctly and completely, not just for the two fields Chapter 7 happened to need.

### 8.2 Design Rationale

Three forces: (1) §1.10 named ten fields at a one-line-each level — sufficient to establish that they exist, not sufficient to build against; (2) Chapter 7 explicitly delegated volatility classification here rather than solving it locally, and an unmechanized delegation is exactly the kind of orphaned requirement this document's discipline forbids; (3) per this revision's standing engineering rule, every field's source is checked against the actual, already-deployed schema (`muendlich_participants`, `muendlich_selections`) rather than assumed — grounding this chapter in what genuinely exists, the same discipline already applied to Chapter 4's persistence model.

### 8.3 The Context Payload as a Realized Structure

The context payload is one structure with exactly ten named fields, assembled fresh for every turn by the Prompt Builder (§7.3) from live reads against its sources — never itself persisted as a standalone record, never cached across turns. Each field below is specified as: **shape** (its concrete form), **source** (the module or existing system that supplies it), and **volatility** (stable for the whole exam, stable for the current turn only, or continuously changing).

### 8.4 Per-Field Specification

**1. Person identity and current addressee.**
Shape: `{ personA: { userId, slot: 'A' }, personB: { userId, slot: 'B' }, currentlyAddressed: 'A' | 'B' | 'both' | 'none' }`. Source: the existing `muendlich_participants` table (`slot` already distinguishes Person A/B, fixed by `UNIQUE(room_id, slot)`; `user_id` is the identity) — this chapter reads that existing structure, it does not invent a new identity model. `currentlyAddressed` is distinct from ownership (field 2): during an Examiner-owned turn, ownership can belong to the Examiner while the utterance itself addresses one specific student — addressee is *who the words are for*, ownership is *who is responsible for what happens next* (§1.8's distinction, carried through here). **This field is a composite with two different volatilities, not one:** the `personA`/`personB` identity sub-fields are **stable for the whole exam** — `slot` is assigned once per participant per room and never reassigned; only `currentlyAddressed` is **stable for the current turn** — set once when a turn is gated, unchanged for that turn's generation and delivery, but free to differ from one turn to the next.

**2. Current state and ownership.**
Shape: exactly §4.11's atomic snapshot, `{ stageId, transitionSequenceNumber, owner, ownershipGrantId }` — reused verbatim, not re-derived. Source: the State Machine, via its existing read interface. Volatility: **stable for the current turn** — this is precisely the property Chapter 7's determinism mechanism already depends on (§7.7), confirmed here as this field's defining characteristic rather than an incidental one.

**3. Current turn's objective.**
Shape: a short, structured directive (e.g., "elicit an opinion on the selected Teil 2 topic," "verify comprehension of the student's prior claim") — distinct from and upstream of Chapter 7's *task instruction* (§7.6): the objective is what the Decision Engine determines this turn should accomplish; the task instruction is what the Prompt Builder assembles *from* the objective plus a selected Prompt Library variation. Source: the Decision Engine, computed once per gated turn (Chapter 10's exact logic, not redesigned here). Volatility: **stable for the current turn** — and, per field 6's finding below, frozen for the duration of any retry of that turn, never recomputed against a fresher read of whatever triggered it.

**4. Selected topics for this room.**
Shape: **not a single flat value** — grounded directly in the existing `muendlich_selections` schema, which is per-*Teil* and sometimes per-participant: for Teil 1, `{ teil: 1, personA: <topic>, personB: <topic> }` (each participant presents on their own selected topic, `slot` populated per row); for Teil 2 and Teil 3, `{ teil: 2 | 3, shared: <topic> }` (`slot` is `NULL` in the existing schema — one shared topic, uniqueness enforced by the existing partial index `muendlich_sel_shared_uidx` specifically because a plain `UNIQUE(room_id, teil, slot)` does not constrain `NULL` slots under standard SQL semantics — a real gap the existing system already found and fixed, confirmed by checking the actual migration rather than assumed). The context payload carries whichever shape applies to the current stage's Teil, read from the existing, unchanged selection records. Source: `muendlich_selections`, populated during Preparation (§5.4), unchanged. Volatility: **stable for the whole exam** — topics are locked (`locked = true` in the existing schema) before the Examination phase begins and never change within a room's lifetime.

**5. Relevant prior questions already asked.**
Shape: an ordered, filtered subset of session memory's conversation record — only the entries that are actual examiner questions, not the full transcript (field 7 carries the fuller history). **Fields 5 and 7 are two different filtered views over the same underlying session-memory conversation log, never two independently-maintained records** — this is stated explicitly so a future implementation doesn't build two trackers that could silently diverge from each other. Source: session memory (§1.10, Chapter 14's Session Object). Volatility: **stable for the current turn** — a snapshot at generation time; changes turn to turn as new questions are asked, but fixed for the duration of any one turn's generation.

**6. Remaining time in the current section.**
Shape: a duration (seconds remaining), computed from the existing `exam_stage_started_at` + `exam_stage_seconds` pattern (§4.4) against the current wall-clock time. Source: the Timing Engine. Volatility: **continuously changing — the one field in this payload that is not stable even within a single turn's generation window.** This is exactly the field Chapter 7 §7.13 flagged as a risk if ever mistakenly treated as a determinism input: it is **not** one of Chapter 7's four hash inputs (room identifier, transition sequence number, category, stage id), and this section confirms explicitly, closing the loop §7.13 opened, that it must never become one — a future chapter must not fold "remaining time" into any determinism-sensitive computation.

> **A subtler version of the same risk, found by tracing retries against this field rather than assumed away: a volatile field can influence a *supposedly stable* hash input indirectly, through a trigger, unless that influence is explicitly frozen at the right moment.** §1.12's time-management intervention, and §1.9's silence/confusion triggers (field 8, also continuously-evaluated in real time even though its *payload value* is turn-stable), can each cause the *category* (one of Chapter 7's four stable hash inputs) to be Encouragement or Silence-recovery rather than a stage's structural default. If a bounded retry (§1.8, §3.8) re-evaluated those triggers against a fresh, later read of remaining time or silence status, a retry could legitimately land on a *different* category than the original attempt — quietly breaking Chapter 7 §7.7's "a bounded retry... deterministically reselects the same variation" claim, which implicitly assumed category stays fixed across a retry without stating why. **This section fixes why: category and objective (field 3) are determined exactly once, at the moment the Decision Engine gates a turn, and are frozen as part of that turn's identity for every subsequent retry of it — a retry never re-evaluates any trigger against a fresh read of a volatile field.** §1.8's "retry with tightened constraints" governs *how* the already-fixed category and objective are phrased on retry, never *whether* a different one is chosen. This is an extension of what Chapter 7 already asserted, not a contradiction of it — Chapter 7 never said retries re-derive category from scratch, and this is the reason that was always true.

**7. Recent speaking history.**
Shape: a bounded, ordered record of recent turns (speaker, brief content reference) — bounded per a Configuration System parameter (Chapter 16), not unbounded growth. Source: session memory, fed by the Fairness Engine's tracking. Volatility: **stable for the current turn.**

**8. Silence / confusion / topic-drift status.**
Shape: `{ silenceDetected: boolean, confusionDetected: boolean, topicDriftDetected: boolean }` plus optional detail per flag. Source: the Silence Management Engine and Decision Engine's own analysis (§1.9's `STUDENT_CONFUSION_DETECTED`/`TOPIC_DRIFT_DETECTED` events). Volatility: **stable for the current turn** — computed once as part of the same gating decision that determines a turn is warranted (§1.14 step 3).

**9. Active persona configuration.**
Shape: `{ personality parameters, voiceGenderIdentity, language }` per §1.5's Personality & Variation Config. Source: room configuration, set once at room-creation/Birth time (§2.5), never redesigned here. Volatility: **stable for the whole exam** — nothing in Chapters 1–7 permits mid-exam persona changes, and this chapter does not introduce one.

**10. Student-progress signal.**
Shape: an enum/scalar value with the default already fixed by §1.10: `'not_yet_assessed'` until the Decision Engine computes a real signal. Source: the Decision Engine (Chapter 10's exact computation, deferred). Volatility: **stable for the current turn** — always present, per §1.10's existing hard requirement, reaffirmed here rather than re-litigated.

### 8.5 Validation & Defaults

§1.10 already fixed one default (student-progress signal's `'not_yet_assessed'`). This section states the general rule the other nine fields fall under, which no chapter through Chapter 7 fully closed:

> **Every one of the ten fields must be populated before a request is assembled. A field that cannot be populated — not "not yet assessed" (a valid, populated value) but a genuine failure to read it from its source — is treated as equivalent to an `LLM_FAILURE`-class condition (§1.8, §3.8): the Prompt Builder does not assemble or send a malformed or partial request. It reuses the existing bounded-retry-then-neutral-fallback mechanism rather than inventing a second failure path for context-assembly specifically.**

This closes a real gap: prior chapters defined what happens when the *vendor* call fails (§3.8) but never what happens when the *payload feeding that call* can't be built in the first place — this section fixes that the two cases resolve through the same existing mechanism, not two different ones.

### 8.6 Explicit Scope Boundaries

Reaffirmed from this chapter's side, matching §7.9 exactly: **Chapter 8 (this chapter)** owns the context payload's field-level schema, sourcing, and volatility classification. **Chapter 7** owns how that payload is consumed — request assembly, stage-to-library mapping, task instruction, variation selection — and is not redesigned here. **Chapter 9 / Chapter 14** own the memory model and the Session Object that fields 5 and 7 read from — this chapter treats that record as a given source, never redesigning its storage. **Behavior Specification** owns no part of this chapter — there is no prompt wording here to claim.

### 8.7 Advantages

Every context field now has a concrete shape and a named source, most of them grounded directly in schema that already exists and runs in production (`muendlich_participants`, `muendlich_selections`, the `exam_stage_*` pattern) rather than invented fresh. The explicit volatility classification — especially field 6's — closes the exact risk Chapter 7 flagged as a standing concern rather than leaving it as a future chapter's problem to rediscover. The topic field's Teil-dependent shape (§8.4, field 4), grounded in the real schema's per-participant-vs-shared structure, is more accurate than a generic flat-list assumption would have been.

### 8.8 Alternatives Considered

**(a) A single flat "topics" field, uniform across all Teils.** Rejected: contradicts the actual, already-deployed `muendlich_selections` schema, which is explicitly per-Teil and per-participant for Teil 1 — a flat field would either lose real data (Teil 1's two distinct topics) or require silently reshaping existing data to fit an invented shape.

**(b) Treat all ten fields as uniformly volatile, refreshed at generation time with no stability guarantee.** Rejected: this is what Chapter 7's determinism mechanism already implicitly assumed was false for state/ownership; generalizing "volatile" to every field would make Chapter 7's guarantee unverifiable rather than merely undocumented.

**(c) Field-by-field shape, source, and explicit volatility classification, grounded in existing schema where one already exists (recommended).** The only option that closes §7.13's standing request and stays consistent with the real, deployed system rather than an idealized one.

### 8.9 Recommended Approach

Option (c): the ten-field schema in §8.4, each field's shape and source grounded in either an already-frozen chapter's mechanism (fields 2, 3, 8, 10) or the actual deployed database schema (fields 1, 4, 6, 9), with volatility classified explicitly for every field — not just the two Chapter 7 happened to use — and a single, reused failure path for context-assembly errors (§8.5) rather than a new one.

### 8.10 Possible Risks

**Field 5 and field 7's "bounded" history size has no number yet.** Named as a Configuration System dependency (Chapter 16), consistent with how every other unbounded-in-principle parameter in this document has been handled — not resolved here.

**Grounding field shapes in the current `muendlich_participants`/`muendlich_selections` schema creates a real dependency on that schema not changing incompatibly.** If a future, non-architectural change to those tables alters `slot`'s meaning or removes the per-Teil structure of `muendlich_selections`, this chapter's field 1 and field 4 shapes would need revisiting — named explicitly as a standing coupling, not hidden.

**Volatility classification is a documentation discipline, not an enforced one.** Nothing in this chapter *mechanically* prevents a future chapter from introducing a volatile field into a determinism-sensitive computation — §8.4's explicit classification is what makes such a mistake visible on inspection, not impossible by construction. Named honestly rather than overclaimed.

### 8.11 Future Improvements

The Teil-dependent shape of field 4 (§8.4) is what would let a future exam format with a different topic-selection structure (e.g., a shared topic for all three Teils) be expressed as a different populated shape from the same schema pattern, without this chapter's field definition changing. The explicit volatility classification (§8.4) is what a future performance-optimization chapter could use to decide which fields are safe to cache briefly within a turn's generation window and which (field 6) never are.

No further weakness survived a second attack pass. No cross-chapter contradiction was found — the category/objective-freezing fix extends and explains Chapter 7's existing claim rather than conflicting with it, so no amendment was needed and no frozen chapter was touched. Passes 1–3 (Adversarial, Constitutional Compatibility, Implementation) re-traced the category-freezing fix against every trigger type named across Chapters 1, 3, and 7 (silence, confusion, topic-drift, time-management) and confirmed the freeze-at-gating-time rule closes all of them uniformly, not just the remaining-time case that surfaced it. ## Chapter 9 — Memory Architecture

### 9.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–8

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–8. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **Session memory's content list and its destruction rule** (§1.10) — this chapter is the model and the rules; Chapter 14 remains the concrete structure, per §1.10's own forward pointer.
- **Destruction tied to Teardown's second step** (§2.5) — this chapter specifies exactly what "destroyed" operationally means, never a different trigger.
- **Memory is never reconstructed on a resumed birth** (§5.7) — this chapter's destruction/creation model is built to make that statement trivially true, not to work around it.
- **Chapter 7's "previous interventions" record** (§7.7) and **Chapter 8's "two filtered views of one shared log"** (§8.4, fields 5/7) — this chapter gives both a real, single underlying definition.
- **The stale-turn gate and turn-overlap/emergency-truncation rules** (§3.6, §3.7, as amended) — this chapter's write discipline is built specifically to stay correct under them, not to assume they don't apply.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 9.1 Purpose

Give session memory an actual model: named record types covering everything §1.10 already requires, precisely when each gets written, how other modules read it, and the exact operational meaning of "destroyed completely" — verified, throughout, against the real, already-deployed relay's own in-memory room state and teardown code, not designed in the abstract.

### 9.2 Design Rationale

Three forces, the third grounded directly in code rather than asserted: (1) §1.10 named memory's content without a model to build against, and Chapters 7 and 8 have already *used* pieces of that content (the "previous interventions" record, the "shared log" fields 5/7 filter) without either giving it a real definition — an unmechanized dependency two chapters deep is exactly what this document's discipline forbids; (2) memory's *write timing* interacts with Chapter 3's turn-overlap and emergency-truncation rules in a way that isn't obvious until traced through a concrete scenario, and getting it wrong would mean memory recording things that were never actually delivered; (3) checking `muendlich-relay/src/server.ts` directly surfaced two independently valuable facts: the current system already holds a per-room in-memory struct (`RoomSession`) destroyed via `rooms.delete(room.roomId)` at the end of a proven lifecycle, and its `endRoom()` function already carries an explicit re-entry guard (`if (room.ended) return`) with a comment stating plainly that the bug it guards against "\[was\] caught by actually running the full exam lifecycle end to end, not by inspection." That is a real precedent this chapter takes seriously rather than rediscovering the hard way.

### 9.3 The Memory Model

One underlying structure, per room, holding four named record types — not four separately-synchronized stores:

1. **Conversation log** — the full, ordered turn-by-turn record (speaker, content reference, timestamp), **plus, per §9.4's interruption-marker rule, entries that record a delivery interruption occurred at a given point without asserting what was said** — a distinct entry kind from an ordinary speaker turn, never a guessed reconstruction of one. This is the *one* shared log Chapter 8 §8.4 already said fields 5 ("relevant prior questions") and 7 ("recent speaking history") both filter — formalized here as its actual source.
2. **Speaking-balance tracking** — per-participant cumulative speaking time and question count, feeding the Fairness Engine (§1.13) directly.
3. **Prompt-variety tracking** — the record of which Prompt Library variation was used, per category, and when. This is the exact structure Chapter 7 §7.7 already assumed existed under the name "the Examiner's own previous interventions" — this section is that assumption's real definition, not a new one.
4. **Understanding/progress tracking** — whatever the Decision Engine has determined about student comprehension so far, feeding Chapter 8 §8.4's student-progress signal (field 10).

All four are read-accessed by different consumers (§9.5) but written through one discipline (§9.4), never four independent write paths that could drift out of sync with each other.

### 9.4 Write Discipline

> **A record is written to memory only once the event it describes is confirmed to have actually happened from the student's perspective — never at the moment it was merely decided or generated.** For an Examiner turn, this means: memory is updated only once that turn's audio has **fully finished delivering** to the client — the exact same moment Chapter 4 §4.10 (as amended) ties the State Machine's own advance to, for turn-bearing transitions, and the general principle this section extends to *every* Examiner turn, not only the four transition-bearing ones. For a student turn, there is no delivery step to wait for — the utterance already happened in the real world the moment it was spoken — so memory is updated as soon as Deepgram's finalized transcript is available, with no additional delay, **regardless of whether the Decision Engine has yet acted on it.** §3.5's "deferred consumption" during an in-flight Examiner turn governs when the Decision Engine *reacts* to that input, never whether the fact of what was said gets recorded — the conversation log is a truthful record of what happened, not a business-logic-filtered one, and conflating the two would make memory silently incomplete for exactly the interruption scenarios it most needs to capture accurately.

**A bounded retry produces at most one written record per logical turn, never more.** A failed attempt (§1.8, §3.8) never reaches "fully finished delivering" — it errored or timed out first — so it is never written; only an eventually-successful retry, if one occurs, satisfies the write condition, exactly once, when *its* delivery completes. This follows directly from the rule above without needing a separate mechanism for retries.

**A turn's memory write and the next turn's read of the same record can never race, because they can never overlap.** Chapter 3 §3.7 already fixes that at most one turn's audio delivery is in-flight at a time — no second turn can begin generating, and therefore no second turn can need to read prompt-variety tracking for its own selection (§7.7), until the first has already resolved (written, or correctly not written, per the rules above). The exclusion set any turn's variation selection reads is therefore always current relative to every turn that came before it, by construction, not by a timing assumption this chapter has to hope holds.

**A mid-stream failure (§3.8's `TTS_FAILURE`, partial delivery then abort) never writes the undelivered content as if it were a completed utterance — but the fact that an interruption occurred is still recorded.** The partial, uncertain content is correctly excluded by the rule above (a broken stream never "fully finishes delivering"), and inventing a guess at how much the student actually heard — chunks *sent* are not the same as chunks *played*, given client-side buffering — would overclaim a certainty this architecture doesn't have. But recording nothing at all would leave the recovery turn generated after Chapter 3's "technical delay" reclaim (§1.8) with no memory that an interruption happened here, risking a recovery turn that sounds as if nothing occurred. This section fixes the resolution: the conversation log (record type 1, §9.3) gains a distinct **interruption marker** entry at this point — noting *that* a delivery was interrupted, never a reconstruction of *what* was said — giving the next turn's generation the context it needs without fabricating content the system was never actually certain of.

**Why this matters, traced through a concrete failure this rule prevents:** if memory were instead written at Safety-Layer-approval time — mirroring the real relay's current pattern of writing the durable transcript immediately alongside the `broadcast()` call — an emergency transition (§3.7) truncating that same turn's audio mid-delivery would leave memory recording an "intervention" the student never actually heard. The next turn's anti-repetition tracking (§7.7) and speaking-history field (§8.4) would then be built on a fact that isn't true. Tying the write to full-delivery-completion instead of generation-or-approval-time closes this by construction: a truncated turn's delivery never completes, so it is never written.

**This is a new rule, not a restatement of anything already fixed.** No chapter through Chapter 8 specified session-memory write timing; this section fills that gap rather than contradicting a prior answer, so no amendment is needed. It is consistent with, and a direct generalization of, the same principle behind Constitutional Amendment #1 (ownership/state changes only once delivery is truly complete) — applied here to memory instead of state.

**The durable transcript and this chapter's conversation log are companion writes with the same trigger, for the same reason, not two designs that happen to agree.** The real relay's existing pattern writes the durable record immediately per utterance; this chapter's session-memory write for an Examiner turn is deliberately *later* than that pattern (gated on full delivery, not generation) — a real, deliberate divergence from the precedent it's otherwise grounded in, justified by the emergency-truncation risk that precedent's simpler pipeline never had to account for.

### 9.5 Read Discipline

Every consumer reads the *same* one underlying structure (§9.3), applying its own filter — never a separately-maintained, independently-updated copy:

- The **Prompt Builder** reads the conversation log, filtered to examiner-questions-only (Chapter 8 field 5) or recent-turns-generally (field 7).
- The **Prompt Builder's variation-selection mechanism** (§7.7) reads prompt-variety tracking, filtered to the current category, to compute its exclusion set.
- The **Fairness Engine** reads speaking-balance tracking directly.
- The **Decision Engine** reads and writes understanding/progress tracking as part of computing Chapter 8 field 10.

No consumer caches a private copy across turns — per-turn reads are always against the current, live structure, consistent with §1.10's "nothing not explicitly re-supplied" statelessness rule applying to the LLM, not to the server's own internal reads.

### 9.6 Destruction Mechanics

Chapter 2 §2.5 already fixed *when*: Teardown's second step, after the durable record is already safe. This section fixes exactly *what "destroyed" means* and *how it's made safe to invoke*, grounded directly in the real system's own, already-proven pattern:

> **Destruction is releasing every reference to the room's memory structure — the same operational meaning as the real relay's `rooms.delete(room.roomId)`, extended from a single Map entry to the full four-record structure of §9.3.** Nothing is soft-deleted, archived, or marked inactive; there is no separate "purge" step to get wrong, because there is nothing left holding a reference for a purge to act on.

**Precisely: the Room Runtime itself is not the meaningful holder of this reference — the per-room module instances it composed (§9.5's consumers: Prompt Builder, Fairness Engine, Decision Engine) are.** Consistent with §2.3's rule that the Room Runtime holds no business data of its own, memory becomes unreachable as a *consequence* of the Room Runtime releasing those module instances (§2.5's Teardown step 2) — not because the Room Runtime separately "held" and then dropped a memory reference itself. This is a precision fix over an earlier draft of this section, which risked implying the Room Runtime was itself a data holder — a role Chapter 2 already, deliberately, gives it none of.

**Destruction must be idempotent — guarded against re-entry, exactly as the real system's `endRoom()` already is, for exactly the reason its own comment names.** A room's Teardown can plausibly be triggered more than once in practice (e.g., a client-side socket close firing its own handler while the server-side completion path is already running) — without an explicit guard, a second destruction attempt could run against an already-released structure, or worse, race with a first attempt still in progress. This chapter fixes that destruction is guarded the same way: once triggered, a room is marked destroyed immediately, and any subsequent destruction attempt for that room is a no-op — the same shape as `if (room.ended) return`, generalized from the real relay's specific field to this architecture's memory structure. This is not a hypothetical risk named out of caution; it is a bug class the real, already-deployed system found and fixed, cited here as direct evidence the guard is necessary, not merely tidy.

**Consistent with §5.7 by construction, not by cross-checking after the fact:** because destruction means releasing every reference and nothing is reconstructed from it, a resumed birth (§5.6) necessarily starts with a *new* memory structure — there is nothing left from the old one to accidentally reattach to, even if a future implementation wanted to.

### 9.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapter 14

Stated directly: **Chapter 9 (this chapter)** owns the memory model — what is tracked, when it's written, how it's read, and what destruction operationally means. **Chapter 14 (Session Object)** owns the concrete data structure realizing this model — the literal class, record, or table shape holding the four record types of §9.3. Neither chapter designs the other's territory: this chapter never specifies a field's storage type or memory layout, and Chapter 14 will not be free to redefine what gets tracked, when it's written, or when it's destroyed — those are this chapter's, already fixed above.

### 9.8 Advantages

The "previous interventions" record Chapter 7 already depended on, and the "shared log" Chapter 8 already assumed, both now have one real, named definition instead of two chapters' worth of forward-looking assumptions. The write-discipline rule closes a genuine correctness gap — memory recording undelivered content — that would otherwise have surfaced only under the specific combination of an emergency transition and a mid-delivery truncation, exactly the kind of condition unlikely to be caught by anything short of deliberately tracing it. Destruction's idempotency requirement is grounded in a real, already-fixed production bug rather than a hypothetical, making it a stronger, more credible requirement than an invented one would be.

### 9.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Write session memory at generation or Safety-approval time, mirroring the real relay's existing durable-transcript pattern exactly.** Rejected: traced directly to a real failure mode this architecture's own emergency-truncation rule (§3.7) creates that the existing simpler pipeline never had — memory would record undelivered content.

**(b) Four independently-maintained memory stores, one per record type in §9.3.** Rejected: this is exactly what Chapter 8 §8.4 already ruled out for fields 5/7 specifically ("never two independently-maintained records"); generalizing that same risk across four stores instead of two multiplies it rather than avoiding it.

**(c) No explicit destruction idempotency guard — rely on Teardown only ever being triggered once.** Rejected on direct evidence: the real, already-deployed system needed exactly this guard, discovered through full-lifecycle testing rather than code inspection — assuming single-invocation in a new, more complex architecture would be repeating a mistake already made and fixed once.

**(d) One shared memory structure, write-gated on full delivery completion for generated content and immediate for observed content, with an idempotent, reference-dropping destruction (recommended).** The only option consistent with both this document's own prior rules and the real system's own hard-won lessons.

### 9.10 Recommended Approach

Option (d): the four-record model of §9.3, written per §9.4's delivery-gated discipline (generalizing Constitutional Amendment #1's principle beyond state/ownership to memory), read per §9.5's shared-structure-with-filters pattern, and destroyed per §9.6's idempotent, reference-dropping mechanics — grounded throughout in the real relay's own `RoomSession`/`endRoom()` precedent rather than an idealized design.

### 9.11 Possible Risks

**The write-discipline rule (§9.4) adds a small amount of latency between "turn happened" and "memory reflects it," compared to the real system's immediate-write pattern.** For Examiner turns, memory lags real-time by however long that turn's full delivery takes — negligible for anti-repetition/fairness purposes (which operate at turn granularity, not sub-second granularity), but named explicitly rather than assumed free.

**Four record types sharing one write discipline is simpler than four independent ones, but still requires whatever holds this structure (Chapter 14) to support atomic-enough updates that a partial write across the four types can't be observed by a concurrent reader.** Named as a real constraint on Chapter 14's eventual design, not resolved here.

**The idempotent-destruction guard assumes Teardown-triggering events are themselves deduplicated or safely re-triggerable at the level above this chapter (Chapter 2, Chapter 4's idempotency work).** This chapter's guard is a second, independent safety net — appropriate given the real system needed exactly this belt-and-suspenders combination — not a substitute for correctness further up the stack.

### 9.12 Future Improvements

The four-record model (§9.3) is deliberately structured so a future chapter could add a fifth record type (e.g., a richer emotional-tone tracker) without touching the write-gating or destruction mechanics, both of which are defined generically over "the memory structure," not enumerated per record. The delivery-gated write discipline (§9.4) is the same mechanism a future chapter could reuse if any other subsystem ever needs to record "what actually reached the student" rather than "what was decided," without inventing a second version of the same rule.
