| **The soft escalation level's direct Client consumption of a raw Silence Management Engine event was never checked against §2.7's Chain of Authority**, leaving a real question — does a non-Decision-Engine-mediated client notification bypass a frozen gate? — unaddressed | §12.3 — resolved explicitly: the generation gate does not apply to content that never triggers generation, and the client notification and the Ownership Arbiter's own consumption are independent readers of the same signal, not one bypassing the other |
| **§1.8's "wait for a natural stopping point... whenever time allows" note was cited in §12.0's compatibility list but never actually resolved anywhere in the chapter body** — a citation without a resolution, which a careful reader would reasonably flag as incomplete | §12.3 — traced to already-frozen Chapter 10 gating mechanics (both silence- and confusion-triggered reclaims only ever fire against a genuinely finished or absent utterance) and confirmed the property already holds structurally, with no new mechanism needed |
| **The peer-to-peer transfer trigger's "evaluated continuously" claim did not cite the specific Chapter 10 mechanism that makes continuous, any-event-triggered evaluation correct**, nor did it address the two-condition check's concurrency safety explicitly | §12.6 — cited §10.3's decision-cycle-triggering rule directly, and added the serialization argument (§1.9) closing the specific race a careful reviewer would ask about |
| **The dominance-ratio computation had a real, un-caught degenerate case: a single early turn by one participant produces a 100% share, flagging false "dominance" absurdly early** — a genuine correctness gap, not a style nit | §12.4 — added a minimum-sample guard (a second Configuration System parameter) below which the fairness check contributes no live proposal |
| **`CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED` arriving during an Examiner-owned in-flight turn had no stated handling**, risking the appearance that this signal type was exempt from the general deferred-consumption rule every other student-originated signal already follows | §12.7 — added an explicit cross-reference confirming it is the ordinary "student input during an Examiner turn" case §12.5 and §10.8 already cover, with no new mechanism |

A second attack pass, focused specifically on the two mechanisms this chapter introduces with no real-codebase precedent at all (the Fairness Engine and the peer-to-peer transfer trigger), found no further defect: the Fairness Engine's scope-to-relevant-stages argument was re-checked against all four in-scope stages (6, 7, 9, 10) individually, not just stage 6's cited invariant, and held for each; the peer-to-peer trigger's backchannel-noise gap was confirmed as a genuine, honestly-named residual risk rather than something a slightly cleverer heuristic would have quietly closed. No cross-chapter contradiction was found in either pass — every fix either filled a genuine gap no chapter through Chapter 11 had addressed, or corrected this chapter's own internal inconsistency before it was ever shown for review. Proceeding to the formal validation gauntlet.

### 12.15 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

Passes 1–3 (Adversarial, Constitutional Compatibility, Implementation) re-walked all six self-review findings against the exact frozen text they touch — §2.3, §2.7, §2.8 for the Chain-of-Authority confirmation; §1.8, §3.7, §10.4, §10.7 for the natural-stopping-point resolution; §1.9, §10.3 for the peer-to-peer trigger's concurrency argument; §4.7, §10.3, §10.9 for the Fairness Engine's scope and consumption model — and confirmed each fix is additive or corrective, never a redefinition of frozen content. The adversarial pass specifically tried to find a scenario where the Examiner-turn "never barge in" policy (§12.5) produces a worse outcome than an override would, including a simulated urgent-technical-problem case, and found the buffer-then-defer path still recovers correctly on the very next decision cycle — the policy's cost is perceived immediacy only, never lost information, exactly as §12.5 already argues.

Pass 4 (Five-Engineer Validation) traced whether five independent senior engineers, given Chapters 1–11 plus this chapter alone, would converge on one implementation for: the escalation-level shape and its ownership-model consistency (yes — a client-cue level cannot be confused with a reclaim, and the boundary between them is explicit); what the Fairness Engine tracks and from what source (yes — two figures, both derived from already-frozen data, with vendor-agnosticism argued rather than assumed); when the Examiner's own turn can be interrupted (yes — never, with a reasoned "no correctness cost" argument, not an arbitrary rule); how peer-to-peer transfer actually triggers (yes — a concrete two-condition composition of existing signals, closing Chapter 10's own explicitly-left-open question); and how a clarification request is rate-limited and routed (yes — a distinct Tier-3 event, denied explicitly when exhausted, never silently dropped). The one area five engineers would still plausibly diverge on numerically, not structurally: the real escalation-level timings, dominance ratio, minimum-sample size, and clarification cap — all explicitly and correctly deferred to Chapter 16.

Pass 5 (Production-Readiness Validation) walked the full conversation-management lifecycle under load and failure: a fully silent student during Teil 3 (soft client cue at the configured threshold, firm reclaim after the debounce interval, both derived from clock-only computation); a lopsided Teil 2 discussion where one participant answers first (dominance check correctly withholds a proposal until the minimum-sample guard is satisfied, avoiding the false-positive this round's self-review caught); a participant beginning to speak while their partner is still finishing a thought during Teil 2 (peer-to-peer trigger correctly defers the transfer proposal until completeness resolves, per the two-condition check); a clarification request arriving mid-Examiner-turn (deferred per §12.5/§10.8's existing rule, honored on the next cycle); and a third clarification request after the cap is exhausted (explicitly denied, not silently dropped). No scenario produced an unhandled case or a contradiction with a frozen chapter.

**Constitutional compatibility explicitly confirmed:** no frozen chapter required modification this round. Every point of contact with frozen content — Chapter 10's consumption model, Chapter 4's stage contracts, Chapter 1's ownership model, Chapter 2's Chain of Authority — is read from and composed with, never redefined.

## Chapter 13 — Event System

### 13.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–12

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–12. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§1.5's Event Bus charter** ("Routes events between modules with an ordered, per-room stream; delivery semantics... an open question for Ch.13") — this chapter is that design.
- **§1.9's event-driven backbone** — the representative (non-exhaustive) event category list, the ordering/serialization guarantees, the per-event four-property requirement (producer, consumer set, idempotency rule, failure/retry behavior), and "the AI is never a producer of events" — this chapter fully realizes all of it, changes none of it.
- **§2.3's producer-independence and direct-read/event-mediated split** ("Timing Engine, Silence Management Engine, Fairness Engine — each subscribes... independently"; "direct reads of authoritative state permitted; proposals/notifications must be event-mediated") — this chapter states the boundary precisely (§13.5), never redraws it.
- **§2.4's acyclic-instantiation-vs-cyclic-runtime-feedback distinction** — this chapter's ordering mechanism (§13.4) is built to support normal feedback loops, never to eliminate them as if they were a defect.
- **§2.9's no-distributed-broker confirmation** — this chapter's Event Bus is in-process and per-Room-Runtime (§13.4), consistent with, not an exception to, that already-frozen fact.
- **§3.6/§3.7's stale-turn-gate atomicity and the ordinary/emergency interruption policy**, and **§3.8's pipeline-local vendor-failure reactions** — this chapter supplies the full event-lifecycle design those sections already assumed exists, never redesigns the pipeline-local mechanics themselves.
- **§4.8/§4.9/§4.10/§4.11's sequence numbers, ownership-grant identifier, `requestAdvance`/`confirmAdvance`/`proposeOwnershipChange`, and the atomic state+ownership read** — this chapter clarifies exactly how these already-frozen mechanisms relate to event delivery (§13.5), never redesigns any of them.
- **§5.7's `ROOM_RESUMED`-class signal**, named but left to this chapter's full design — absorbed into the catalog (§13.6).
- **§6.4's Client local-signal resolution**, which depends on "the exact event/signal shape... left to Chapter 13" — supplied at §13.6.
- **Chapter 10's already-frozen "a decision cycle initiates on any event in the coordinator's consumer set" rule (§10.3)** and its per-event consumption already fixed for `STUDENT_CONFUSION_DETECTED`/`TOPIC_DRIFT_DETECTED`/`TIME_WARNING`/`TIME_LIMIT_REACHED`/`STT_FAILURE` — this chapter's catalog is what that rule ranges over; nothing here narrows or contradicts it.
- **Chapter 11's `TIME_WARNING`/`TIME_LIMIT_REACHED` payload shapes and Chapter 12's `CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED` payload/consumer relationship** — absorbed into the catalog verbatim, never redefined.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 13.1 Purpose

Resolve the single question named as open since Chapter 1 (delivery semantics) with real reasoning; supply the concrete per-room ordering mechanism §1.9 assumed but never built; state a clean, checkable rule for when data flows as a direct read versus an event; and produce the full producer/consumer/idempotency/retry specification for every event category named across Chapters 1–12, including the two named-but-undesigned signals (`ROOM_RESUMED`, `CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED`) — closing the largest, most-referenced open surface remaining in the document.

### 13.2 Design Rationale

Three forces shape this chapter.

**First, this is the most heavily-deferred-to chapter in the document, and the debt is real, not decorative.** A direct grep of "Chapter 13"/"Ch.13" across Chapters 1–12 surfaces more than thirty distinct forward-pointers — more than any other chapter has accumulated by the time its turn arrived, including Chapter 10 and Chapter 12. Discharging that debt honestly means resolving delivery semantics with real reasoning (§13.3), not restating it as still open, and producing a genuinely complete event catalog (§13.6), not a partial one that quietly defers half its entries again.

**Second, like Chapter 12's Fairness Engine, this chapter has no internal-messaging precedent to formalize.** A direct grep of `muendlich-relay/src/server.ts` and `geminiLive.ts` for any event-bus or pub-sub pattern finds none — the real system wires every callback directly, once, at session-creation time (`MuendlichLiveCallbacks`: `onOpen`, `onAudioChunk`, `onOutputTranscript`, `onInputTranscript`, `onTurnComplete`, `onError`, `onClose`), plus direct `ws.on('message', ...)` handling and direct function calls (`broadcast()`, `send()`) for everything else. The Event Bus this chapter designs is genuinely new architecture, not a formalization of anything already running — stated honestly rather than manufacturing a false precedent the way every other chapter through Chapter 11 was able to.

**Third, every consumer-side mechanism this document has already frozen was built assuming duplicate-safe delivery, which settles this chapter's central question before it is even argued in detail.** The transition sequence number (§4.8), the ownership-grant identifier (§4.9), the stale-turn gate (§3.6), and the per-stage-instance checkpoint-fired set (§11.5) are each, independently, an idempotency mechanism a *consumer* runs — none of them was designed assuming the Event Bus itself guarantees exactly-once delivery. This is strong, converging evidence for what §13.3 argues explicitly: the architecture this document has already built does not need, and was never actually assuming, a stronger delivery guarantee than at-least-once.

### 13.3 Delivery Semantics: At-Least-Once, Idempotency Pushed to Consumers

> **The Event Bus guarantees at-least-once delivery within a room's lifetime — an event, once produced, is delivered to every subscribed consumer at least once, but may be delivered more than once under retry or reconnect conditions. Exactly-once delivery is explicitly not attempted. Every consumer that requires it supplies its own idempotency mechanism; this chapter's job is to confirm one exists for every event that needs it (§13.6), not to make the bus itself stronger than the architecture requires.**

**Why at-least-once, reasoned against what the architecture already assumes, not asserted as a default.** Exactly-once delivery is a substantially harder distributed-systems guarantee — it typically requires either a persistent, deduplicated log with consumer-side offset tracking, or a two-phase commit between producer and every consumer, neither of which this architecture's in-process, per-Room-Runtime Event Bus (§13.4, consistent with §2.9's no-distributed-broker confirmation) has any other reason to need. Meanwhile, every consumer-side mechanism already frozen in this document — cited in §13.2's third force — was independently built to tolerate a duplicate. Choosing exactly-once now would mean building real additional infrastructure to provide a guarantee none of the already-frozen consumers actually asked for, purely for its own sake. At-least-once, with idempotency pushed to consumers, is the strictly cheaper option that is already sufficient, and is not a compromise relative to what §1.9 required — §1.9 named the choice as open, not as requiring the stronger guarantee.

**This closes §1.18/§1.19's risk #63 with a decision, not a restatement.** "Event delivery semantics (at-least-once vs. exactly-once) must be decided" is answered here definitively: at-least-once, chosen because it is what the rest of the architecture was already built to assume, confirmed by tracing that assumption through four independently-designed mechanisms rather than declared by fiat.

**What this requires of every future event this document or a later chapter introduces.** Any new event added after this chapter must either be naturally idempotent (a pure notification of current state, safely re-appliable) or be paired with an explicit consumer-side idempotency key (a sequence number, a grant identifier, a per-instance fired-set, or equivalent) — this chapter fixes that requirement as a standing design constraint on every future event, not merely a retrospective description of the ones already named.

### 13.4 The Per-Room Ordering and Serialization Mechanism

> **Each Room Runtime owns exactly one ordered event queue. Every event produced for that room — regardless of which module produced it — is appended to that one queue and dispatched to its full consumer set strictly one at a time, in arrival order, before the next queued event is dispatched.**

**This is what makes §1.9's "effectively serialized" a real mechanism, not an assumption a later chapter has to keep re-deriving.** §1.9 already fixed that per-room event processing is serialized and that this rules out two concurrent Decision Engine evaluations racing against stale state — this section supplies the concrete structure (one queue, one dispatcher, per room) that makes that true by construction. No module — including the Decision Engine's own coordinator — ever processes a second event for the same room while a first is still being dispatched.

**The simultaneous-`VOICE_STARTED` tie-break, resolved by construction rather than a new rule.** §1.9 names two near-simultaneous `VOICE_STARTED` events from both participants as a case requiring one deterministic outcome. Because both events are appended to the same single queue as they arrive at the Room Runtime's transport boundary, whichever one's underlying network frame is physically received and enqueued first is processed first — no timestamp comparison, no randomness, and no new tie-break logic is needed beyond the queue's own arrival order, which is already deterministic for any given real execution.

**One queue per room, never a shared cross-room structure — consistent with, not a new instance of, §2.6's isolation guarantee.** A slow consumer or a burst of events in one room's queue has no effect on any other room's queue or dispatch cadence; this is the same per-room isolation §2.6 already establishes for failure, applied here to ordering.

**Cyclic runtime feedback through this queue is normal and expected, never something this mechanism tries to eliminate.** §2.4 already distinguishes acyclic module *instantiation* from cyclic-by-design runtime *event flow* — a Decision Engine proposal that results in a new event that the Decision Engine itself later consumes (e.g., its own `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` output eventually informing a later decision cycle) is not a bug this queue guards against; it is the normal shape of a reactive system, and the single-queue-per-room design supports it without special-casing. This is also why `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED`'s Decision Engine consumer entry in §13.6 is correct and not a violation of §13.5's direct-read rule below: the coordinator consumes the *notification* to know a new decision cycle should run at all (per §10.3's already-frozen "any consumer-set event" trigger rule), never as a substitute for reading *current* ownership, which it always does through §4.11's direct read once a cycle is already running.

**Vendor-agnosticism, confirmed explicitly rather than left to be assumed from Chapters 11–12's precedent.** The Event Bus itself is a pure internal message-routing mechanism — it holds no adapter binding, makes no vendor call, and every one of its own mechanics (the per-room queue, arrival-order dispatch, at-least-once delivery) is defined purely in terms of when an event arrives at the Room Runtime's boundary, never in terms of a vendor's own processing behavior or latency. This is trivially true for this chapter's own mechanism, but is stated explicitly rather than silently skipped, consistent with the standing practice §12.14 established: a guarantee argued rigorously for one chapter's mechanism is not assumed to transfer to the next without its own check.

### 13.5 Direct Reads vs. Event-Mediated Notifications

> **A module reads another module's current authoritative state directly, through an explicit read interface, when one exists — never through the Event Bus. A module reacts to something having happened — a value changed, a threshold crossed, an external input arrived — exclusively through the Event Bus. State is never a notification; a notification is never state.**

**§4.11's atomic snapshot is the canonical example of a direct read, confirmed rather than redesigned.** Every module that needs current stage id, transition sequence number, owner, or ownership-grant identifier — the Decision Engine's coordinator, the Prompt Builder, the Timing Engine — reads it directly via that interface, as already fixed. This chapter does not route that read through an event; doing so would add latency and a staleness window to the single most latency-sensitive read in the whole architecture (§1.10's budget) for no benefit, since the interface already guarantees atomicity and currency.

**`OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` and `TRANSITION_STARTED`/completion are notifications about a direct-read value having changed, not the value itself — a distinction that matters and is stated explicitly here.** A module that needs to know current ownership *right now* uses §4.11's direct read. A module that needs to know *that ownership just changed*, in order to react to the change itself (the Client re-rendering, the Logging/Observability Layer recording it) subscribes to `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED`. Both are correct, simultaneously, for different needs — this section fixes that neither is the "wrong" way to learn about ownership, because they answer different questions.

**How Event-Bus-delivered proposals relate to `requestAdvance`/`confirmAdvance`/`proposeOwnershipChange`, stated precisely.** These three operations (§4.10, §10.5, both frozen) are direct calls the Decision Engine's coordinator makes against the State Machine's own interface — they are not events, and are never routed through the queue described in §13.4. Once one of them completes, the resulting state change is what the corresponding notification event (`OWNERSHIP_CHANGED`, `TRANSITION_STARTED`) reports; the call and the notification are two different things serving two different purposes, exactly as this section's opening rule already distinguishes.

### 13.6 The Full Event Catalog

Every event named across Chapters 1–12, given all four properties §1.9 requires. Grouped by §1.9's own categories; nothing here renames or redefines a category, only completes it.

**Lifecycle — with a real boundary correction found during final audit, stated before the table rather than silently folded into it.** §1.9's own "Lifecycle" list groups `ROOM_CREATED`, `ROOM_JOINED`, `ROOM_READY`, `TOPICS_SELECTED`, and `ROOM_FINISHED` together, but they are not all the same *kind* of thing once §2.4/§2.5's already-frozen instantiation order is traced precisely. §2.4 fixes that the Event Bus is instantiated *at Birth*, first among all modules. §2.5 fixes that Birth is *triggered by* "the existing room becoming ready (prep complete, both participants present)." That means room creation, both participants joining, readiness, and topic selection — everything that happens during Preparation — necessarily **precedes the Event Bus's own existence**. They cannot be per-Room-Runtime Event Bus events, no matter which category §1.9's representative list files them under, because there is no Event Bus yet to carry them. Resolving this precisely — not assuming it away — is exactly the kind of boundary question §1.9 left open for this chapter.

> **`ROOM_CREATED`, `ROOM_JOINED`, and `TOPICS_SELECTED` are pre-Birth signals belonging to the existing Preparation/matchmaking system (§1.6, already grounded as "the existing room mechanism") — never per-Room-Runtime Event Bus events, and not redesigned here.** Any post-Birth module that needs a pre-Birth fact reads it directly from already-persisted state, exactly per §13.5's direct-read rule, never via a subscription to an event that would have already fired before the module existed to receive it. This is what §8.4 field 4 already implied without this chapter having said so explicitly: field 4's source is "`muendlich_selections`, populated during Preparation... unchanged," read directly, not delivered via a `TOPICS_SELECTED` event the Prompt Builder — a module that doesn't exist until Birth — could never have received. The same reasoning applies to participant identity: the Fairness Engine reads slot/identity from already-persisted `muendlich_participants` data at its own Birth-time instantiation (the same pattern §2.4 already establishes for Personality & Variation Config being "read... once at room-start to parametrize... per-room instances"), never by subscribing to a `ROOM_JOINED` event that predates it.

**`ROOM_READY` is a genuine exception to the three above, precisely because Chapter 4's own frozen text gives it a second, later occurrence — found only by re-checking §4.7's stage-1 contract directly, not by pattern-matching it against its three siblings.** Stage 1 ("Waiting for Exam Start") is entered *at* Birth, once the pre-Birth "prep complete, both present and ready" condition triggers it — but §4.7 fixes stage 1's own **exit** condition as "both participants confirmed ready (**or** a short server-driven grace period elapses)" and explicitly lists `ROOM_READY` among its **valid events**. Since stage 1 is a state the State Machine — and therefore the Event Bus — only occupies *after* Birth, this second confirmation is necessarily a genuine, post-Birth Event Bus event: each client's live (re-)confirmation of readiness to the now-instantiated Room Runtime, distinct in *timing* from the coarser, pre-Birth signal of the same name that triggered Birth in the first place. `ROOM_READY` therefore appears twice in this document with two different natures — once, pre-Birth, as part of the existing Preparation system (out of this chapter's scope, like its three siblings above); and once, post-Birth, as the genuine Event Bus event stage 1 already names as valid. Only the second is catalogued below.

| Event | Producer | Consumer(s) | Idempotency | Failure/Retry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ROOM_READY` (post-Birth occurrence only — stage 1's own live readiness re-confirmation, §4.7) | Client, via the WebSocket transport, per participant | State Machine (stage 1's exit condition) | Keyed by connection instance; a duplicate re-confirmation from the same client is a no-op against an already-satisfied exit condition | If not received within stage 1's own grace period, the grace period elapsing is itself the alternate, already-frozen exit path (§4.7) — no separate retry is needed |
| `ROOM_FINISHED` | Room Runtime, Teardown (§2.5) — the Room Runtime and its Event Bus still exist throughout Teardown, so this is a genuine, post-Birth Event Bus event, unlike the pre-Birth signals above | Logging, evaluation generation | Guarded by the real, already-cited re-entry guard (§9.6: `if (room.ended) return`) | N/A |

**Nothing above redefines a category's meaning; every entry only completes the four properties §1.9 already required and left unfilled.**

### 13.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapter 16 and Chapter 20

Stated directly, matching the pattern §10.10, §11.8, and §12.8 already establish: **Chapter 13 (this chapter)** owns delivery semantics (§13.3), the ordering/serialization mechanism (§13.4), the direct-read/event-mediated boundary (§13.5), and the full event catalog (§13.6). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines: **Chapter 16**'s exact retry counts, backoff intervals, and rate-limit values for every event this chapter names as retriable or capped — this chapter fixes *that* these are Configuration System parameters, never their values. **Chapter 20**'s cross-instance/multi-process event coordination should this architecture ever need it — this chapter's Event Bus remains explicitly in-process and per-Room-Runtime (§13.4, §2.9), and introducing a distributed broker is a new, separately-evaluated dependency Chapter 20 alone may take on, never assumed here.

### 13.8 Advantages

The delivery-semantics decision (§13.3) is argued from evidence already present across four independently-designed, already-frozen mechanisms, not declared by convention — the strongest form this document's "reasoned, not asserted" discipline can take. The single-queue-per-room mechanism (§13.4) makes §1.9's ordering and serialization guarantees real, checkable structure rather than a standing assumption every later chapter had to re-derive on faith. The direct-read/event-mediated rule (§13.5) closes a real ambiguity risk — without it, a future chapter could plausibly route a latency-critical read through an event out of habit, quietly violating §1.10's budget. The full event catalog (§13.6) discharges more accumulated forward-reference debt than any other single section in this document, and does so without silently under-specifying any of the four required properties for any entry.

### 13.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Exactly-once delivery, via a persisted, deduplicated event log.** Rejected (§13.3): a real, non-trivial infrastructure commitment this document's already-frozen consumer-side mechanisms never actually required, chosen only because it sounds stronger — not because anything needs it.

**(b) A shared, cross-room event queue with room-id filtering per consumer.** Rejected (§13.4): reintroduces exactly the cross-room interference §2.6's per-room isolation guarantee exists to prevent — a slow or bursty room's events could delay dispatch for every other room sharing the structure.

**(c) One ordered queue per Room Runtime, at-least-once delivery, idempotency pushed to consumers (recommended).** The only option that is both cheap to build and already sufficient for every consumer mechanism this document has frozen.

**(d) Route latency-critical state reads (e.g., §4.11's snapshot) through the Event Bus for architectural uniformity.** Rejected (§13.5): would add a queue-traversal latency and staleness window to the single most time-budget-sensitive read in the architecture, for the sake of consistency alone — a real cost for no real benefit.

### 13.10 Recommended Approach

Option (c) for delivery semantics and ordering; the direct-read/event-mediated rule fixed per option (d)'s rejection; the full catalog (§13.6) adopted as the complete, honestly-sourced specification for every event named through Chapter 12, with every retry-count/threshold value correctly deferred to Chapter 16 rather than guessed here.

### 13.11 Possible Risks

**At-least-once delivery still requires every *future* event, introduced by a chapter not yet written, to actually supply an idempotency mechanism — this chapter can mandate the requirement (§13.3) but cannot enforce it retroactively on content it doesn't yet know exists.** Named as a standing discipline for every remaining chapter, not a risk this chapter itself can fully close.

**The single-queue-per-room mechanism (§13.4) has a real, unaddressed throughput question at scale.** A room with an unusually bursty event pattern (many rapid `VOICE_STARTED`/`VOICE_STOPPED` transitions, for instance) could see dispatch latency for later events in the same burst — this chapter fixes the mechanism's correctness, not its throughput characteristics under real load, which is a legitimate input to Chapter 20's scaling work.

**The catalog (§13.6) is complete relative to every event named through Chapter 12, but is not claimed exhaustive for the whole document.** §1.9 itself frames its own list as "representative... not exhaustive," and later chapters (14 onward) may still name new events this chapter cannot anticipate — this chapter's contribution is completeness *as of Chapter 12*, and the idempotency-by-design requirement (§13.3) any such future event must satisfy, not a claim that no chapter will ever add another event again.

### 13.12 Future Improvements

The single-queue-per-room mechanism (§13.4) is what would let a future chapter (20) introduce per-room sharding across multiple worker threads or processes, if real throughput data ever justified it, without changing this chapter's ordering guarantee — only the physical location of each room's one queue would change. The direct-read/event-mediated rule (§13.5) is a small, reusable litmus test a future chapter can apply to any new cross-module data need without re-deriving the reasoning each time. The event catalog's per-category structure (§13.6) is what would let a future chapter add a new category (rather than shoehorning a new concern into an existing one) cleanly, following the same four-property template every existing entry already uses.

### 13.16 Final Pre-Freeze Audit

Per standing practice (established at this chapter's freeze, applying to every chapter from here forward): before recommending any chapter for freeze, it is re-read start to finish as an independent, adversarial pass — not a re-assertion of the self-review and gauntlet already run above — actively re-checking every claim against the real codebase and every citation against the exact frozen text it invokes, hunting specifically for contradictions, missing ownership, orphan references, duplicated responsibilities, and scope leaks the original passes may have missed precisely because they were looking for different things.

**This pass found one significant, genuine structural defect the original self-review and gauntlet both missed.** Re-tracing §13.6's Lifecycle category against §2.4's and §2.5's exact, already-frozen instantiation-order text — not merely against §1.9's category list, which is all the original passes checked it against — found that `ROOM_CREATED`, `ROOM_JOINED`, and `TOPICS_SELECTED` were catalogued as ordinary per-Room-Runtime Event Bus events, when §2.4 fixes the Event Bus as instantiated *at* Birth and §2.5 fixes Birth as *triggered by* "prep complete, both participants present" — meaning all three necessarily occur before the Event Bus exists to carry them. A further check against §4.7's own frozen stage-1 contract (not merely assumed to already agree with the corrected framing) found that `ROOM_READY` is a genuine exception, appearing twice with two different natures: once as Birth's own pre-Birth trigger (out of scope, like its three siblings), and once as a distinct, real post-Birth Event Bus event stage 1 itself lists as valid — a nuance that would have been lost by a blanket fix applied without checking Chapter 4's text specifically. This finding was also checked against §1.6's and §4.7's separate treatment of `TOPICS_SELECTED` as an *invalid* event for in-exam stages ("a prep-stage event... logged and dropped") — confirmed consistent, not contradictory: an already-frozen defensive policy for a stray or racy message arriving post-Birth is exactly what a chapter would write if it already implicitly understood `TOPICS_SELECTED` as fundamentally a pre-Birth concept, which is independent, if indirect, supporting evidence for this pass's finding rather than a conflict with it.

**A second, smaller finding: §13.0 claimed to "supply" the exact event/signal shape Chapter 6 §6.4 deferred to this chapter, but §13.6's original text never explicitly closed that loop** — it listed `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED`/`TRANSITION_STARTED` with Client as a consumer without stating that these two, specifically, are what Chapter 6's already-frozen local-audio-signal resolution depends on. Fixed with an explicit closing note directly under the `OWNERSHIP_CHANGED` row.

**Both fixes were re-verified against every other catalog entry, not applied in isolation.** Every remaining producer/consumer pairing in the catalog was individually re-checked against §2.4's instantiation order for a timing problem of the same kind — none were found; every other event's producer and every other event's consumers are all provably instantiated, per §2.4, before any real-world condition that could cause that event to fire (an active STT connection, a running exam stage, a vendor call in flight) can exist. The Lifecycle category's boundary problem — three entries wholly pre-Birth, one (`ROOM_READY`) split across a pre-Birth and a post-Birth occurrence — was the only instance of this defect class in the whole catalog, not the first of several.

## Chapter 14 — Session Object

### 14.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–13

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–13. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§9.3's memory model** ("one underlying structure, per room, holding four named record types — not four separately-synchronized stores") — this chapter gives that structure its concrete shape; it does not add, remove, or redefine a single record type.
- **§9.4/§9.5/§9.6's write discipline, read discipline, and destruction mechanics** — all fully fixed by Chapter 9; this chapter supplies the structure those rules already operate on, never re-decides when something is written, how it's filtered on read, or what triggers its destruction.
- **§9.3's own named constraint** ("whatever holds this structure (Chapter 14) [must] support atomic-enough updates that a partial write across the four record types can't be observed by a concurrent reader") — resolved at §14.5, by composition with an already-frozen guarantee, not a new mechanism.
- **§1.10's forward pointer** ("The concrete data structure holding this memory — the Session Object — is formalized in Chapter 14; this chapter only fixes its content and destruction rule, not its shape") — this chapter is that shape.
- **§2.3's "Room Runtime holds no business data of its own"** and **§2.4's instantiation order** (the Prompt Builder, item 4, already assumes "the room's Session Object" exists by the time it is wired) — this chapter fixes precisely where the one canonical instance is created and how references reach each consumer without the Room Runtime ever holding it directly.
- **§2.6's cross-room containment guarantee**, explicitly flagged as "verified against Ch.14's Session Object design" — re-verified explicitly at §14.4, not assumed.
- **§5.7/§9.6's "session memory is never reconstructed on resume"** — this chapter's creation-time design (§14.4) is built to make that trivially true, not to add a new rule enforcing it.
- **Chapter 13's per-room event-processing serialization** (§13.4, frozen) — reused directly at §14.5 to resolve §9.3's atomicity concern, never redesigned.

If anything below had appeared to require editing a frozen chapter, work would have stopped and the conflict would have been reported before any change — that did not happen here.

### 14.1 Purpose

Give the Session Object — named since §1.10, used by name since Chapters 7–9, never given a concrete shape — an actual design: one structure per room holding Chapter 9's four record types as named fields; fixed creation timing and reference-sharing that respects the Room Runtime's "no business data" rule; atomicity across the four record types resolved by composition with Chapter 13's serialization guarantee rather than new locking; and destruction/non-reconstruction confirmed as a direct consequence of this chapter's own creation-time design, not a separately-argued rule.

### 14.2 Design Rationale

Three forces shape this chapter, the narrowest and most precisely pre-scoped in the document so far.

**First, the real, already-deployed system already answers this chapter's central shape question, successfully, in production.** `muendlich-relay/src/server.ts`'s `RoomSession` interface — already cited by Chapters 9 and 11 — is one single struct per room holding heterogeneous typed fields (`examStage`, `lastSenderSlot`, `repeatCount`, `teil1HandoffSent`, and more), not four independently-managed stores. §9.3 already reasoned toward "not four separately-synchronized stores" in the abstract; the real system is direct, concrete evidence that this is not merely a tidy convention but a proven, working pattern.

**Second, §2.4's instantiation order creates a real, precise ordering constraint this chapter cannot leave implicit.** The Decision Engine (§2.4 item 2) reads and writes understanding/progress tracking (§9.5); the Prompt Builder (item 4) reads session memory to assemble context (§8.4). Both facts, already frozen, mean the Session Object must exist *before* the Decision Engine is wired — earlier than either chapter that assumed its existence ever had to say explicitly, because neither Chapter 9 nor Chapter 2 owned the question of *when*, precisely, a Session Object begins to exist relative to the ten-module instantiation sequence.

**Third, §9.3's atomicity concern is a real, named, unresolved question — closing it correctly means finding the right already-frozen guarantee to compose with, not inventing a new one.** A chapter that reached for a new locking primitive here would be solving a problem Chapter 13 already solved one layer up (per-room event processing is strictly serialized) — this chapter's job is to recognize that and cite it precisely, closing §9.3's flagged constraint as a consequence of already-frozen architecture rather than new machinery.

### 14.3 The Session Object Shape: One Structure, Four Named Fields

> **The Session Object is a single per-room structure, created once per room instance, with exactly four named fields — one per record type §9.3 already fixed — never four independently-instantiated stores.**

- **`conversationLog`** — an ordered list of entries, each either a speaker-turn entry (`speaker`, a content reference, a timestamp) or, per §9.4's already-frozen interruption-marker rule, a distinct interruption-marker entry (a timestamp only, never a guessed reconstruction of content). One list, two entry kinds — never two separate lists a consumer would have to merge and re-sort.
- **`speakingBalance`** — per-participant (`slot: 'A' | 'B'`) cumulative speaking time and question count, scoped to the *current stage instance* exactly as Chapter 12 §12.4 already fixed ("resets per stage instance... via a stage-id change observed via §4.11's atomic read") — this chapter stores what Chapter 12 already defined the reset behavior for; it does not reintroduce a whole-exam-cumulative shape Chapter 12 never asked for.
- **`promptVariety`** — per-category, turn-ordered record of which variation was selected, exactly the structure Chapter 7 §7.7 already assumed existed under the name "the Examiner's own previous interventions." Ordered by turn, not by a separate timestamp field: §7.7's own recency language ("variations used in this category within the last *N* turns," "least-recently-used") is phrased in terms of turn count, so this field's own append-order already carries the recency information Chapter 7 needs — this chapter does not add a wall-clock timestamp Chapter 7 never asked for.
- **`understandingProgress`** — the Decision Engine's running qualitative assessment, feeding context payload field 10 (§8.4). This chapter gives it a named storage slot; it does not define the assessment's internal composition, which §10.9 already, deliberately, left to Behavior Specification/evaluation-rubric territory.

**Why one structure, tested against the alternative rather than merely asserted.** Four independent stores would need their own independent lifecycle (creation, reference-sharing, destruction) each separately re-derived — quadrupling the surface area §14.4–§14.6 have to cover for no benefit, since every consumer already reads a *filtered view* of one or more fields (§9.5), never an entire field wholesale. A single structure with four named fields gives every consumer exactly the same access it would have had to four independent stores, at a quarter of the lifecycle-management cost.

### 14.4 Creation, Reference-Sharing, and the Consumer Boundary

> **Exactly one Session Object instance is created per room, at Birth, immediately alongside the State Machine and Event Bus (§2.4 item 1) — before any module that reads or writes it is instantiated. Every consuming module (Decision Engine, Fairness Engine, Prompt Builder, per §9.5) receives a reference to that one instance at its own instantiation time; none of them creates its own copy, and the Room Runtime itself never holds a reference to it directly.**

**The Session Object is not an eleventh module, and creating it early does not silently expand §2.4's fixed ten-module list.** §2.4 enumerates exactly ten named per-room modules — decision-making components wired through the Event Bus. The Session Object introduces no decision logic of its own; it is data, created as part of the same foundational construction step as the substrate, in the same sense Personality & Variation Config data is "read... once at room-start to parametrize... per-room instances" (§2.4) without being counted as an eleventh module. This chapter's design adds a data-creation step to Birth's existing procedure; it does not add an eleventh entry to §2.4's module list.

**Why this early, precisely against §2.4's own ordering.** The Decision Engine (§2.4 item 2, instantiated immediately after the substrate) already reads and writes `understandingProgress` (§9.5) — meaning the Session Object cannot be created any later than the Decision Engine's own wiring without violating an already-frozen consumer relationship. Creating it alongside the State Machine and Event Bus, as part of the same foundational step, is the only timing that satisfies every consumer's instantiation-order requirement simultaneously, including the Prompt Builder's (item 4), the latest of the three.

**Birth's existing atomicity/fail-closed guarantee extends to this creation step too, not only to the ten named modules.** §2.5 already fixes that if instantiating or wiring any module fails partway, every instance already created is released immediately and the room is reported as failed to create — this chapter's Session Object creation step is subject to that exact same guarantee: a Birth attempt that fails after the Session Object is created but before, say, the Safety/Validation Layer finishes wiring releases the Session Object along with every module instance already created, never leaves it dangling as an exception to §2.5's all-or-nothing rule.

**Why the Room Runtime never holds it directly, closing the one way this design could have silently violated §2.3 — a distinction worth drawing precisely, since §2.3 itself already permits a related but different kind of reference-holding.** §2.3 already fixes that the Room Runtime "holds references to" all ten per-room module instances, in order to wire and later release them (§2.5) — that is not what "holds no business data of its own" forbids. What it forbids is the Room Runtime retaining the *business data itself* (the Session Object's actual content) as part of its own ongoing state. This chapter's design keeps that line clean: the Room Runtime holds references to *module instances* (already established, unchanged by this chapter) but never additionally holds a direct reference to the Session Object as one of its own fields — the Session Object is created *by* the Birth sequence but *held by* each consuming module as an injected reference, never retained by the Room Runtime itself once wiring completes. This is the same reference-holding pattern §9.6 already fixed for the *destruction* side, stated with the same precision §9.6 already used: "the Room Runtime is not the meaningful holder of this reference... not because the Room Runtime separately 'held' and then dropped a memory reference itself." This chapter fixes the *creation* side of the identical pattern, not a different one.

**Cross-room containment, explicitly re-verified per §2.6's own forward-pointer, not assumed compliant by default.** Each room's Session Object is created fresh, per room, as part of that room's own Birth sequence — there is no module-level, process-wide, or static reference anywhere in this design that any two rooms' Session Objects could ever share. This holds by the same construction §2.6 already relies on for every other per-room module instance (§2.4): no shared mutable state exists, so there is nothing for one room's session memory to leak through into another's.

### 14.5 Atomicity Across Record Types, Resolved via Chapter 13's Serialization Guarantee

§9.3 named this constraint and left it for this chapter: a partial write across the four record types must never be observable by a concurrent reader. This section closes it.

> **No new locking or transaction mechanism is introduced. Every write to any field of the Session Object originates from a module reacting to an event dispatched through that room's one ordered queue (§13.4, frozen) — and because that queue dispatches strictly one event at a time, no two writes to the Session Object, whether to the same field or different fields, can ever be in flight concurrently. Atomicity across the four record types is therefore a direct, free consequence of Chapter 13's already-frozen serialization guarantee, not a property this chapter has to build.**

**Why this is a genuine resolution and not a restatement of the problem.** §9.3's concern was real: if two module instances could write to different fields of the same Session Object at genuinely the same time, a reader could observe, for instance, an updated `conversationLog` alongside a stale `speakingBalance` from a half-completed logical operation. Chapter 13's guarantee rules this out structurally — every write-triggering event for a given room is already processed one at a time, in order, before the next begins — so there is no moment at which two writes are simultaneously in progress to observe a partial state between. This is the same reasoning Chapter 11 already used for its own per-stage checkpoint state and Chapter 12 for its per-stage-instance Fairness tracking; this chapter applies it to the Session Object as a whole, closing §9.3's specific, named concern rather than leaving it as a standing risk.

### 14.6 Destruction and Resumed-Birth Non-Reconstruction, Confirmed

**Destruction is exactly what §9.6 already fixed, with this chapter supplying only the missing precondition — that there is exactly one instance for every consumer's reference to point to.** §9.6 already fixes that the per-room module instances (Prompt Builder, Fairness Engine, Decision Engine) hold the references being released at Teardown's second step, and that memory becomes unreachable as a consequence of releasing *them*, never a separate Session-Object-specific release step. Because §14.4 fixes that all three consumers share references to the *same* one instance, releasing all three consumers' references is sufficient to make that one instance fully unreachable — there is no fourth reference anywhere (the Room Runtime holds none, per §14.4) that could keep it alive past Teardown.

**Resumed-birth non-reconstruction is trivial by construction, not a separately-argued rule.** §5.7/§9.6 already fix that session memory is never reconstructed on resume. Because §14.4 fixes that a Session Object is created fresh, every Birth — including a resumed one, which is still "instantiate the per-room module set" per §2.5's own Birth procedure, just entered via a different detection path (§2.5's "fresh vs. resumed birth" distinction) — there is no code path in this design that could reach back to a previous room instance's now-destroyed Session Object. A resumed birth gets a new instance for the same reason a fresh birth does: because creation, in this design, is simply what Birth does, every time.

### 14.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapter 9, Chapter 2, and Chapter 20

Stated directly, matching the pattern §12.8 and §13.7 already establish: **Chapter 14 (this chapter)** owns the Session Object's concrete shape (§14.3), creation timing and reference-sharing (§14.4), atomicity (§14.5), and destruction/non-reconstruction confirmation (§14.6). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines: **Chapter 9**'s memory model — what is tracked, when it's written, how it's read, what destruction operationally means (all already fixed; this chapter only gives them a shape to operate on). **Chapter 2**'s Room Runtime lifecycle and instantiation order — this chapter fits its one creation step into Birth's already-fixed sequence, never adds a new lifecycle phase or reorders anything §2.4/§2.5 already fixed. **Chapter 20**'s per-room memory footprint at scale — already named as a real, open concern at §2.13 ("many concurrent Room Runtimes, each holding 10 per-room module instances plus a Session Object, has real memory cost... a genuine input to Chapter 20's scaling design") — this chapter fixes the Session Object's shape, never its footprint budget at the "thousands of concurrent exams" target.

**Vendor-agnosticism, briefly confirmed per standing practice.** The Session Object is a pure in-memory data structure — no field, no read, no write, and no part of its creation or destruction touches a vendor call or vendor-produced data directly (the *content* some fields hold, e.g. a conversation-log entry's content reference, may ultimately trace back to something a vendor produced, but the Session Object itself only ever stores and returns references, never computes from or depends on vendor timing or behavior). Trivially compliant, stated explicitly rather than silently assumed.

### 14.8 Advantages

The single-structure shape (§14.3) is directly grounded in a real, already-proven production pattern (`RoomSession`) rather than an abstract preference, and gives every consumer exactly the same filtered access four independent stores would have, at a quarter of the lifecycle-management surface area. The creation-timing fix (§14.4) closes a real ordering gap neither Chapter 2 nor Chapter 9 had to resolve precisely, since neither owned the question of exactly when a Session Object begins to exist relative to the ten-module sequence. The atomicity resolution (§14.5) closes a named, real constraint (§9.3) for free, by composition with Chapter 13's already-frozen guarantee, rather than adding new locking machinery this architecture has never otherwise needed. The destruction and non-reconstruction confirmations (§14.6) required no new rules at all — both are direct, provable consequences of this chapter's own creation-time design, which is itself evidence the design is a clean fit for the rules it has to satisfy.

### 14.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Four independently-instantiated stores, one per record type.** Rejected (§14.3): quadruples the lifecycle-management surface area (creation, reference-sharing, destruction, each separately re-derived) for no benefit, since every real consumer already reads a filtered view of one or more fields, never an entire independent store wholesale.

**(b) One structure per room, created once at Birth alongside the substrate, shared by reference to every consumer (recommended).** The only option that satisfies every consumer's instantiation-order dependency (§2.4) simultaneously and reuses, rather than duplicates, §9.6's already-fixed reference-holding pattern.

**(c) A new locking/transaction mechanism to guarantee atomicity across the four fields.** Rejected (§14.5): solves a problem Chapter 13 already solved one layer up; adding a second mechanism for the same guarantee would be redundant machinery this architecture has no other reason to need.

**(d) The Room Runtime holds the canonical Session Object reference and hands out read/write proxies to consumers.** Rejected (§14.4): would make the Room Runtime a business-data holder in substance even if not in name, directly in tension with §2.3's already-frozen rule — a proxy layer doesn't change what's actually being held.

### 14.10 Recommended Approach

Option (b): one Session Object per room, four named fields per §14.3, created once at Birth alongside the State Machine and Event Bus, shared by direct reference injection to every consuming module at its own instantiation — never held by the Room Runtime (per option (d)'s rejection) — with atomicity resolved via Chapter 13's serialization (per option (c)'s rejection) and destruction/non-reconstruction following as direct consequences of this same creation-time design.

### 14.11 Possible Risks

**Per-room memory footprint, already named as an open concern this chapter does not close.** §2.13 already flags "many concurrent Room Runtimes, each holding 10 per-room module instances plus a Session Object, has real memory cost" at the "thousands of concurrent exams" scale §1.5 targets — this chapter fixes the Session Object's shape, not its size budget; an unbounded `conversationLog` across a very long exam is a real, named input to Chapter 20's scaling design, not resolved here.

**Reference-sharing depends on disciplined wiring, not a structural guarantee this chapter can enforce by itself.** Nothing in this chapter's design *prevents* a future implementation from accidentally giving one consumer a stale or copied reference instead of the shared one — the design fixes the correct pattern and names it precisely, but, like §2.13's "composition-root erosion" risk, disciplined adherence during implementation is what actually keeps the guarantee true, not a compiler-enforced property this chapter can claim outright.

**The `understandingProgress` field's internal composition remains genuinely undefined**, consistent with §10.9's own deliberate deferral to Behavior Specification/evaluation-rubric territory — this chapter gives it a storage slot, but a future implementation reading only this chapter would not know what shape to put inside that slot without also reading the (not-yet-written) Behavior Specification.

### 14.12 Future Improvements

The single-structure shape (§14.3) is what would let a future chapter add a fifth record type (should Chapter 15's AI Modules or a later chapter ever need one) as a fifth named field, without touching this chapter's creation, reference-sharing, atomicity, or destruction design at all — those are all generic over "the structure," never hardcoded to exactly four fields. The reference-injection creation pattern (§14.4) is what would let a future chapter (20) introduce a pooled or size-bounded variant of the structure for extreme-scale scenarios without changing which modules hold references or when they receive them — only the structure's own internal implementation would change.
