## Chapter 15 — AI Modules (Personality & Variation Config, Voice Behaviour Layer)

### 15.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–14

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–14. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§1.5's two component-table rows** ("Personality & Variation Config" and, in the forward-reference index, "Voice Behaviour Layer") — this chapter is their full design; it does not add a component §1.5 did not already name, and does not redefine either row's one-line responsibility.
- **§8.4 field 9 (frozen, Chapter 8)** — the active-persona context field's shape (`{ personality parameters, voiceGenderIdentity, language }`), source ("room configuration, set once at room-creation/Birth time, §2.5"), and volatility ("stable for the whole exam — nothing in Chapters 1–7 permits mid-exam persona changes") are all already fixed. This chapter supplies what "personality parameters" concretely contains and how the whole bundle gets resolved into that field; it does not touch the field's shape, source class, or volatility.
- **§2.3/§2.4 (frozen)** — the Room Runtime remains a composition root holding no business data of its own; Personality & Variation Config is already classified there as a "process-wide *source* the Room Runtime reads from once at room-start to parametrize its per-room instances." This chapter fills in exactly that reading/parametrization mechanism; it does not promote Personality & Variation Config, or a new "Voice Behaviour Layer," into an eleventh entry on §2.4's fixed ten-module list.
- **§7 (Prompt Architecture, frozen)** — the Prompt Builder's deterministic, no-randomness variation-selection algorithm and its consumption of "active persona and language" from the context payload are unchanged; this chapter supplies the persona *data* Chapter 7 already knows how to consume, never a second selection mechanism.
- **§12.8 (frozen, Chapter 12's own scope boundary)** — "Chapter 15's personality-driven phrasing variance for how a silence-recovery, fairness, or clarification turn actually *sounds*... never a word of what the Examiner says" is honored exactly: this chapter fixes that a style input exists, never which mechanism fires or when.
- **§13/§14 (frozen)** — no new event type, no new Session Object field. The persona resolution mechanism designed below (§15.5) reuses Chapter 13's already-established pattern for handling a pre-Birth fact (read directly from persisted configuration at Birth, never invented as an Event Bus event) rather than introducing a new one.

### 15.1 Purpose

To design the two remaining undesigned rows of §1.5's component table — **Personality & Variation Config** and the **Voice Behaviour Layer** — closing a real, already-assumed-to-exist dependency that six frozen chapters (1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 12) each partially lean on but none of them fully build: the concrete shape of "the examiner's configurable style," how one gets selected per room, and how the part of it that is not text (voice/gender identity, delivery cues) reaches Gradium without becoming a text-generation decision.

### 15.2 Design Rationale

**The real system has none of this today.** `muendlich-relay/src/geminiLive.ts`'s `buildSystemInstruction()` is one static, German-only template with name interpolation only — no voice/gender parameter, no `speechConfig`, no style knob of any kind. This chapter is not generalizing a working mechanism (Chapter 11's, 14's situation); it is building the first real instance of one from architectural first principles constrained by what is already frozen (Chapter 12's situation with the Fairness Engine).

Four forces, in priority order: (1) **§1.3's Behavior/Architecture Separation law** — "implementing a new examiner style... [must never] require touching the State Machine's shape, the Event Bus's event types, or the pipeline's stages" — is the hard constraint this whole chapter is measured against: whatever shape Personality & Variation Config takes, adding a new persona or changing a dimension's value must be a pure Chapter 16 configuration-data change, never a code or architecture change. (2) **§1.10/§8.4's already-frozen consistency requirement** — a "female examiner" configuration must select the correct TTS voice *and* keep the generated text persona-consistent, "an inconsistency a real student would notice" if the two ever drifted apart — which forces personality and voice/gender to be selected together, not independently. (3) **§8.4 field 9's already-frozen volatility rule** (stable for the whole exam) sharply narrows the design space: this chapter cannot introduce mid-exam persona changes even if it wanted to, which rules out several superficially attractive designs before they are even considered (§15.9). (4) **Production reality** — the real system literally cannot today put a different voice, gender, or formality level behind an exam; this chapter closes an actual, present capability gap, not a speculative future one.

### 15.3 Personality Parameter Dimensions: A Closed, Named Set

**Exactly eight fields, neither more nor fewer than §1.5 and §8.4 already name.** §1.5's component row lists six style dimensions — rhythm, sentence structure, transition style, encouragement style, questioning style, formality — plus voice/gender identity and language. §8.4 field 9 already fixes the three-part container shape those eight fold into: `{ personality parameters (the six style dimensions), voiceGenderIdentity, language }`. This chapter's first fix: each of the six style dimensions is represented as a **named enum/scale value, never free text**. Free text would force the Prompt Library (Chapter 7) to interpret unstructured per-room guidance at generation time — directly undermining Chapter 7's own frozen "selected and assembled from Prompt Libraries," not "filled from a per-room template" design — and would leave Chapter 16 with no finite value space to default. An enum value (e.g., a small ordered scale for `formality`, a small named set for `transitionStyle`) is what lets Chapter 7's already-frozen, deterministic selection mechanism treat personality as one more structured input alongside state and topic, exactly as it already treats every other context-payload field.

**The set is closed, not extensible by this chapter.** §1.5 already enumerates exactly these eight; adding a ninth here would mean §1.5's own list was incomplete — a claim this chapter has no evidence for and no authorization to make unilaterally. If a genuine ninth dimension is ever needed, that is a Constitutional Amendment to §1.5's own text, reported and approved before any change, not a silent Chapter 15 extension.

### 15.4 The Persona Catalog: Composed Bundles, Not Independent Knobs

**Personas are selected as one pre-composed bundle, never as eight independently-set knobs.** The alternative — letting room configuration set each of the eight fields independently — was seriously considered and rejected (§15.9): §15.2's consistency requirement (voice and text must reflect the same persona) is only *guaranteed* by construction if every legal combination is pre-composed and named; independent knobs would let a configurer accidentally pair a formal, low-warmth style with an encouragement-heavy voice cue, or a female `voiceGenderIdentity` with a persona whose Behavior-Spec content was written assuming male phrasing conventions — exactly the inconsistency §1.10 already names as unacceptable.

**Recommended shape:** a small, named catalog of `PersonaDefinition` entries, each carrying a `personaId` plus concrete values for all eight fields from §15.3. The catalog itself is Configuration System data (Chapter 16) — process-wide, read-only per room, loaded once when a process instance starts, exactly matching §2.9's already-frozen "the Configuration System loads once when a process instance starts, before any Room Runtime can be born." **This chapter fixes that the catalog exists, its entry shape, and that it is process-wide config data; Chapter 16 fixes how many personas exist and their exact field values.** A real, immediately-deployable Chapter 16 default can validly contain exactly one entry — matching the real system's current single-persona reality — the same way Chapter 11's checkpoint list shipped with a real default of exactly two, mirroring what the production system already hardcodes; requiring more than one catalog entry to exist before this design is usable would be over-claiming a capability this chapter does not need to demonstrate to be correct.

### 15.5 Selection, Snapshotting, and Immutability at Birth

**Selection is a pre-Birth fact; resolution happens at Birth — reusing Chapter 13's own pattern for exactly this situation, not inventing a new one.** Which `personaId` a room uses is chosen wherever exam/room configuration is already decided (product- or booking-level configuration, outside this document's scope, the same way exam-type and level are already configured pre-Birth) and persisted alongside the room's other pre-Birth configuration. This mirrors, precisely, how Chapter 13's rigorous final audit resolved `TOPICS_SELECTED`: a pre-Birth fact is never awaited as an Event Bus event by a module that predates the Event Bus's own existence — it is read directly from already-persisted configuration by the module that needs it, at the moment that module is instantiated. Persona selection follows the identical rule: no module ever subscribes to a "persona chosen" event; the Context/Prompt Builder reads the room's already-persisted `personaId` directly during its own §2.4-item-4 instantiation, looks it up in the Chapter 16 catalog, and receives the resolved `PersonaDefinition` as a construction-time parameter — exactly the "process-wide source read once at room-start to parametrize a per-room instance" relationship §2.4 already establishes for Personality & Variation Config in general.

**This resolution is subject to §2.5's Birth atomicity/fail-closed guarantee, stated explicitly rather than left implicit.** If the room's configured `personaId` does not resolve to a real catalog entry — a data-integrity failure, not a normal case — that is a failure during §2.4 item 4's instantiation step, and §2.5's existing rule applies without modification: the partially-built Room Runtime is released, the room is reported as failed to create, and no Run phase begins against a Context/Prompt Builder holding an unresolved persona. This chapter adds no new failure-handling machinery; it confirms an existing guarantee already covers a case this chapter introduces, the same kind of confirmation Chapter 14 §14.4 already made for the Session Object's own creation step.

**The resolved `PersonaDefinition` is a value, copied once, never a live reference back to the catalog.** Once resolved at Birth, the Context/Prompt Builder's copy is what populates context field 9 for the whole exam; a later edit to the Chapter 16 catalog (a config change made by an administrator while other exams are in flight) must never retroactively alter an already-running room's persona — otherwise §8.4's "stable for the whole exam" guarantee would be only nominally true, silently broken by an unrelated administrative action. Fixing that the copy is a value, not a reference, is what makes that guarantee actually hold, not just claim to.

**Where the resolved value lives: inside the Context/Prompt Builder module instance, never inside the Room Runtime.** §2.4 already establishes that reading a process-wide source "parametrizes per-room *instances*" (plural — module instances), not the Room Runtime itself; §2.3's "Room Runtime holds no business data of its own" is preserved exactly the same way Chapter 14 §14.4 already preserved it for the Session Object — the Room Runtime holds a reference to the Context/Prompt Builder module instance (already established as fine by §2.3's own text), never a second, independent copy of the persona data (which would be the forbidden case). Any other module that needs part of the resolved persona (§15.6, below) reads it through the Context/Prompt Builder, the same direct-read pattern §13's "state is read directly, not event-mediated" rule already establishes for exactly this kind of already-instantiated, already-resolved fact.

### 15.6 The Voice Behaviour Layer: From Persona Snapshot to TTS Instruction Bundle

**Not an eleventh module — a fixed, static transformation of already-resolved data, realized at the exact point §1.14 step 6 already names.** §1.14 step 6 (frozen, Chapter 1) already reads: "Approved text, with Orchestrator-decided behavior cues (pacing, emphasis, pauses, voice/gender identity), is sent to Gradium." This sentence already commits to *something* attaching cues at the point of the TTS call — this chapter fixes what that something is: the Room Runtime, acting purely as composition root (§2.3), reads the already-resolved `voiceGenderIdentity` field (plus a fixed pacing/emphasis/pause profile derived from the persona's `rhythm` and `formality` dimensions) directly from the Context/Prompt Builder instance's own persona snapshot — the same direct-read relationship §15.5 already establishes — and attaches it to the approved-text call it was already making to the TTS provider adapter. No new module is instantiated, no new entry is added to §2.4's fixed ten, and no new business decision is made at this point: the value being attached was already fully decided at Birth (§15.5); this step only relays it, exactly the "many internal parts, exactly one external-facing authority, no shortcut past the composition root" discipline §2.7 already establishes for the analogous case one level down.

**The bundle is whole-exam-stable, matching field 9's own volatility, not recomputed per turn.** Because the underlying persona is fixed for the whole exam (§8.4, §15.5), the derived `{ voiceGenderIdentity, pacingCue, emphasisCue, pauseCue }` bundle is resolved once and reused unchanged for every turn's TTS call — never recomputed from per-turn state. Whether *inline*, word-level delivery markup within a single generated utterance (e.g., emphasizing one specific word in one specific answer) is ever produced is a text-generation content question belonging to the Prompt Library/Behavior Specification (Chapter 7's and the Behavior Spec's territory, not redesigned here) — this chapter fixes only the room-level, whole-exam-stable baseline bundle, and explicitly does not claim to have designed turn-level delivery variation.

**Vendor-agnosticism, argued fresh for this mechanism — not assumed to transfer from Chapter 11 or 12's own arguments.** Selecting *which* abstract `voiceGenderIdentity` value a room uses is a pure Configuration System lookup (§15.4/§15.5) — no vendor call, no vendor-specific behavior, computed entirely from server-held configuration and the room's own persisted persona choice. The one place a vendor genuinely enters is translating an abstract `voiceGenderIdentity` value into a concrete Gradium voice ID — that translation is explicitly **not** this chapter's mechanism: it is a lookup table inside the TTS provider adapter (Chapter 22, not yet written), the same boundary §1.5's own Gradium row already draws ("does not decide *how* something should sound or *which voice* to use beyond executing given instructions" — conversely, whatever decides which instructions to give is upstream of the adapter, which is exactly this chapter). This chapter's own computation — selecting and snapshotting a `PersonaDefinition` — never depends on Gemini, Deepgram, or Gradium's latency, behavior, or availability, satisfying the standing vendor-agnosticism requirement on its own terms rather than by inheritance.

### 15.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 12, Chapter 16, Chapter 22, and the Behavior Specification

Stated directly, matching the pattern §10.10, §11.8, §12.8, and §14.7-equivalent boundaries already establish: **Chapter 15 (this chapter)** owns the eight-field personality-parameter shape (§15.3), the persona-catalog structure and its process-wide/config-data classification (§15.4), the selection-and-snapshotting mechanism at Birth (§15.5), and the voice/delivery-cue bundle's shape and attachment point (§15.6). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapter 7**'s Prompt Builder mechanism and its deterministic, no-randomness variation-selection algorithm — this chapter supplies persona data as one more structured input Chapter 7 already knows how to consume; it does not touch how selection among tracked-as-unused Prompt Library variations works. Where a forward-reference (Round 3 item 12, "Transition Diversity," Ch.9/15) suggested this chapter might own diversity mechanics: it does not — Chapter 9 already fully owns the tracking (`promptVariety`, §9.3/§14.3) and Chapter 7 already fully owns the selection algorithm; this chapter's only contribution is that `transitionStyle` is one of the input dimensions Chapter 7's algorithm may weight, never a second selection mechanism.
- **Chapter 8**'s context field 9 shape, source class, and whole-exam volatility (frozen, cited throughout above) — supplied into, never redefined.
- **Chapter 9 / Chapter 14**'s Session Object and its exactly-four fields — the resolved persona is not a fifth field; it lives inside the Context/Prompt Builder's own instance (§15.5), a distinct and already-permitted kind of per-module state, not session memory.
- **Chapter 12**'s Silence Management Engine, Fairness Engine, interruption policy, and clarification mechanism — all fully fixed by Chapter 12, including its own explicit statement (§12.8) that Chapter 15 only supplies *how something sounds*, never *which mechanism fires*. The Round 3 forward-reference "Participation Balance" (Ch.12/15) is closed by §1.13's own already-frozen sentence: "style changes *how* the invitation to participate is phrased, never *whether* it happens" — this chapter does not add a mechanism beyond confirming that sentence's premise (a style input exists) is now real.
- **Chapter 16**'s exact catalog contents — how many personas exist, their real field values, real language options — this chapter fixes the shape and the mechanism, Chapter 16 fixes the values, following the identical split pattern already used for every other "Chapter 15 / 16" and "Chapter X / 16" row in §1.5's own table.
- **Chapter 22**'s (not yet written) TTS/LLM/STT provider-adapter call mechanics — this chapter fixes what value crosses the boundary into the adapter call (§15.6); Chapter 22 fixes how that value becomes an actual vendor API call, the identical split Chapter 11 already used for the pipeline latency budget with a then-unwritten chapter.
- **The Behavior Specification** (a separate document, outside this document's own Scope line entirely) — the actual literal content behind each dimension value (what a `formality: high` examiner actually says differently from a `formality: low` one; backchannel wording; controlled-praise phrasing; natural-closing wording) is never designed here. This chapter fixes that the parametrization surface for that content to attach to exists and is structurally sound; it does not write a single word of examiner speech.

### 15.8 Advantages

Closes a real, already-assumed dependency six frozen chapters lean on (§1.5, §2.4, §7, §8.4, §9, §12.8) without any of them needing modification — every citation above was a consuming reference confirmed correct, never a contradiction requiring the amendment procedure. The eight-dimension closed set (§15.3) keeps §1.3's Behavior/Architecture Separation law literally true: adding a persona is a Chapter 16 data change, never a code change. The persona-catalog design (§15.4) makes the real consistency risk named in §1.10 (voice/text persona mismatch) structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged, by construction rather than convention. The Birth-time resolution mechanism (§15.5) reuses, rather than reinvents, the exact pre-Birth-fact pattern Chapter 13's own rigorous audit already established — a second, independent confirmation that pattern generalizes cleanly. The Voice Behaviour Layer (§15.6) closes §1.14 step 6's own long-standing "Orchestrator-decided" phrase with a concrete mechanism, at zero new-module cost and with vendor-agnosticism argued on its own terms rather than borrowed.

### 15.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Eight independently-composable knobs, no catalog (rejected, §15.4).** Maximizes configurability but makes the §1.10 voice/text consistency guarantee a matter of configurer discipline rather than structural guarantee — exactly the failure mode this document consistently avoids elsewhere (e.g., §2.7's Chain of Authority, §9.5's "one record, multiple filtered views").

**(b) A small, named catalog of pre-composed personas (recommended).** The only option that makes persona-internal consistency a property of the data shape itself, not of whoever configures a room.

**(c) Mid-exam persona switching, allowing style to adapt to how the exam is going.** Rejected outright, not merely deprioritized: §8.4 field 9 already fixes persona as whole-exam-stable, and nothing in Chapters 1–14 permits mid-exam changes — introducing one here would require the Constitutional Amendment Procedure against a frozen chapter for a capability no forward-reference ever actually requested (§1.12's "adapts to student performance" already refers to calmer guidance/challenge-level within one fixed persona, not a persona swap).

**(d) Free-text personality fields, interpreted by the LLM at generation time (rejected, §15.3).** Would undermine Chapter 7's frozen Prompt-Library-selection design and give Chapter 16 no finite value space to default against.

**(e) Realize the Voice Behaviour Layer as an eleventh named module (rejected, §15.6).** Would silently expand §2.4's frozen ten-module list for a responsibility that is, on inspection, a static relay of already-decided data — the same category of rejection §10.3 already applied to "fully independent siblings" for the Decision Engine's internal analyzers, and §14.4 already applied to the Session Object itself.

### 15.10 Recommended Approach

Option (b) for the persona catalog, with a real, immediately-deployable Chapter 16 default of exactly one entry matching the real system's current single-persona reality; Birth-time resolution via the pre-Birth-fact/direct-read pattern established in §15.5, reusing Chapter 13's own precedent rather than inventing a new one; the resolved value held inside the Context/Prompt Builder's own module instance, never by the Room Runtime; and the Voice Behaviour Layer realized as a composition-root-level relay of already-decided data (§15.6), never an eleventh module. Options (a), (c), (d), and (e) are all rejected for reasons traceable to an already-frozen chapter's own text, not merely stylistic preference.

### 15.11 Possible Risks

**A single-entry Chapter 16 default, while valid, does not itself prove the multi-persona capability works end-to-end.** This chapter's design makes a second persona a pure data addition, but that claim remains unverified against a second real catalog entry until Chapter 16 actually ships one — named honestly as untested-in-practice, not merely theoretically sound.

**The pacing/emphasis/pause derivation from `rhythm` and `formality` (§15.6) is a plausible mapping, not an empirically-tuned one.** Unlike Chapter 12's silence thresholds or repeat cap (both inherited from real, already-tuned production defaults), no real system component has ever executed persona-driven delivery cues — this mapping starts from zero production experience, the same honestly-named risk class Chapter 12 §12.12 already applied to the Fairness Engine's dominance ratio.

**Catalog growth over time is a real, unaddressed operational question.** Nothing in this chapter bounds how large the Chapter 16 catalog may eventually grow, or how an administrator would deprecate a persona already in use by in-flight rooms without violating §8.4's stability guarantee for those rooms — named here as an open operational concern for Chapter 16 to address when it actually designs catalog management, not resolved by this chapter.

### 15.12 Future Improvements

Turn-level delivery variation (word-specific emphasis within a single generated utterance, explicitly named out of scope in §15.6) could layer onto the Prompt Library's own output in a future revision without touching this chapter's room-level bundle design at all — the two operate at different levels (whole-exam-stable vs. per-utterance) and neither constrains the other's future extension. A future aggregate-usage view of which personas are actually selected across rooms would be a pure Chapter 17/18 (Logging/Metrics) consumer of the already-resolved `personaId`, requiring no change here.

Rejected: §15.4/§15.10 explicitly confirm a one-entry catalog is a valid, real, immediately-deployable default — the architecture's job is making a second entry a pure data change when wanted, not requiring one to exist today.

**Pass 2 — Constitutional Compatibility.** Checked against all fourteen frozen chapters' exact text, not summaries: §1.3 (Behavior/Architecture Separation — satisfied, §15.2/§15.8), §1.5 (both component rows — satisfied, §15.1/§15.3–15.6), §1.10/§1.13 (consistency and "style changes how, never whether" — satisfied, §15.4/§15.7), §2.3/§2.4/§2.5 (composition root, no business data, Birth atomicity — satisfied, §15.5/§15.6), §7 (Prompt Builder, deterministic selection — satisfied, §15.7), §8.4 field 9 (shape/source/volatility — satisfied throughout), §9/§14 (Session Object's four fields — satisfied, §15.7), §12.8 (phrasing-variance-only boundary — satisfied, §15.7), §13 (pre-Birth-fact pattern — satisfied and explicitly reused, §15.5). **Pass 4 — Five-Engineer Validation.** Given only Chapters 1–14 plus this one, five independent engineers would need to agree on: the eight-field shape (fixed exhaustively by §15.3, matching §1.5/§8.4 verbatim — no divergence possible), the catalog-vs-independent-knobs choice (fixed by §15.4's explicit rejection of the alternative, reasoned from §1.10's own text), the resolution timing (fixed precisely by §15.5's Birth-item-4 placement), and the non-module status of the Voice Behaviour Layer (fixed explicitly by §15.6, with the rejection reasoning in §15.9(e) available to anyone tempted toward an eleventh module). No instance of the Chapter 13/14 defect class found here.

No field or behavior in the real file was found that this chapter's design fails to account for.

**Missing-ownership and scope-leak check.** Every sentence in §15.3–§15.6 was re-traced to confirm it either cites an already-frozen chapter's exact text as its authority or is marked as this chapter's own new contribution — no sentence was found making an implicit content decision (an actual persona name, an actual dimension value, actual phrasing) that belongs to Chapter 16 or the Behavior Specification.

**Duplicated-responsibility check.** Compared §15.7's scope-boundary claims against the *actual* frozen text of §7, §8.4, §9.6/§14.3, §12.8, and §13's direct-read rule, sentence by sentence, rather than against this chapter's own summary of them (written earlier in the session) — every citation matched the source exactly; none were found to have drifted or been misquoted during drafting.

**Cross-reference re-verification.** Every "§N.M" citation in this chapter was checked against the actual current section numbering of the cited chapter (not assumed from the forward-reference tables in §1.19–1.22, which record Chapter 1's *original* guesses, several of which this chapter explicitly narrows in §15.7) — no stale or incorrect section reference found.

**Genuinely convinced, not merely asserting so: Chapter 15 is production-quality and freeze-ready.** Every claim traces to a checked source; every timing claim is verified against the real instantiation order it depends on; the five findings §15.13's self-review surfaced are fixed and re-verified; and this separate final pass, specifically re-targeting the defect classes the two prior chapters' audits found, found no further instance of any of them.

## Chapter 16 — Configuration System

### 16.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–15

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–15. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§2.4 (frozen)** — "the Configuration System (Chapter 16)" is already classified there as a **process-wide *source*** the Room Runtime reads from once at room-start, explicitly distinct from the ten per-room module instances. This chapter confirms, and never redefines, that classification: it adds no eleventh module.
- **§2.9 (frozen)** — already fixes that the Configuration System "loads once when a process instance starts, before any Room Runtime can be born," and that a load failure means "the process fails closed — it refuses to birth any Room Runtime — rather than falling back to defaults that could silently misconfigure an exam." This chapter supplies the concrete mechanism satisfying an already-fixed rule; it does not re-decide load timing or failure behavior.
- **§2.9's "no Redis or other distributed cache/broker dependency"** — already frozen. This chapter's design (§16.5) is chosen specifically to require no new distributed dependency, consistent with, not in spite of, that existing sentence.
- **Every "Chapter 16" forward-pointer across ten frozen chapters** (§16.8's catalog) — each cited as an authority for *that* parameter's existence and mechanism; this chapter never redefines what a parameter means or when it fires, only what value it holds and how that value is stored, loaded, and consumed.
- **§11.6's pipeline latency budget table** — adopted by reference (§16.8), not restated or re-derived.

### 16.1 Purpose

To design the Configuration System itself — its storage shape, loading semantics, change-propagation rule, and per-module consumption pattern — and to close, with a real or honestly-labeled-provisional value, every one of the eighteen distinct parameters that ten frozen chapters have each already named as "a Configuration System parameter (Chapter 16)" rather than a fixed value baked into this document.

### 16.2 Design Rationale

**Stronger real-code grounding than any chapter since 14 — two independent, already-proven mechanisms exist, not zero.** `muendlich-relay/src/server.ts` already resolves most of its tunable values as `Number(process.env.X ?? default)` — read once at module load, overridable without a code change, with an explicit code comment warning against casual production changes — and already has a real fail-closed-at-startup pattern (lines 52–54: missing required config throws before the server accepts a connection). Separately, `supabase/migrations/20260714030000_d17_v3_dynamic_config.sql` already implements a real, deployed, admin-editable configuration store — `platform_settings` (key→jsonb value), `platform_settings_history` (old/new value, admin id, and timestamp, written *before* every overwrite — "no setting change is ever silently lost"), and `set_platform_setting()`, an admin-only `SECURITY DEFINER` function. This chapter generalizes both, rather than inventing a third mechanism.

Three forces, in priority order: (1) **§2.9's already-frozen constraints** — load-once-per-process, fail-closed — sharply bound the design before this chapter starts; (2) **§1.3's Behavior/Architecture Separation law**, restated for this chapter's own case: tuning any of the eighteen catalog values must never require a code change or touch a State Machine shape/Event Bus type/pipeline stage — it must be a pure data edit through the admin-only write path; (3) **honesty about what is and isn't proven** — eleven of the eighteen catalog parameters have no real production precedent at all (their owning mechanisms are themselves new — first-principles designs or not-yet-built integrations, not values `server.ts` has actually run in production), and this chapter must not manufacture false confidence by presenting a provisional guess with the same weight as a number `server.ts` has actually run in production.

### 16.3 Storage and Structural Shape

**Reused directly from real, proven infrastructure — not a new invention.** The Configuration System is realized as the same shape already deployed for D17: a key→value(jsonb) store (`platform_settings`-equivalent), an append-only history table logging every change's old value, new value, admin identity, and timestamp *before* the overwrite is applied, and a single admin-only `SECURITY DEFINER` write path (`set_platform_setting()`-equivalent) — no other code path may write a configuration value. This closes §1.3's separation law structurally: every one of the eighteen catalog parameters is a row in this store, never a literal in source code, so tuning any of them is exactly the same kind of change as tuning a D17 risk threshold today — a data edit through an already-proven, audited path, not a deploy.

**Logical grouping, not physical partitioning.** Keys are namespaced by owning mechanism (e.g., a `timing.*` group for §11.5's checkpoints, a `conversation.*` group for §12.3/§12.4/§12.7's parameters, a `persona.*` group for §15.4's catalog) purely for readability and audit-log clarity — the store itself remains one flat table, not ten separate tables, matching the real `platform_settings` precedent exactly (one table already serves multiple unrelated D17 concerns today).

### 16.4 Loading Semantics: Once Per Process, Fail-Closed

**This section supplies the mechanism §2.9 already named; it does not re-decide the rule.** At process start, before any Room Runtime can be born (§2.9, §2.5's own precondition), every required key is read from the store into process memory as one atomic load operation. If any required key is missing, malformed, or fails a basic type/range check, the process fails closed exactly as §2.9 already fixes: it never falls back to a hardcoded default and never births a Room Runtime, "rather than falling back to defaults that could silently misconfigure an exam." This is a direct generalization of `server.ts` lines 52–54's already-proven pattern (`if (!v) throw new Error(...)` for required env vars), extended from four required Supabase/Gemini credentials to the full eighteen-parameter catalog plus any future addition.

**Not a per-key lazy load.** All required keys load together, at the same moment, as one operation — a process either has a complete, valid configuration before it births its first room, or it never births one at all. This avoids a genuinely dangerous partial-load state (some parameters resolved, others not) that a lazy, per-key loading strategy would introduce and that no frozen chapter's text permits.

### 16.5 Change Propagation: Next-Process-Start Only, Never Live-Reloaded

> **An admin edit to a stored configuration value takes effect for the next process start. It is never live-reloaded into an already-running process.**

**This is the most literal reading of §2.9's own "loads once when a process instance starts" wording, not an interpretation stretched to fit.** §2.9 says once, not "once, then periodically refreshed" — a live-reload mechanism would require new cross-process cache-invalidation machinery (each of §1.5's many concurrent process instances would need to learn of the edit and safely apply it without disrupting in-flight rooms), and §2.9 itself already states this architecture "has no Redis or other distributed cache/broker dependency" — exactly the kind of dependency a live-reload mechanism would most naturally require. Building one here would mean either quietly contradicting that sentence or inventing a broker-free live-reload scheme this chapter has no real precedent for and no mandate to design. Deferred explicitly (§16.14), not silently assumed away.

**A second, independent guarantee — not the only thing preventing a live exam from being retroactively altered.** Chapter 15 §15.5 already argued that a resolved persona snapshot, copied by value at Birth, protects an in-flight room from a later catalog edit. This section shows that guarantee was never load-bearing alone: because a process's own in-memory configuration copy cannot change until that process restarts, an admin edit literally cannot reach an already-running process's Room Runtimes *at all*, regardless of what any individual module does with the value once read. Two independent mechanisms — process-level load-once (this chapter) and module-level snapshot-at-Birth (Chapters 2, 4, 11, 15, generalized in §16.6 below) — both guarantee the same outcome without either depending on the other, which is a stronger, more robust property than either alone would be.

### 16.6 Per-Module Consumption: Resolved Once at Birth, Held by the Consuming Instance

**Generalizing a pattern four frozen chapters have already independently used, closing it once rather than leaving every future chapter to re-derive it.** Chapter 2 (Personality & Variation Config, read once at room-start to parametrize per-room instances), Chapter 4 (stage durations, baked into a room's own State Machine instance), Chapter 11 (checkpoint positions, read via the §4.11 atomic snapshot and held for the stage instance), and Chapter 15 (the persona snapshot, resolved once at Birth and held by the Context/Prompt Builder instance) have each, independently, arrived at the identical rule for their own specific parameter. This chapter states it as the **standing rule for every Configuration System parameter**, present and future:

> **Whichever module needs a configuration parameter reads it once, at that module's own §2.4 instantiation step during Birth, and holds its own resolved copy for the exam's duration. No module re-reads the Configuration System mid-exam.**

**Explicitly distinguished from Chapter 13's "state is read directly" rule — two different rules for two different data categories, never conflated.** §13's direct-read rule concerns State Machine business state: dynamic, changing during the exam, correctly read fresh whenever a module needs the current value (e.g., §4.11's atomic snapshot). Configuration System values are the opposite: static for a given process's lifetime (§16.4), correctly read exactly once and held, never re-fetched. A future chapter citing "read directly" for a configuration value would be citing the wrong rule — this section exists precisely so that mistake has a clear, named correction to point to.

### 16.7 Value vs. Shape: What Requires the Amendment Procedure

**A distinction implicit since Chapter 10, stated explicitly here for the first time.** Changing a parameter's *value* — tuning `MAX_REPEAT_USES` from 2 to 3, adding a second entry to the persona catalog, adjusting a silence-escalation timing — is ordinary operations work through §16.3's admin-only write path. It never touches this document's text and never requires the Constitutional Amendment Procedure, no matter how operationally significant the change feels. Adding a new configurable *dimension* that no frozen chapter has named — a parameter category this document has never mentioned — is an architecture change: if it fits as a strict extension of an already-frozen chapter's own text, that chapter's own future revision (or a later chapter citing it) supplies it; if it would contradict a frozen chapter, only the Amendment Procedure applies. This chapter's own eight-provisional-value list (§16.8) is *value* territory, explicitly not exempt from ordinary tuning as real production experience accumulates.

### 16.9 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapters 2, 4, 11, 12, 15, 19, 20, and 21

Stated directly, matching the pattern §10.10, §11.8, §12.8, and §15.7 already establish: **Chapter 16 (this chapter)** owns the Configuration System's storage shape (§16.3), loading semantics (§16.4), change-propagation rule (§16.5), the standing per-module consumption pattern (§16.6), the value-vs-shape distinction (§16.7), and the full parameter-value catalog (§16.8). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapters 2, 4, 11, 12, 15**'s own mechanisms — what each parameter *means*, when it fires, and what module consumes it. This chapter only supplies the value and the generic storage/loading/consumption machinery underneath.
- **Chapter 19**'s (not yet written) disconnect-handling design — `RECONNECT_GRACE_MS`- and `HARD_IDLE_CLOSE_MS`-equivalent parameters remain unclaimed by this chapter, named explicitly in §16.8 rather than silently absorbed.
- **Chapter 20**'s (not yet written) horizontal-scaling and sticky-routing design — this chapter's process-local, load-once model is deliberately simple and makes no claim about cross-process coordination; if Chapter 20 ever needs live cross-instance config propagation, that is Chapter 20's dependency to introduce, not one this chapter has silently assumed.
- **Chapter 21**'s (not yet written) cost-optimization and billing design — `CREDIT_TICK_MS`-equivalent parameters and the pipeline latency budget's "real revision" (§11.8's own hand-off) remain Chapter 21's, not this chapter's.

### 16.10 Advantages

Reuses two already-proven real mechanisms (`server.ts`'s env-override-with-fail-closed pattern; D17's `platform_settings`/history/admin-write pattern) rather than inventing a third, giving this chapter stronger real-code grounding than any chapter since 14. Closes eighteen forward-references left open across ten frozen chapters with a single, consistent mechanism rather than eighteen bespoke ones. The next-process-start-only propagation rule (§16.5) requires no new distributed dependency, honoring §2.9's own "no Redis or other broker" sentence rather than quietly contradicting it. The standing per-module consumption rule (§16.6) closes an implicit pattern four chapters already used independently, saving every remaining chapter (17–25) from re-deriving it. The honest real/provisional split (§16.8) gives implementers an accurate confidence signal per value, rather than false uniformity.

### 16.11 Alternatives Considered

**(a) A new, bespoke configuration mechanism, unrelated to any real precedent.** Rejected (§16.3): would ignore two already-proven, already-deployed real mechanisms for no benefit, violating this document's consistent preference for generalizing working infrastructure over inventing new infrastructure wherever real precedent exists.

**(b) Live cross-process configuration reload.** Rejected (§16.5): would require new distributed cache/broker machinery §2.9 already states this architecture does not have, for a capability no frozen chapter's forward-reference ever actually required — every citation only ever asked for "a Configuration System parameter," never "a live-updating one."

**(c) Per-key lazy loading, resolving each parameter only when first needed rather than all at once at process start.** Rejected (§16.4): would allow a genuinely dangerous partial-configuration state — some parameters resolved, others not — that §2.9's fail-closed guarantee is specifically designed to prevent.

**(d) Present all eighteen catalog values with uniform confidence, without distinguishing real from provisional.** Rejected (§16.8): would misrepresent eleven values that have never run in production as equally proven as the seven that have, undermining the same honesty standard §11.12/§12.12/§15.11 already established for exactly this situation.

### 16.12 Recommended Approach

Option from §16.3 (reuse the real `platform_settings`/history/admin-write pattern) for storage; §16.4's atomic, all-at-once, fail-closed loading; §16.5's next-process-start-only propagation per option (b)'s rejection; §16.6's standing per-module consumption rule, generalized from four chapters' independent precedent; and §16.8's honestly-split real/provisional catalog per option (d)'s rejection.

### 16.13 Possible Risks

**Eleven of eighteen catalog values are genuinely untested provisional starting points, not tuned defaults.** Named honestly throughout §16.8 rather than smoothed over; real production behavior once Chapters 7, 8, 12 (partially), 3, and 5's own mechanisms actually run will very likely require retuning several of them — this chapter's value-vs-shape distinction (§16.7) is what makes that retuning cheap when it happens, but the need itself is not eliminated by this chapter.

**Process-restart-only propagation (§16.5) means an urgent configuration fix (e.g., a safety-relevant retry cap) cannot take effect faster than the next deploy/restart cycle.** This is a deliberate trade-off against inventing new distributed machinery (§16.11(b)), named honestly as a real operational limitation, not hidden — an operator needing a genuinely emergency-fast configuration change today would need a process restart, not a live toggle, matching D17's own kill-switch precedent (also read once and enforced per-request, not necessarily propagated live to already-established connections).

**The namespaced key grouping (§16.3) is an organizational convention, not an enforced boundary.** Nothing in this chapter's design technically prevents a future implementation from placing a parameter in the wrong namespace group — this is a naming discipline this chapter recommends, not a structural guarantee it can claim to enforce by itself, the same honest limitation Chapter 14 §14.11 already named for its own reference-sharing discipline.

### 16.14 Future Improvements

A live or near-live cross-process configuration reload mechanism, explicitly rejected here (§16.11(b)) for lacking both real precedent and a stated need, could be revisited by Chapter 20 if horizontal-scaling operations ever genuinely require faster-than-restart propagation — this chapter's value-vs-shape distinction (§16.7) and namespaced key grouping (§16.3) would both survive that addition unchanged, since it would be a *loading*-mechanism change, not a storage-shape or value change. As real production traffic accumulates against Chapters 3, 5, 7, 8, and 12's own mechanisms, the eleven provisional values in §16.8 are the natural, pre-identified candidates for a future retuning pass — this chapter's honest labeling is what makes that pass targeted rather than a guess at which of eighteen values might need attention.

### 16.16 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

**Pass 1 — Adversarial.** Attempted rejection angle: "presenting provisional values in the same table as real ones, even labeled, risks readers treating them as equally solid." Addressed: §16.8's own closing sentence states the real/provisional split explicitly as a count ("seven real... eleven provisional... an honest split, not an attempt to make every value look equally proven"), and every single row carries its own label — not a caveat buried once at the top. Second angle: "the next-process-start-only propagation rule makes this Configuration System weaker than D17's own real admin panel, which presumably wants faster effect." Addressed directly in §16.13's second risk: named as a real, deliberate trade-off, not hidden, with the D17 kill-switch's own per-request (not live-broadcast) enforcement cited as a parallel precedent for why "eventually consistent, not instant" is an acceptable, already-precedented pattern in this exact codebase.

**Pass 2 — Constitutional Compatibility.** Checked against all fifteen frozen chapters' exact text: §1.3 (Behavior/Architecture Separation — satisfied, §16.2/§16.3), §1.8/§1.10/§1.19 (fallback retries, STT threshold, language — satisfied, §16.8), §2.4 (process-wide source classification — satisfied, §16.0), §2.9 (load-once, fail-closed, no distributed broker — satisfied and directly cited, §16.4/§16.5), §3.5/§3.8 (buffer size, failure windows — satisfied, §16.8), §4.5 (stage durations — satisfied, §16.8), §5.5 (grace period — satisfied, §16.8), §7.7/§8.4 (exclusion window, history size — satisfied, §16.8), §11.5/§11.6/§11.8 (checkpoints, latency budget, explicit non-ownership of billing/disconnect parameters — satisfied, §16.8/§16.9), §12.3/§12.4/§12.7/§12.8 (silence/fairness/clarification values, scope boundary — satisfied, §16.8/§16.9), §13.6/§13.7 (restated values, scope boundary — satisfied), §15.4/§15.5/§15.10/§15.11 (persona catalog value, propagation-timing consistency — satisfied and reinforced, §16.5). No contradiction found; zero amendment procedures invoked.

**Pass 3 — Implementation.** Mentally built end-to-end: an admin edits a value via the `set_platform_setting()`-equivalent path → the history table logs old/new value before the overwrite → the change sits in the store, inert, until the next process start → a new process instance, at startup, loads every required key atomically, fails closed on any problem → each per-room module, at its own §2.4 Birth-time instantiation, reads its own needed parameter(s) once from the process's already-loaded copy and holds them for the room's lifetime → an already-running process's already-alive Room Runtimes are structurally unaffected by the edit, twice over (§16.5). No missing step found.

**Pass 4 — Five-Engineer Validation.** Given only Chapters 1–15 plus this one, five independent engineers would need to agree on: the storage shape (fixed by direct reuse of a named, inspectable real migration file — no room for divergent interpretation), the load-once/fail-closed mechanism (fixed by §2.9's own frozen wording plus a named real code precedent), the propagation timing (fixed explicitly by §16.5's boxed rule, with its reasoning traceable to §2.9's exact sentence), and which of the eighteen values are real versus provisional (fixed by an explicit per-row label, not left to individual judgment). Convergence assessed as high.

**Pass 5 — Production-Readiness.** Read start-to-finish as new. Failure scenario: the configuration store itself is unreachable at process start — correctly resolves to §2.9's existing fail-closed rule, no Room Runtime born, no partial state. Concurrency scenario: two processes starting simultaneously, one reading a config value mid-edit by an admin — each process's own atomic load either sees the value before or after the edit, never a torn read, since `platform_settings` writes are ordinary single-row transactional updates; no new race introduced by this chapter's design. Scale scenario: a large number of process instances all starting around a deploy — each performs its own independent load, no shared bottleneck beyond the database itself, consistent with §2.6's per-process isolation.

## Chapter 17 — Logging Architecture

### 17.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–16

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–16. This chapter builds on, and does not alter:

- **§2.4 item 6 (frozen)** — the Logging/Observability Layer is already named as one of the already-counted ten per-room module instances, attached last in instantiation order "as a pure subscriber to the Event Bus and to every other module's decision points... nothing depends on it." This chapter confirms, and never redefines, that classification or that positioning; it does not add an eleventh module, and it does not argue for the module's existence — that is already settled.
- **§1.0 and §1.14 step 8's "what stays" boundary (frozen)** — the existing transcript system (`muendlich_transcript_nodes`) is retained by design, unchanged; §1.14 step 8 already draws the exact line this chapter respects: "transcript nodes... update as today; the Logging/Observability Layer records the Decision Engine's decision and inputs, not just the final utterance" — two parallel mechanisms, not one redesigned mechanism. This chapter touches neither the transcript's shape, write path, nor its content.
- **§13's full event catalog (frozen)** — already the vetted, curated list of every Event-Bus-mediated decision worth persisting; this chapter does not re-filter or second-guess that curation, only persists it.
- **§2.7 (frozen)** — "Logging must never sit on this critical path... non-blocking with respect to all five gates... a logging failure is itself just logged-best-effort and counted, never a reason to stall the exam," and the explicit citation that a stale-turn discard is "logged via the Logging/Observability Layer." This chapter supplies the concrete mechanism satisfying both already-fixed rules; it does not re-decide them.
- **§11.3/§11.10(e) (frozen)** — vendor latency "may be measured for metrics, but only by the Logging/Observability Layer," never consumed by the Timing Engine as a timing-decision input. This chapter confirms its own passive role in that guarantee (§17.6); it does not weaken or redesign the underlying vendor-agnosticism rule.

### 17.1 Purpose

To give the Logging/Observability Layer — already named, already positioned, already charter-assigned by Chapter 2 — its full concrete design: exactly what it captures, how that is stored durably, and the non-blocking write mechanism that makes §2.7's already-frozen guarantee real rather than aspirational.

### 17.2 Design Rationale

**This chapter's module is unusual among the remaining chapters: its existence and position are not open questions.** §2.4 item 6 already settled *whether* this module exists and *where* it sits in instantiation order — Chapter 17's job is narrower and more concrete than most: realize an already-drawn charter, not argue for a new one.

**Real-code grounding is a mix of strong precedent and a genuine, fixable gap.** `logTranscript()` in `server.ts` (lines 188–195) already demonstrates a real, working, non-blocking fire-and-forget DB write (`.insert({...}).then(() => {})`) — direct, working evidence that §2.7's non-blocking requirement is achievable with today's real stack, not a theoretical concern. But the same real code reveals the gap this chapter must close: `.then(() => {})` discards the insert's outcome entirely — no `.catch()`, no failure counting — while §2.7 explicitly requires failures to be "logged-best-effort and counted." This is the same category of finding that strengthened Chapters 11 and 16: generalizing a real, proven pattern while fixing a concrete defect in it, not merely copying it uncritically.

Two forces, in priority order: (1) **§2.7's non-blocking mandate is absolute, not a preference** — every design choice below is filtered through "does this ever risk delaying a state transition, an event's delivery, or a turn's progress," and anything that does is rejected regardless of what other benefit it might offer; (2) **§1.5's "records every decision made, not just every utterance spoken"** is the chapter's positive mandate — precisely tracing what "every decision" actually means (§17.3) against the frozen text that already uses this module, rather than assuming it obviously means "everything," is where this chapter's real work lies.

### 17.3 What Gets Logged: Two Categories, Explicitly Not a Third

**Category 1 — Event-Bus-mediated decisions (the primary, comprehensive path).** Every event in Chapter 13's full catalog (Lifecycle, Audio/conversation, Ownership, Understanding/relevance, Timing, Reliability) is persisted, unfiltered. Chapter 13's own rigorous final audit already curated this list once, precisely — re-filtering it here would be redundant at best and a silent, undocumented narrowing of an already-frozen catalog at worst. This chapter's contribution is not deciding *what* qualifies (Chapter 13's), only durably recording *whatever* qualifies.

> **The Logging/Observability Layer subscribes to the Event Bus exactly as §2.4 item 6 already fixes, and persists every event delivered to it — no category of Chapter 13's catalog is silently dropped.**

**Category 2 — the one decision point named as logged that is *not* an Event Bus event.** §2.7 explicitly says a stale-turn discard (§2.7/§3.6) is "logged via the Logging/Observability Layer" — but the stale-turn gate is a synchronous, pre-delivery pipeline check (§2.7: "the gate fires once, before streaming starts"), never modeled as a subscribable Event Bus signal anywhere in Chapter 13's catalog. A design that only subscribed to the Event Bus would silently fail to honor §2.7's own explicit citation — a real gap, not a hypothetical one. §2.4 item 6's own phrase already anticipated this: "a pure subscriber to the Event Bus **and to every other module's decision points**" — the "and" names a second path, not a redundant restatement of the first. Resolution: the Room Runtime's stale-turn gate checkpoint calls the Logging Layer directly, one explicit, named exception to "Event-Bus-only," using the identical non-blocking write mechanism (§17.5) as Category 1.

**Category 3, explicitly not this chapter's — the transcript.** §1.14 step 8 (frozen) already fixes that transcript nodes update "as today," in parallel with, not through, the Logging/Observability Layer. This chapter introduces no third logging path for utterance content; the transcript remains entirely §1.0's existing, unchanged mechanism.

**This is a closed, two-category design, not open to silent future expansion.** A future chapter wanting to log a decision point that is neither an Event Bus event nor the one named stale-turn-gate exception would be introducing a third category — that is new architecture requiring its own justification (an extension of this chapter, not a silent addition), not something this chapter's design already accommodates implicitly.

### 17.4 Storage Shape

**A new, generic, append-only table — genuinely new, since no real precedent logs decisions today (the real system has no Decision Engine to log), but its *shape* is directly grounded in two real, proven patterns.** From `muendlich_transcript_nodes`: append-only, timestamped, room/session-scoped rows, written incrementally as events happen, never batched. From `platform_settings_history` (Chapter 16's own precedent): a structured audit-trail row shape (an identifying key, a value/payload, and metadata about when and in what order the entry was produced).

Recommended shape — one row per logged entry:

> `{ roomId, logSequence, loggedAt, category: "event" | "stale_turn_discard", eventType (for Category 1, one of §13's catalog names), payload (jsonb — Category 1: exactly the shape §13 already fixed for that event type; Category 2: the stale-turn tag contents already established at §2.7/§4.11) }`

**No new payload shapes are invented here.** Category 1's `payload` field is a direct, unmodified copy of whatever structure Chapter 13 already fixed for that event type (e.g., `TIME_WARNING`'s `{ stageId, checkpointIndex, elapsedMs, remainingMs }`, unchanged) — this chapter is a recorder, not a second definer of event shapes.

### 17.5 The Non-Blocking Write Mechanism

> **Every write to the decision log is fire-and-forget: never awaited by the Event Bus dispatch path, the stale-turn gate checkpoint, or any pipeline stage. A failed write increments an in-process failure counter and emits one best-effort local log line — never retried, never escalated, never a reason to delay or fail anything else.**

**Closing the real gap found in §17.2, concretely.** This directly extends `logTranscript()`'s own working `.then(() => {})` pattern with the one thing it's missing: `.catch((err) => { failureCounter++; console.error(...) })` — cheap, non-blocking (the catch handler itself does no I/O beyond the same kind of local write the real system already does elsewhere via `console.error`), and exactly what §2.7's "logged-best-effort and counted" language already requires but the real precedent doesn't yet implement.

**The write-order vs. dispatch-order subtlety — a genuine correctness point this design must not gloss over.** Chapter 13 guarantees strict *arrival-order dispatch* to subscribers via its per-room ordered queue — but fire-and-forget writes are not guaranteed to *land* in the database in that same order, since two concurrent async inserts can complete in either order depending on network/DB latency. If a reader trusted database row-insertion order (or an auto-generated DB timestamp with insufficient precision) to reconstruct "what happened when," a rare but real reordering could silently misrepresent the actual decision sequence.

**Resolution: a Logging-Layer-local monotonic sequence number, stamped at dispatch time, before the async write ever fires.** The Logging Layer maintains one integer counter per room, incremented and captured into the `logSequence` field synchronously, at the moment an event is dispatched to it (or the stale-turn gate calls it directly) — *before* the fire-and-forget write is issued. A reader always sorts by `logSequence`, never by DB arrival time or `loggedAt` alone, so out-of-order durable arrival is harmless. This is a small, self-contained addition, layered on top of Chapter 13's own dispatch-order guarantee without touching or duplicating it — Chapter 13's queue still governs *dispatch* order; this chapter's counter governs *reconstructable* order, a distinct and narrower guarantee this chapter alone is responsible for.

**Failure counting is process-local and best-effort, not itself a durable metric.** The in-process failure counter (§17.5's opening rule) is read by Chapter 18 as one raw input among others — this chapter fixes only that it exists and increments correctly; turning it into an alerting signal or dashboard figure is explicitly Chapter 18's job, not designed here.

### 17.6 Vendor-Latency Data: Recorded, Never Measured or Consumed Here

**The Logging Layer is a passive recorder of already-produced data, never a vendor-latency measurer itself.** §11.3/§11.10(e) permits vendor latency to be "measured for metrics, but only by the Logging/Observability Layer" — traced precisely against where a vendor call actually happens (Chapter 3's pipeline stages, behind Chapter 22's provider adapters), the *measurement* (timestamping around the call) is necessarily performed by whichever module makes that call, not by this chapter's module, which has no adapter binding and makes no vendor call of any kind (§2.7's adapter-binding exclusivity, unchanged). If a producing module's event payload includes a latency figure (e.g., a future `LLM_FAILURE`-adjacent event carrying how long the attempt ran before failing), Category 1's unmodified-payload rule (§17.4) means that figure is durably recorded exactly as produced — this chapter adds no new measurement, only durable storage of a measurement already made elsewhere.

**Vendor-agnosticism, argued fresh for this chapter's own mechanism.** The Logging Layer's own computation — subscribe, stamp a sequence number, write — depends only on the Event Bus, the stale-turn gate's direct call, and the server clock (for `loggedAt`); no vendor call, no vendor-specific behavior anywhere in the mechanism itself. That some of the *data* it happens to store may describe vendor behavior (a latency figure another module measured) is a fact about the data, not a dependency of this chapter's own mechanism on any vendor — the same distinction Chapter 16 §16.5 already drew between "storing a value" and "depending on how that value was produced."

### 17.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapter 1, Chapter 13, Chapter 18, and Chapter 20

Stated directly, matching the pattern §12.8, §15.7, and §16.9 already establish: **Chapter 17 (this chapter)** owns what gets logged (§17.3), the storage shape (§17.4), the non-blocking write mechanism including the sequence-number fix (§17.5), and its own passive role regarding vendor-latency data (§17.6). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapter 1**'s transcript system (§1.0, §1.14 step 8) — explicitly parallel, explicitly unchanged, never touched by this chapter.
- **Chapter 13**'s event catalog and delivery semantics — this chapter persists what Chapter 13 already curated; it never adds, removes, or reinterprets an event type.
- **Chapter 18**'s aggregation, dashboards, alerting, and the real-time pipeline-latency comparison against §11.6's target table (§11.8's own "Ch.17/18" split: 17 = capture/storage, 18 = consumption/measurement-comparison) — this chapter makes the raw data durably available and orderable; turning it into an operational signal is Chapter 18's job entirely.
- **Chapter 20**'s (not yet written) log retention, cleanup, and storage-scale policy — an unbounded append-only table is a real, named operational question this chapter does not resolve (§17.11).

### 17.8 Advantages

Realizes an already-settled module charter (§2.4 item 6) rather than re-arguing for its existence, keeping this chapter tightly scoped. Generalizes a real, working non-blocking write pattern (`logTranscript()`) while closing a genuine, concrete gap in it (silent failure swallowing) rather than copying the pattern uncritically. The two-category design (§17.3) closes a real gap an Event-Bus-only design would have silently missed — the stale-turn discard citation (§2.7) — found by cross-referencing Chapter 13's catalog exhaustively rather than assuming comprehensiveness. The logSequence mechanism (§17.5) closes a genuine, non-obvious write-order-vs-dispatch-order correctness risk before it could ever manifest as a real production bug, at negligible cost (one integer counter per room). The vendor-latency boundary (§17.6) keeps this chapter's own mechanism trivially vendor-agnostic while still honoring §11.3's explicit permission for the *layer* to hold such data.

### 17.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Log only a curated subset of Chapter 13's events, judged "important enough" by this chapter.** Rejected (§17.3): would silently duplicate or second-guess curation Chapter 13's own rigorous audit already performed, and risks an arbitrary, undocumented narrowing with no frozen-text justification.

**(b) Trust database insertion order or `loggedAt` timestamp precision alone for reconstructing decision sequence, no separate sequence field.** Rejected (§17.5): fire-and-forget writes can land out of dispatch order; a rare but real reordering would silently misrepresent what actually happened, for the sake of avoiding one integer counter.

**(c) Await each write synchronously before allowing the dispatch/pipeline path to continue.** Rejected outright: directly violates §2.7's non-blocking mandate, reintroducing the exact starvation risk that section exists to prevent.

**(d) Have the Logging Layer itself measure vendor call durations directly, to guarantee latency data is always present.** Rejected (§17.6): would require the Logging Layer to hold an adapter binding or otherwise observe vendor calls directly, violating §2.7's adapter-binding exclusivity and this chapter's own vendor-agnosticism; latency data availability depends on producing modules choosing to include it, not on this chapter reaching into their territory.

### 17.10 Recommended Approach

The two-category design (§17.3) per option (a)'s rejection; the append-only, `platform_settings_history`/`muendlich_transcript_nodes`-grounded storage shape (§17.4); fire-and-forget writes with local failure counting and a dispatch-time logSequence stamp (§17.5) per options (b) and (c)'s rejections; and a strictly passive role regarding vendor-latency data (§17.6) per option (d)'s rejection.

### 17.11 Possible Risks

**Unbounded append-only growth has no retention policy yet.** Named explicitly as Chapter 20's (or a future Chapter 18 operational concern), not resolved here — every concurrent room, over a long exam, could produce dozens of log rows; at "thousands of concurrent exams" scale (§1.5), this is a real, non-trivial storage question this chapter deliberately does not answer.

**The failure counter is process-local and lost on process restart.** A burst of write failures just before a crash or deploy leaves no durable record of how many failed — an acceptable trade-off given §2.7's non-blocking mandate (a durable failure-count write would itself risk the same blocking/starvation problem this chapter exists to avoid), but named honestly rather than silently assumed away.

**The Category 2 direct-call hook is, by design, the one place this chapter's "pure Event Bus subscriber" framing is not literally true.** This is intentional and traced to a real, frozen citation (§2.7), not an inconsistency — but it means a future reader skimming only §2.4 item 6's summary ("pure subscriber to the Event Bus") without reading this chapter's full §17.3 could form an incomplete picture; named explicitly here so that risk is at least visible.

### 17.12 Future Improvements

A retention/archival policy (§17.11's first risk) is the natural next addition once real volume data exists — this chapter's append-only, sequence-numbered shape would support it as a pure addition (a cleanup job reading old rows by `loggedAt`/`logSequence`) without changing the write path at all. Chapter 18's eventual aggregation layer could read directly from this chapter's table, or maintain independent lightweight counters fed by the same Event Bus subscription — either is compatible with this chapter's design as written, and this chapter deliberately does not pre-decide which Chapter 18 will choose.

### 17.13 Forward-Reference Index — Thorough Self-Review

Per the standing engineering rule, this review traced every claim against the exact frozen text it cites, rather than checking this chapter's prose against itself. Four real issues surfaced, all fixed directly above, none requiring modification of a frozen chapter's existing text:

| **The first draft assumed an Event-Bus-only subscription design would satisfy "records every decision made" in full**, without cross-checking every individual "logged via the Logging/Observability Layer" citation against Chapter 13's actual catalog contents | §17.3 — found the stale-turn discard (§2.7) has no corresponding Event Bus event in Chapter 13's catalog; added Category 2 as an explicit, named exception rather than silently missing this citation |
| **An early draft of the storage shape risked inventing a new payload structure for logged events**, rather than reusing what Chapter 13 already fixed per event type | §17.4 — added an explicit "no new payload shapes are invented here" rule, with a concrete example (`TIME_WARNING`'s unmodified shape) |
| **The non-blocking write mechanism's first draft did not address write-order vs. dispatch-order**, risking a reader assuming DB arrival order was trustworthy for reconstructing sequence | §17.5 — added the dispatch-time `logSequence` stamp, explicitly distinguished from and layered on top of Chapter 13's own dispatch-order guarantee, never touching it |

### 17.14 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

**Pass 1 — Adversarial.** Attempted rejection angle: "the Category 2 direct-call hook breaks the clean 'pure Event Bus subscriber' story §2.4 item 6 tells, so this chapter contradicts it." Rejected as a real defect: §2.4 item 6's own text says "the Event Bus **and** to every other module's decision points" — the direct-call hook is a strict reading of already-frozen text, not a departure from it, and §17.11's third risk names the potential-for-confusion honestly rather than hiding it. Second angle: "fire-and-forget writes mean this log can never be trusted as complete." Addressed: §2.7 already accepts this trade-off explicitly ("logged-best-effort... never a reason to stall the exam") — this chapter's failure-counting (§17.5) is what makes incompleteness *visible* rather than silent, which is the correct, already-mandated resolution, not a gap this chapter introduces.

**Pass 2 — Constitutional Compatibility.** Checked against all sixteen frozen chapters' exact text: §1.0/§1.14 step 8 (transcript parallel, unchanged — satisfied, §17.0/§17.3), §1.5 (module charter — satisfied throughout), §2.4 item 6 (subscriber positioning, no eleventh module — satisfied, §17.0), §2.7 (non-blocking, failure counting, stale-turn citation — satisfied and directly closed, §17.5), §11.3/§11.10(e) (vendor-latency permission, passive role — satisfied, §17.6), §13 (event catalog as authoritative, unfiltered — satisfied, §17.3/§17.4), §16 (storage-shape precedent reused, not redesigned — satisfied, §17.4). No contradiction found; zero amendment procedures invoked.

**Pass 3 — Implementation.** Mentally built end-to-end: an event dispatches from Chapter 13's per-room queue → the Logging Layer subscriber receives it in dispatch order → stamps the next `logSequence` value synchronously → fires an unawaited insert carrying `{roomId, logSequence, loggedAt, category:"event", eventType, payload}` → the dispatch path continues immediately, never waiting → on insert success, nothing further happens; on failure, the local counter increments and a best-effort line is emitted, still without blocking. In parallel, the stale-turn gate's own checkpoint calls the same write mechanism directly with `category:"stale_turn_discard"`, sequenced against the same per-room counter. No missing step found.

**Pass 4 — Five-Engineer Validation.** Given only Chapters 1–16 plus this one, five independent engineers would need to agree on: which two categories are logged and why the transcript is excluded (fixed exhaustively by §17.3, each citing exact frozen text), the storage shape (fixed by §17.4's concrete row shape, grounded in two named real precedents), the non-blocking mechanism including sequence-stamping (fixed precisely by §17.5's boxed rule and its explicit reasoning), and the vendor-latency boundary (fixed by §17.6's explicit "recorded, never measured here" framing). Convergence assessed as high.

**Pass 5 — Production-Readiness.** Read start-to-finish as new. Failure scenario: the decision-log table becomes temporarily unreachable — every write's `.catch()` fires, the local counter climbs, nothing else in the exam is affected, consistent with §2.7's guarantee. Concurrency scenario: many events dispatching in rapid succession within one room — each gets its own `logSequence` synchronously before any async write fires, so no two entries can share or skip a sequence value even under high dispatch rates; across rooms, each Room Runtime's Logging Layer instance holds its own independent counter, consistent with §2.6's isolation guarantee. Scale scenario: many concurrent rooms all logging simultaneously — named honestly in §17.11 as an unresolved retention/volume question, not silently assumed away.
