## Chapter 21 — Cost Optimization

### 21.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–20

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–20. This chapter closes hand-offs across eight chapters, each honored as an extension, never a redefinition:

- **§1.5's Cost Controller row (frozen)** — realized exactly as charted ("filters/batches so the LLM is invoked only when genuinely needed"); this chapter narrows *what* gets filtered/batched with precision, never redefines the one-line charter itself.
- **§2.4 (frozen)** — the Cost Controller's per-room-only classification, already corrected once by Chapter 2's own self-review after an earlier draft's process-wide shared-counter design was rejected, is honored exactly; this chapter introduces no cross-room in-process state for the Cost Controller itself.
- **§2.5 (frozen)** — the fail-closed Birth guarantee is reused exactly as fixed; this chapter adds a second legitimate trigger (budget exhaustion) alongside Chapter 20's instance-capacity trigger, never a new failure mode.
- **§2.7 (frozen)** — the closed, five-gate enumeration is unchanged; the Cost Controller is confirmed, not merely assumed, to never become a sixth.
- **§10.3/§10.7 (frozen)** — the Decision Engine's "modulating input" pattern (already established for time pressure) and the escalation-path auxiliary call (already named as a real, conditional, additional cost) are both reused exactly as designed; this chapter adds one more modulating input to an already-existing judgment, never a new sub-analyzer or a new call.
- **§11.6/§11.8 (frozen)** — the pipeline latency budget table and its "real revision" hand-off are honored; this chapter fixes the revision *methodology*, never restates or alters §11.6's own provisional figures.
- **§16.8/§16.9 (frozen)** — the excluded billing-tick parameter is supplied (§21.6) without altering Chapter 16's loading/consumption mechanism.
- **§17.5/§18.5 (frozen)** — the non-blocking write mechanism and the aggregator/alerting shape are both reused exactly, as a second sanctioned instance (§18.8's own explicit invitation), never redesigned.
- **§20.6/§20.10 (frozen)** — Chapter 20's admission-control failure mode is reused; its heartbeat/registry pattern is confirmed unnecessary for this chapter's own, simpler aggregation need.

### 21.1 Purpose

To design the Cost Controller's precise per-room responsibility and the platform's aggregate AI-vendor spend budget — formalizing an already-deployed, working real mechanism for the latter, and resolving a genuinely constrained first-principles design question for the former, while keeping the two, and the wholly separate student-facing credit system, cleanly distinct.

### 21.2 Design Rationale

**A chapter of two very different groundedness levels, named honestly from the start.** The aggregate vendor-spend budget (§21.5) has the strongest real-code precedent of any remaining chapter — `server.ts`'s preflight `get_today_api_usage()`/`GEMINI_DAILY_TOKEN_CAP` check and `record_api_usage` ledger write, plus D17's already-generalized-once `checkBudget80Percent()`, are a complete, working, already-deployed mechanism this chapter formalizes rather than invents. The per-room Cost Controller (§21.4) has zero real precedent — today's system calls Gemini Live's continuous audio stream directly, with no discrete "should this LLM call happen" cost decision anywhere — and must be designed within a space Chapters 1, 2, and 10 have already tightly constrained.

**The central constraint, stated once and governing every design choice below.** §2.7's five-gate enumeration is closed and does not name a Cost Controller gate; §2.4's own self-review already rejected a process-wide shared-counter design for exactly this module. Together these mean the Cost Controller cannot be a new gate and cannot hold cross-room state — its only remaining architectural shape is a per-room producer of advisory input to an *already-existing* gate, exactly the role §10.3 already built a slot for with the Timing Engine's own time-pressure modulation.

### 21.3 Two Distinct Cost Concerns, Never Conflated

> **The student-facing credit/minutes balance (`deduct_muendlich_minutes_dual`, real, atomic, per-minute, hard-stopping on insufficient balance) and the platform's own AI-vendor spend (Gemini/Deepgram/Gradium usage cost) are two wholly separate mechanisms. Chapter 21 owns only the second. The first is §1.0's "what stays" — real, working, and entirely unchanged by this chapter.**

**Why this distinction matters enough to state explicitly.** A student running out of credits and the platform approaching its own daily Gemini budget are both "cost" events but have nothing else in common — different triggers, different consequences (one ends a single room for one pair of students; the other refuses new rooms platform-wide), different owners (existing real code vs. this chapter), and different failure semantics (insufficient-balance is a per-room, expected, already-handled outcome; budget-exhaustion is a platform-wide, rare, alerting-worthy event). Conflating them, even in naming, risks a future implementation accidentally coupling two mechanisms that must remain independent.

### 21.4 The Per-Room Cost Controller: Modulating the Escalation-Path Auxiliary Call

> **The Cost Controller's entire per-room responsibility is modulating whether Chapter 10's escalation-path auxiliary confusion/topic-drift call fires — never the main turn-generation call, which remains unconditional. "Filters" means suppressing the auxiliary call under real, configured budget pressure; "batches" means coalescing multiple near-simultaneous ambiguous-escalation triggers into one auxiliary call rather than firing one per trigger.**

**Why the main turn-generation call is never in scope, structurally, not by policy choice.** §1.14 steps 3–5 gate the Examiner's actual response to the student on the Decision Engine's completeness determination alone — a live exam cannot decline to respond in order to save money without breaking the fundamental premise of a real-time conversation. §2.7's five gates do not include a cost gate on this path, and this chapter does not propose adding one; the main call is out of scope by construction, not by a policy this chapter merely chooses not to exercise.

**Why the escalation-path auxiliary call is the correct, and only, target.** §11.6 already independently named this call as "a real, conditional, additional cost... not folded into the headline total" — the one place in the entire architecture a genuinely discretionary, cost-bearing LLM call already exists. Chapter 10's own coordinator (§10.3) already treats time pressure as a modulating input to an existing judgment rather than a new sub-analyzer; the Cost Controller supplies a second, independent modulating input to the *same* escalation-path decision — reusing an already-designed slot rather than inventing a new decision point.

**Mechanically:** the Cost Controller, instantiated per-room (§2.4, unchanged), holds the room's own share of a configured cost-pressure threshold (Chapter 16 parameter) and a small debounce window. When the heuristic pass's confidence in a confusion/drift signal is genuinely ambiguous (the same "minority, ambiguous-escalation case" §11.6 already names as the auxiliary call's trigger condition), the Cost Controller's threshold — not a new one Chapter 10 must separately consult — determines whether that ambiguity is worth resolving via an auxiliary vendor call right now, or whether the debounce window should first check for other near-simultaneous ambiguous signals to potentially resolve together in one call. This is communicated to Chapter 10's coordinator via the same Event Bus channel every other producer already uses (§2.3) — the Cost Controller never calls a vendor adapter itself, and never bypasses the coordinator to reach the Prompt Builder or Gradium directly, honoring §2.7's adapter-binding exclusivity exactly as every other advisory producer already does.

**Real-world basis, honestly named as absent.** No real precedent exists for this exact mechanism (the auxiliary call itself is new, first designed in Chapter 10) — this section is genuinely first-principles, constrained tightly by frozen text rather than generalized from working code, the same honest category Chapters 12 and 15 were in.

### 21.5 The Aggregate Vendor-Spend Budget: Formalizing Real, Already-Deployed Infrastructure

> **Before Birth, the room's process instance checks aggregate platform-wide vendor usage against a configured daily budget cap. If exceeded, Birth fails closed — the same general mechanism §2.5 already fixes, with budget exhaustion as a second, legitimate trigger alongside Chapter 20's instance-capacity trigger. At session end, actual usage is recorded to a durable ledger, fire-and-forget, non-blocking. A dedicated aggregator instance (Chapter 18's shape, reused exactly) alerts at a configured threshold before the cap is reached.**

**This is not new design — it is a direct, careful formalization of real, working code.** `get_today_api_usage()`/`GEMINI_DAILY_TOKEN_CAP`'s preflight check, `record_api_usage`'s fire-and-forget usage recording, and `checkBudget80Percent()`'s threshold alert are adopted essentially as-is, with each piece attributed to the already-frozen mechanism it now formally belongs to: the preflight refusal is §2.5's fail-closed Birth guarantee (a second trigger, not a new one); the usage recording reuses Chapter 17's exact non-blocking write discipline (§17.5); the threshold alert is a second, explicitly-sanctioned instance of Chapter 18's aggregator/alerting shape (§18.4/§18.5, per §18.8's own invitation), never a redesign of it.

**Why no new coordination mechanism (heartbeat or otherwise) is needed here, unlike Chapter 20.** Chapter 20's problem — "which instance currently owns this room" — has no natural single source of truth without an explicit registry, because room ownership is a discrete, per-room fact. This chapter's problem — "what is today's aggregate usage total" — is a running sum any instance can compute directly from the durable usage ledger via an ordinary SQL aggregate query, with no liveness/staleness question involved at all. Confirming this explicitly (rather than reflexively reusing Chapter 20's registry pattern out of habit) is this chapter's own contribution to closing §2.9's "evaluate explicitly" spirit a second time.

**Attribution of Birth failure, made precise.** A room refusing to start because of instance capacity (Chapter 20) and a room refusing to start because of budget exhaustion (this chapter) are both "Birth failed closed" from a client's perspective, but the two conditions are checked independently and can be distinguished in the failure's own reported reason — reusing the real system's own already-distinct `"budget_exceeded_preflight"` reason string as the precedent for this distinction, never merging the two into one undifferentiated "unavailable" outcome.

### 21.6 Billing-Tick Configuration Values

**Closes §16.8/§16.9's explicit exclusion with the real, already-tuned value.**

| Parameter | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Credit-deduction tick interval | 60,000 ms | **Real** — `CREDIT_TICK_MS`, already governing the existing, unchanged `deduct_muendlich_minutes_dual` mechanism (§21.3) |
| Aggregate vendor-spend alert threshold | 80% of daily cap | **Real** — `BUDGET_ALERT_FRACTION`, already governing `checkBudget80Percent()` |

Both values live in the Configuration System (Chapter 16), loaded and consumed exactly per its already-fixed mechanism — this chapter supplies values, never a second loading or consumption path.

### 21.7 Pipeline Latency Budget: Revision Methodology, Not Fabricated Numbers

> **§11.6's provisional latency targets are revised, when real Deepgram/Gradium integration data eventually exists, as a pure Configuration System value change (Chapter 16) — never a change to Chapter 11's Timing Engine mechanism, and never a change that lets the Timing Engine begin consuming vendor latency as a timing-decision input.**

**Honestly, no revision happens in this chapter.** Neither Deepgram nor Gradium is wired into the real system today — the real relay uses Gemini Live's own built-in audio-in/audio-out, with no separate STT/TTS vendor calls to measure. Proposing revised numbers here would be exactly the kind of fabricated precision this document's standing honesty practice (§11.12, §16.13, §20.8, and others) already rejects. This section fixes the *process* — real measurements, once they exist (via Chapter 18's own latency-measurement mechanism, §18.3), feed a Chapter 16 value update, reviewed against real cost data this chapter is positioned to evaluate (is a faster, more expensive Gradium tier worth it against the vendor-spend budget in §21.5?) — without ever touching §11.3's vendor-agnosticism guarantee, which governs the Timing Engine's own computation, not this chapter's cost-driven value-tuning decision.

### 21.8 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapters 1, 2, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18, and 20

Stated directly, matching the pattern §18.8, §19.13, and §20.10 already establish: **Chapter 21 (this chapter)** owns the Cost Controller's escalation-call-modulation responsibility (§21.4), the aggregate vendor-spend budget mechanism (§21.5), billing-tick values (§21.6), and the latency-budget revision methodology (§21.7). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapter 1**'s student-facing credit/minutes system — entirely unchanged (§21.3).
- **Chapter 2**'s Room Runtime lifecycle, Birth fail-closed mechanics, and the closed five-gate enumeration — reused exactly; this chapter adds a trigger and a modulating input, never a new gate or failure mode.
- **Chapter 10**'s escalation-path auxiliary call, its firing condition, and its consumption model — unchanged; this chapter supplies one more modulating input to an already-designed decision point.
- **Chapter 11**'s Timing Engine mechanism and vendor-agnosticism guarantee — untouched; §21.7 fixes only how its *target table's values* eventually get revised, never how the Timing Engine itself computes anything.
- **Chapter 16**'s Configuration System mechanism — this chapter supplies values and a revision trigger; Chapter 16 governs storage/loading unchanged.
- **Chapter 17**'s non-blocking write mechanism — reused exactly for usage-ledger recording.
- **Chapter 18**'s aggregator/alerting mechanism — reused exactly, as its own explicitly-sanctioned second instance, never redesigned.
- **Chapter 20**'s admission-control failure mode and heartbeat/registry pattern — the former reused as a second trigger; the latter explicitly evaluated and confirmed unnecessary for this chapter's simpler aggregation need, not silently ignored.

### 21.9 Advantages

The aggregate vendor-spend budget (§21.5) is the most direct, complete formalization of real, already-deployed infrastructure of any chapter — three real mechanisms (preflight check, usage ledger, threshold alert) adopted with precise attribution to the already-frozen mechanisms they now belong to, rather than redesigned. The per-room Cost Controller (§21.4) resolves a genuinely constrained design question — where §2.7's closed gate list and §2.4's own rejected-shared-counter precedent together leave exactly one architecturally coherent answer — by reusing Chapter 10's already-built modulating-input slot rather than inventing new machinery. The explicit "no heartbeat needed here" confirmation (§21.5) demonstrates this document's §2.9 evaluation discipline is applied freshly each time a coordination question arises, not reflexively pattern-matched from the most recent chapter. The latency-budget revision methodology (§21.7) closes a three-chapter-old hand-off honestly, refusing to fabricate numbers this document has no basis to assert.

### 21.10 Alternatives Considered

**(a) Give the Cost Controller its own gate on the main turn-generation path, skipping a response under severe budget pressure.** Rejected outright (§21.4): would contradict §2.7's closed five-gate enumeration and break the fundamental real-time-conversation premise this entire document is built on — a live exam cannot go silent to save money.

**(b) A process-wide, shared in-memory budget counter for simplicity.** Rejected (§21.5, and previously by Chapter 2's own self-review): directly contradicts §1.5's per-room scoping rule and §2.6's isolation guarantee; the durable-ledger-plus-aggregate-query approach achieves the same outcome without any shared mutable state.

**(c) Reuse Chapter 20's heartbeat/registry mechanism for the aggregate budget, for consistency with the most recent scaling chapter.** Rejected (§21.5): the two problems are genuinely different (discrete room ownership vs. a running numeric total) and a durable SQL aggregate already solves this chapter's need with strictly less machinery — reusing a heavier mechanism than necessary "for consistency" would be exactly the kind of unjustified complexity this document's standing discipline rejects elsewhere.

**(d) Fabricate revised pipeline-latency numbers now, based on estimated Deepgram/Gradium pricing tiers.** Rejected (§21.7): would present unearned precision as if it were measured fact, violating this document's established honesty practice for exactly this kind of provisional-value situation.

### 21.11 Recommended Approach

The escalation-call-modulation design (§21.4) per option (a)'s rejection; the durable-ledger aggregate budget mechanism (§21.5) per options (b) and (c)'s rejections, formalizing real production code with precise attribution to already-frozen mechanisms; real billing-tick values (§21.6); and an honest, process-only latency-budget revision methodology (§21.7) per option (d)'s rejection.

### 21.12 Possible Risks

**The escalation-call debounce window (§21.4) trades a small amount of response latency for reduced auxiliary-call cost — a real trade-off, not free.** Named honestly: coalescing near-simultaneous ambiguous signals into one call necessarily delays acting on the first of them slightly; the exact window duration (a Chapter 16 parameter) is a genuine tuning question with no real production data behind it yet, the same honest limitation this document has now named for several first-principles mechanisms in a row.

**The aggregate vendor-spend budget is a single, platform-wide daily figure — it says nothing about per-room or per-time-of-day distribution.** A legitimate burst of concurrent exams late in a UTC day could exhaust the daily cap and refuse new rooms even though average daily usage is well within budget — a real, already-present limitation in the real system this chapter formalizes rather than newly introduces, named here rather than silently inherited without comment.

**The latency-budget revision methodology (§21.7) has never actually been exercised**, since no real Deepgram/Gradium integration data exists to revise against — the process is sound, but, like several of this chapter's siblings, untested against a real instance of the situation it's designed for.

### 21.13 Future Improvements

Once real Deepgram/Gradium integration exists, §21.7's revision methodology becomes immediately exercisable without any change to this chapter's own design. A more granular, time-of-day-aware or per-instance-share budget (addressing §21.12's second risk) is a natural refinement of the single daily figure, achievable as a pure Chapter 16 value/shape change once real usage-distribution data justifies the added complexity — this chapter's aggregate-query mechanism would support a finer-grained window without redesign. The debounce window's real duration (§21.12's first risk) is the clearest candidate for tuning once real auxiliary-call volume data exists.

### 21.15 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

**Pass 1 — Adversarial.** Attempted rejection angle: "modulating the escalation-path auxiliary call based on cost pressure risks degrading exam quality (missed genuine confusion) to save money — isn't this a Behavior Specification concern this chapter has no business deciding?" ## Chapter 22 — Vendor Independence

### 22.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–21

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–21. This chapter closes citations across six chapters, each honored as an extension, never a redefinition:

- **§1.5/§2.8 (frozen)** — "every vendor swappable behind a provider-adapter layer" and "one pattern, four boundaries" are realized exactly as already committed; this chapter gives the AI-vendor instance of that already-general pattern its concrete shape, never redefines the pattern itself.
- **§2.7's adapter-binding exclusivity (frozen, the most structurally significant citation this chapter closes)** — "the Gemini Flash adapter binding... held exclusively by the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer-to-Gradium pathway... [the Decision Engine's auxiliary call is] a separate, distinctly-bound capability" is realized precisely (§22.4) as a wiring-level guarantee, not merely restated as a rule.
- **§3.8 (frozen)** — `STT_FAILURE`/`LLM_FAILURE`/`TTS_FAILURE` classification is reused exactly; this chapter fixes only what raw signal each adapter surfaces, never how that signal is classified or handled.
- **§6.5/§6.7 (frozen)** — each vendor's one-line contract and boundary-contract citation are given interface shape, never redefined.
- **§15.6 (frozen)** — the voice-identity lookup table, already named as living "inside the TTS provider adapter (Chapter 22)," is supplied exactly there (§22.5).
- **§16.6 (frozen)** — the standing "resolved once, held for the consuming instance's lifetime" pattern is reused directly for vendor selection (§22.6), not reinvented.

### 22.1 Purpose

To give the provider-adapter layer — referenced by name as "fully designed Chapter 22" since Chapter 1's own front matter, and cited by six later chapters as the boundary where vendor-specific behavior stops — its concrete interface shape, closing every named dependency precisely.

### 22.2 Design Rationale

**A chapter formalizing a target architecture, not generalizing an already-compliant real system — an honest distinction from most chapters since 16.** `geminiLive.ts`'s `MuendlichLiveCallbacks` interface is real, working, streaming-callback code — but it wraps one combined Gemini Live session doing STT+LLM+TTS together, not the three-stage decomposed pipeline Chapter 1 designed. Its *style* (callbacks for streaming interaction) is directly reusable evidence; its *shape* (one interface, three roles combined) is exactly what this chapter's decomposition must not inherit. The real code's direct `@google/genai` import — with zero adapter abstraction — is a genuine, named gap between today's system and this document's target, not a defect this chapter pretends doesn't exist.

**§2.7's adapter-binding exclusivity is the chapter's central, non-negotiable constraint.** Every design choice below is checked against "does this let two logically-separate call sites ever reach through the same binding," and rejected if so — this is what elevates §2.7's rule from a convention a future implementer could accidentally violate to a structural impossibility.

### 22.3 Three Adapter Interfaces, Shaped by Contract

**Not a uniform template — each interface's shape follows directly from §6.7's already-fixed contract for that vendor.**

> **STT adapter (Deepgram): streaming, callback-based.** Audio chunks in; interim and final transcript events out, plus a connection-health signal. Modeled directly on `MuendlichLiveCallbacks`'s proven streaming-callback style — the one piece of real code this chapter generalizes stylistically, not structurally.

> **LLM adapter (Gemini Flash): simple async request/response.** One context payload in; one complete text response out. No session object, no adapter-held state between calls — a direct, literal realization of §6.7's "no memory between calls," which this chapter satisfies by construction (there is no field in the adapter for memory to occupy), not by convention.

> **TTS adapter (Gradium): streaming output.** Approved text plus the §15.6 instruction bundle (`voiceGenderIdentity`, pacing/emphasis/pause cues) in; a stream of audio chunks out, to minimize time-to-first-byte against §1.10's latency budget, plus a connection-health signal matching the STT adapter's own shape.

**Each interface's inputs and outputs are exactly what §6.7's table already promises — nothing added, nothing withheld.** Deepgram's adapter has no completeness-judgment output slot (that stays the Decision Engine's, per §6.5); Gemini Flash's adapter has no state-reference or instruction-shaped output slot the Safety/Validation Layer wouldn't already be inspecting for; Gradium's adapter has no "creative interpretation" input — only the cues already given to it.

### 22.4 Two Distinct LLM Adapter Bindings: §2.7's Exclusivity, Realized at the Wiring Level

> **Two independent instances of the LLM adapter interface exist per room, never one shared instance. The first is held exclusively by the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer-to-Gradium pathway, for main turn generation. The second is held exclusively by the Decision Engine, for its own private auxiliary confusion/topic-drift analysis (§10.7). Neither module holds, imports, or can reach the other's binding.**

**Why two instances, not one instance with two callers.** §2.7 does not say "the LLM adapter is used carefully by two callers" — it says the main-generation binding is held *exclusively* by one pathway, and the Decision Engine's capability is *separately and distinctly bound*. A single shared adapter instance, even with disciplined calling conventions, would leave open the possibility of a future code change accidentally letting the Decision Engine's output reach Gradium, or the main pathway's output leak into the Decision Engine's advisory analysis — exactly the kind of convention-only guarantee this document has consistently rejected in favor of structural ones (e.g., §2.7's own "no shorter wiring path" framing for every other gate). Two separately-constructed instances make this impossible at the composition-root level (§2.3), not merely disallowed by discipline.

**Both instances may select the same concrete vendor (Gemini Flash) without contradiction.** §22.6's vendor-selection mechanism is independent of binding count — two adapter *instances* of the same interface, both configured to call Gemini Flash, remain two distinct bindings; "distinctly-bound" (§2.7's own phrase) describes wiring-level separation, not a requirement that the two calls reach different vendors.

### 22.5 The Voice-Identity Mapping: Closing §15.6's Named Boundary

> **The TTS adapter owns one lookup table: abstract `voiceGenderIdentity` value (Chapter 15's persona-catalog field) → concrete Gradium voice identifier. This is the entire mechanism by which Chapter 15's persona snapshot becomes an actual vendor API parameter — no other translation step exists.**

**Exactly where Chapter 15 already said it would live.** §15.6: "a lookup table inside the TTS provider adapter (Chapter 22)" — this chapter supplies that table, nothing more. The table's *values* (which Gradium voice ID corresponds to which abstract identity) are Configuration System data (Chapter 16), following the identical "Chapter 22 fixes the mechanism, Chapter 16 fixes the values" split already used throughout this document for every other adapter-adjacent parameter. Pacing/emphasis/pause cues pass through to Gradium's own API parameters directly, requiring no lookup — only the voice identity needs translation, since it alone is expressed as this architecture's own abstract vocabulary rather than a value Gradium's API already understands natively.

### 22.6 Vendor Selection: A Configuration System Choice, Resolved Once Per Process

> **Which concrete adapter implementation backs each interface (which STT vendor, which LLM vendor, which TTS vendor) is a Configuration System parameter, read once at process start — reusing Chapter 16's own standing "resolved once, held for the lifetime of the consuming scope" pattern (§16.6), not a new selection mechanism.**

**This is what makes "vendor independence" a code-level property, not an aspiration.** Every module that needs an adapter depends only on the interface type (§22.3) — never a concrete vendor class, never a direct SDK import. Swapping Deepgram for a different STT vendor is: write a new class implementing the same STT adapter interface, change one Configuration System value, redeploy. No Room Runtime wiring, no module's own code, changes — directly realizing §1.15's "vendor independence (Chapter 22)" and §1.17's "all vendor calls through thin provider adapters" as literal, checkable code properties rather than restated intentions.

**Confirmed: this is swappability, not simultaneous multi-provider redundancy.** No frozen chapter requires two STT vendors to be live at once for the same room, and this chapter does not design that capability — named explicitly as a Future Improvement (§22.14), not silently assumed out of scope by omission.

### 22.7 Failure Surfacing, Not Failure Handling

> **Each adapter surfaces raw vendor-level signals through its own interface — a connection-drop or error callback for the streaming (STT/TTS) adapters, a rejected promise for the LLM adapter — and does nothing more. Chapter 3's already-fixed `STT_FAILURE`/`LLM_FAILURE`/`TTS_FAILURE` classification, timing, and handling (§3.8) are what interpret these raw signals; this chapter never re-decides what counts as a failure.**

**Why the boundary is drawn exactly here.** An adapter is, by this chapter's own design (§22.2), a thin translation layer with no decision-making role — deciding *whether* a dropped connection constitutes `STT_FAILURE` (versus, say, a benign reconnect within some grace window) is exactly the kind of judgment §3.8 already owns in full. The adapter's contract is symmetric with every other vendor contract this document fixes: report what happened, decide nothing.

### 22.8 The Real-Code Gap, Named Honestly

**Today's real system has no adapter layer at all — this is disclosed explicitly, not smoothed over.** `geminiLive.ts` imports `@google/genai` directly; there is no Deepgram or Gradium integration anywhere in the real codebase, because the real system uses one combined Gemini Live session rather than the three-stage decomposed pipeline this document's Chapter 3 already designed. This chapter's adapter interfaces describe the target this decomposition requires; building them is real, unstarted implementation work, not a refactor of already-compliant code. Named here in the same honest spirit as Chapter 19's "AI plays both roles" disclosure and Chapter 20's "no real precedent" framing — this document does not claim more grounding than actually exists.

### 22.9 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapters 1, 2, 3, 6, 15, 16, and 23

Stated directly, matching the pattern §20.10 and §21.8 already establish: **Chapter 22 (this chapter)** owns the three adapter interface shapes (§22.3), the two-binding LLM realization of §2.7's exclusivity (§22.4), the voice-identity lookup table (§22.5), vendor-selection mechanics (§22.6), and failure-signal surfacing (§22.7). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapter 1**'s fixed technology stack and vendor-independence claims — this chapter is their literal realization, never a redefinition of which vendors are named or why the guarantee exists.
- **Chapter 2**'s adapter-binding exclusivity rule and composition-root discipline — reused exactly; this chapter's two-instance design is how §2.7's rule becomes true at the wiring level, not a modification of the rule.
- **Chapter 3**'s pipeline mechanics and vendor-failure classification — entirely unchanged; adapters surface signals Chapter 3 already knows how to interpret.
- **Chapter 6**'s vendor contracts — given interface shape, never redefined.
- **Chapter 15**'s persona catalog, cue-bundle shape, and Voice Behaviour Layer relay mechanism — unchanged; this chapter owns only the one lookup table §15.6 already named as living here.
- **Chapter 16**'s Configuration System mechanism — this chapter supplies vendor-selection and voice-mapping parameters; Chapter 16 governs their storage/loading unchanged.
- **Chapter 23**'s (not yet written) security design — whether an adapter implementation's own credential handling (API keys, connection security) needs security-specific treatment is named as an open question for Chapter 23, not resolved here.

### 22.10 Advantages

Closes §2.7's structurally most significant remaining citation with a genuine wiring-level guarantee (two separate instances) rather than a restated convention. Gives every one of Chapter 6's already-precise vendor contracts a concrete interface shape without redefining any of them. Realizes §15.6's own named boundary (the voice-identity lookup table) exactly where that chapter said it would live, with no ambiguity about which chapter owns what. Reuses Chapter 16's already-proven "resolve once, hold for the scope's lifetime" pattern for vendor selection rather than inventing a fourth variant of the same idea. Names the real gap between today's combined-session system and this document's decomposed target honestly, consistent with this document's established practice for every chapter in this position.

### 22.11 Alternatives Considered

**(a) One shared LLM adapter instance, with calling discipline enforced by code review/convention rather than by structure.** Rejected (§22.4): exactly the kind of convention-only guarantee this document has consistently rejected elsewhere; a future code change could silently violate §2.7's exclusivity with no compiler or wiring-level barrier to catch it.

**(b) A single, uniform adapter interface template applied identically to all three vendor roles.** Rejected (§22.3): would force Gemini Flash's stateless request/response contract into an unnecessary streaming-callback shape (or vice versa for Deepgram/Gradium), adding complexity neither contract requires.

**(c) Voice-identity mapping performed upstream, in the Context/Prompt Builder or Room Runtime, rather than inside the TTS adapter.** Rejected (§22.5): would contradict §15.6's own explicit placement of this mechanism, and would leak vendor-specific voice-ID knowledge outside the one place §2.8's adapter boundary says vendor-specific detail belongs.

**(d) Design true multi-provider redundancy (two STT vendors live simultaneously, failover between them) as part of this chapter's core scope.** Rejected (§22.6): no frozen chapter names this requirement; "vendor independence" as already used throughout this document means swappability, not simultaneous plurality — named as a future capability, not silently assumed in scope.

**(e) Let each adapter attempt its own failure classification (e.g., an adapter deciding internally whether a dropped connection is retryable) rather than only surfacing raw signals.** Rejected (§22.7): would duplicate judgment Chapter 3 already owns in full, risking two independently-evolving failure-classification schemes for the same underlying events.

### 22.12 Recommended Approach

Three contract-shaped adapter interfaces (§22.3) per option (b)'s rejection; two independently-instantiated LLM bindings (§22.4) per option (a)'s rejection; the voice-identity lookup table placed inside the TTS adapter (§22.5) per option (c)'s rejection; Configuration-System-driven vendor selection reusing Chapter 16's existing pattern (§22.6); swappability-only scope, with multi-provider redundancy named as future work (§22.14) per option (d)'s rejection; and pure signal-surfacing with all classification left to Chapter 3 (§22.7) per option (e)'s rejection.

### 22.13 Possible Risks

**This chapter's design is entirely unbuilt and unverified against any real vendor integration beyond Gemini Live's combined session.** Named honestly per §22.8 — Deepgram and Gradium have never been called by this codebase in any form; the adapter shapes proposed here are reasoned from each vendor's publicly-contracted behavior (per §6.5's own framing) and this document's own constraints, not validated against a real integration attempt.

**Two separate LLM adapter instances, both potentially configured to the same vendor, could double real vendor-side rate limits or connection overhead compared to a shared-instance design.** A real, named cost/complexity trade-off for the correctness guarantee §22.4 provides — not free, and not claimed to be.

**The voice-identity lookup table (§22.5) has no real entries yet, since Chapter 15's own catalog currently ships with exactly one persona.** A one-entry lookup table is trivially valid but does not exercise the mapping mechanism's real behavior under multiple entries — the same "untested until a second catalog entry exists" limitation Chapter 15 §15.11 already named for the catalog itself, inherited here rather than newly introduced.

### 22.14 Future Improvements

True multi-provider redundancy — two STT (or LLM, or TTS) vendors live simultaneously with automatic failover between them — is the clearest candidate for future work this chapter explicitly declines to design (§22.6, §22.11(d)). It would build directly on this chapter's interface-based design (a redundancy-aware composite adapter implementing the same interface, invisible to every consuming module) without requiring any change to §22.3's contracts or §22.4's binding-count guarantee. Once real vendor integration exists, the adapter shapes proposed here should be validated against real Deepgram/Gradium behavior and revised if real API contracts diverge from what §6.5's already-fixed responsibilities assumed.

### 22.15 Forward-Reference Index — Thorough Self-Review

Per the standing engineering rule, this review traced every claim against the exact frozen text it cites, rather than checking this chapter's prose against itself. Four real issues surfaced, all fixed directly above:

| **The STT/TTS adapter interfaces' first draft did not explicitly confirm they add no output slot beyond what §6.7's contract table already promises**, risking scope creep (e.g., an adapter that also judges completeness) | §22.3 — added an explicit "nothing added, nothing withheld" confirmation against each contract row |

### 22.16 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

**Pass 1 — Adversarial.** Attempted rejection angle: "two separate LLM adapter instances add real operational cost (§22.13) for a guarantee that could be achieved just as safely with one instance and a runtime assertion checking the caller's identity." Addressed: a runtime assertion is itself a convention-enforced-at-runtime check, not a structural one — it could be bypassed by any code path that doesn't happen to trigger the assertion (e.g., a new caller added without updating the check), whereas two physically separate instances make the violation impossible to construct in the first place, regardless of what new code is later added — a stronger guarantee for a real, disclosed, bounded cost, not a redundant one. Second angle: "the voice-identity lookup table is trivial for a one-entry catalog — why does it need its own named section?" Addressed: because §15.6 explicitly named this exact mechanism and its exact location, closing that specific citation requires a specific, checkable answer regardless of how many entries currently populate it — the section's value is in closing the citation precisely, not in its current operational complexity.

**Pass 2 — Constitutional Compatibility.** Checked against all twenty-one frozen chapters' exact text: §1.5/§1.15/§1.17 (vendor independence claims — satisfied and literally realized, §22.6), §2.3/§2.7/§2.8 (composition root, binding exclusivity, adapter boundaries — satisfied and structurally realized, §22.4/§22.9), §3.8 (failure classification — satisfied, §22.7), §6.5/§6.7 (vendor contracts — satisfied, §22.3), §15.6 (voice-identity lookup table placement — satisfied precisely, §22.5), §16.6 (resolve-once pattern — satisfied, §22.6). No contradiction found; zero amendment procedures invoked.

**Pass 3 — Implementation.** Mentally built end-to-end: at process start, Chapter 16's config resolves which concrete vendor backs each of the three adapter interfaces → at Birth, the Room Runtime constructs two separate LLM adapter instances, handing one exclusively to the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer-to-Gradium pathway and the other exclusively to the Decision Engine → during a turn, the main pathway's LLM call, the TTS adapter's voice-identity lookup, and (when triggered) the Decision Engine's private auxiliary call all proceed through their own, non-overlapping bindings → any adapter-level failure (a dropped Deepgram connection, a rejected Gemini Flash promise, a Gradium stream error) surfaces through the adapter's own interface and is classified by Chapter 3's already-fixed logic, never by the adapter itself. No missing step found; no module invented beyond the already-counted ten, and no new per-room module added for the adapter layer itself (adapters are held *by* modules, not modules in their own right).

**Pass 4 — Five-Engineer Validation.** Given only Chapters 1–21 plus this one, five independent engineers would need to agree on: each adapter's exact interface shape (fixed precisely by §22.3's boxed contracts, each traceable to §6.7's own table), why two LLM bindings exist and what "distinctly-bound" does and doesn't require (fixed by §22.4's explicit clarification), where voice-identity mapping lives (fixed unambiguously by §22.5, citing §15.6's own placement), and how vendor selection works (fixed by §22.6's direct reuse of §16.6). Convergence assessed as high.

**Pass 5 — Production-Readiness.** Read start-to-finish as new. Failure scenario: a vendor connection drops mid-turn — the relevant adapter's error/close signal fires, Chapter 3's already-fixed classification takes over; this chapter's own role ends at the signal surfacing. Concurrency scenario: the main-pathway and Decision-Engine LLM calls potentially in flight simultaneously (the main call generating a turn while an auxiliary confusion-check runs) — since they are structurally separate instances (§22.4), no shared state or binding could ever create a race between them; each proceeds independently. Scale scenario: vendor-side rate limits under high concurrent-room load — named honestly in §22.13 as a real, disclosed cost of the two-binding design, not silently assumed absorbable.

## Chapter 23 — Security

### 23.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–22

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–22. This chapter closes citations across nine chapters, each honored as an extension, never a redefinition:

- **§1.5's Safety/Validation Layer row (frozen)** — realized exactly as charted; this chapter narrows the mechanism precisely, never redefines the one-line charter.
- **§1.8 (frozen)** — the bounded fallback path is realized exactly (§23.5); Chapter 16's already-supplied provisional retry count (2) is reused, not re-derived.
- **§1.13 (frozen)** — every named role/content rule and the metadata-leakage concern are given a concrete check category (§23.4), never redefined.
- **§7.5/§7.8 (frozen)** — the structural/cross-cutting mapping framework is extended, not altered, with one new, explicitly-justified third kind of category (§23.6); the metadata-leakage prevention/detection split Chapter 7 already drew is confirmed exactly.
- **§2.7 (frozen)** — the Safety Layer's position as gate 4 and its participation in the shared, single-LLM-binding pathway are both honored precisely; this chapter adds no new binding and no new gate.
- **§6.5/§6.7 (frozen)** — Gemini Flash's contract is given its literal enforcement mechanism (§23.4), never redefined.
- **§10.4/§16.8 (frozen)** — Tier 1's existing Safety-rejection trigger is confirmed, not altered; Chapter 16's provisional value is consumed as-is.
- **§1.3/§12.8 (frozen)** — personality-agnosticism of safety rules is confirmed (§23.4), never newly argued as a design choice this chapter is free to reconsider.
- **§11.6 (frozen)** — the ~30–50ms, no-vendor-call latency assumption is the chapter's central, decisive design constraint (§23.2/§23.3), honored precisely rather than merely cited.
- **§22.9 (frozen, Chapter 22's own hand-off)** — adapter credential handling is addressed (§23.7) without redesigning Chapter 22's own adapter interfaces.

### 23.1 Purpose

To give the Safety/Validation Layer — already fully charted by Chapter 1, already positioned as the fourth of Chapter 2's five gates, and cited by nine other chapters — its complete, concrete mechanism: what it checks, how it checks it within an already-frozen latency budget, and what happens when a check fails.

### 23.2 Design Rationale

**The chapter's central design question was already answered by a citation no prior chapter's own prose stated as a constraint.** §11.6's pipeline latency table — written for an entirely different purpose, closing Chapter 3's reserved latency-budget gap — already fixes the Safety/Validation Layer's check at "~30–50 ms... no vendor call assumed." Read naively, "checks LLM output against role/content boundaries" (§1.5) could easily be designed as a second LLM call (a "judge" model evaluating the first model's output) — a common, reasonable-sounding pattern in adjacent systems. §11.6 makes that design impossible without contradicting already-frozen text: a real vendor round-trip costs 300+ms by that same table's own Gemini Flash row, not 30–50ms. This was found by tracing §11.6's exact wording against what this chapter's charter might naively require, not by any chapter explicitly warning against an LLM-judge design — exactly the kind of cross-reference discovery this document's standing practice exists to surface.

**Zero real precedent — first-principles, the same category as Chapters 12, 15, 20, and 22.** The real system inspects nothing; Gemini Live's raw output goes directly to synthesis and the client. Every design choice below is derived from frozen constraints, not generalized from working code.

**The chapter's two halves — detection and recovery — are designed together, not sequentially, because the first's honest limitations directly justify the second's existence.** A fast, non-LLM text check cannot achieve semantic-level accuracy; this is not a flaw to engineer away, but the reason §1.8's retry-and-fallback path exists at all.

### 23.3 The Inspection Mechanism: Fast, Deterministic Text Analysis — Never an LLM Judge Call

> **The Safety/Validation Layer's check is pure, non-vendor text analysis over two already-available inputs — the generated text and the context payload that produced it — completing within §11.6's ~30–50ms budget. It never invokes an LLM, never holds an adapter binding of its own, and never adds a vendor round-trip to any turn.**

**Why this is a hard boundary, not a starting preference this chapter might relax under pressure.** Any design requiring a vendor call here would silently blow through §11.6's already-frozen total (~630–880ms) by roughly half again — a genuine cross-chapter contradiction, not a tuning question. This chapter treats §11.6's figures as a real constraint to design within, exactly as Chapter 21 treated them as a real constraint to eventually revise (never redefine) once real data exists.

**The Safety Layer holds no LLM adapter binding at all — it inspects text already produced by the pathway's one shared binding (§2.7), never calls a vendor itself.** This is consistent with, and does not extend, Chapter 22's two-binding design (§22.4): the main pathway's single LLM binding belongs to the Prompt-Builder-to-Safety-Layer-to-Gradium pathway as a whole; the Safety Layer's role within that pathway is inspection of already-generated output, not a second generation act requiring its own binding.

### 23.4 Two Check Categories: Metadata-Leakage (Mechanical) and Role/Content Violations (Heuristic, Honestly Imperfect)

> **Metadata-leakage detection: mechanical string/pattern-containment checks comparing the generated text against the context payload's own internal field representations — the exact enforcement backstop §7.8 already anticipated for the structural leakage-prevention rule Chapter 7 put in place. Role/content-violation detection: a curated pattern/keyword rule set targeting the specific behaviors §1.13 names (grammar-correction phrasing, explicit vocabulary-definition constructs, coaching language, decision-resembling output per §6.5's contract) — an honest heuristic, not a semantic guarantee.**

**Metadata-leakage is the more mechanically tractable of the two, and is treated accordingly.** Because Chapter 7 §7.8 already structures internal signals (student-progress, silence/confusion status, fairness data) as demarcated fields the model has "no natural reason to describe," a leak is, in practice, the model reproducing something close to that field's own internal representation (a raw number, a field name, a characteristic phrase like "confidence score") — checkable via direct containment/similarity comparison against the exact context payload values this turn's generation call received, no semantic judgment required.

**Role/content violations are named honestly as the harder, imperfect half.** "No grammar correction," "no coaching," "no hidden hints," "no revealing expected answers" are semantic judgments a keyword/pattern rule set can only approximate — a curated set can catch clear textual markers (e.g., explicit correction phrasing, direct answer-revealing constructs) but cannot reliably catch a subtly-phrased violation a human reviewer would recognize instantly. This limitation is not hidden in Possible Risks as an afterthought — it is the direct justification for §23.5's retry-and-fallback design existing at all, stated here where the limitation is introduced.

**Personality-agnosticism, confirmed exactly as already fixed, not re-argued.** §1.3/§12.8 already establish that personality changes *how* something is phrased, never *whether* Safety/Fairness/Ownership rules apply — this chapter's checks read no persona-specific field and apply identically regardless of which Chapter 15 persona is configured for the room. No exception path exists for any personality value.

### 23.5 The Bounded Retry Path: Tightened Constraints, Same Pathway, No New Binding

> **On rejection, the Prompt Builder is re-invoked with the original task instruction plus one additional, specific corrective instruction naming the detected violation category — using the same pathway's existing LLM adapter binding (§2.7, §22.4), never a new instance. This may happen up to a configured maximum (Chapter 16: 2, provisional, already supplied). Exhausting the maximum resolves deterministically to §23.6's fallback utterance — never a third retry, never silence.**

**Why reusing the existing binding, not a new one, is correct — not merely convenient.** A retry is still generation within the same pathway §2.7 already scopes to one binding; it is not a second, parallel capability the way the Decision Engine's auxiliary call is (§22.4). Treating a retry as requiring its own binding would misclassify it as a different kind of call than it structurally is.

**"Tightened constraints," made concrete.** The corrective instruction names the specific violated category (e.g., "avoid providing direct corrections to the student's language") rather than a generic "try again" — giving the regeneration attempt a genuine, targeted chance to pass, not merely repeating the same generation under identical constraints and hoping for a different heuristic outcome.

**This closes §10.4's existing Tier 1 trigger, never opens a new one.** A rejection — whether resolved by a successful retry or by falling through to the fallback utterance — is already named in §1.8's own reclaim-trigger list ("an AI-generated response failing the Safety/Validation Layer's check"); this chapter supplies the mechanism producing that already-anticipated trigger, never a new ownership-reclaim path.

### 23.6 The Fallback Utterance: A Seventh Prompt Library Category, a Justified Extension of §7.5

**A real, honestly-found gap: Chapter 7's own six Prompt Library categories (Greeting, Encouragement, Transition, Follow-up, Silence-recovery, Closing) have no home for §1.8's own required "neutral pre-approved... utterance."** Neither of Chapter 7's two defined mapping kinds fits: not "structural" (tied to one specific stage's default turn — a fallback can be needed at any stage) and not "cross-cutting" as Chapter 7 defined it (triggered by a Decision Engine condition — a fallback is triggered by retry-exhaustion, a Safety Layer outcome, not a Decision Engine trigger).

> **A new, seventh Prompt Library category — Fallback — is added: available from any in-scope stage (2 through 11, matching §1.8's own ownership scope exactly), triggered exclusively by retry-exhaustion (§23.5), never by a Decision Engine condition. Its content — the actual neutral wording — remains entirely Behavior Specification territory, per Chapter 7 §7.6's own already-frozen rule that content is never this document's to write.**

**Reported as an extension, following established precedent, not silently assumed already covered.** This mirrors exactly how Chapter 17 added a justified third logging category and Chapter 18 added a justified third direct-call category to already-frozen, seemingly-closed lists — a real gap, closed by extension, cited transparently rather than smoothed over or treated as requiring the Constitutional Amendment Procedure (which is reserved for genuine contradictions, not gaps a later chapter is positioned to fill).

**Reconciliation with §10.9's earlier "closed-list" wording (Constitutional Amendment #2).** Chapter 10 §10.9 originally stated, in passing, that "§1.11 fixes the library list as closed" and that the "six-library list has no room for" a seventh — used there only to establish the narrower, correct point that no *Decision-Engine-triggered* intervention (topic-drift especially) needs its own new category. Read literally, that global "closed" phrasing would have contradicted this section's seventh category. The document-wide audit surfaced this; the resolution (Constitutional Amendment #2, logged in §10.9 and the front matter) narrowed §10.9's wording to its actual scope rather than weakening this section: §10.9 governs Decision-Engine-triggered categories and needs no new entry for them; the Fallback category is triggered by a Safety/Validation Layer outcome (retry-exhaustion), a genuinely different axis §10.9 never spoke to. The two chapters are now consistent — §1.11's list is not, and never literally was per §1.11's own text, a globally closed set; it admits exactly the one Safety-Layer-triggered extension this section adds.

**Selection within the Fallback category still uses Chapter 7's own deterministic mechanism, unmodified.** §7.7's hash-based, no-randomness variation selection applies to this seventh category exactly as it already applies to the other six — this chapter adds a category, never a second selection mechanism.

### 23.7 Explicit Scope Boundary with Chapters 1, 2, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, and 22

Stated directly, matching the pattern §21.8 and §22.9 already establish: **Chapter 23 (this chapter)** owns the inspection mechanism (§23.3), the two check categories (§23.4), the bounded retry path (§23.5), and the new Fallback Prompt Library category (§23.6). It does not own, and this chapter introduces no content that redefines:

- **Chapter 1**'s role/content rules and metadata-leakage concern — given mechanism, never redefined.
- **Chapter 2**'s five-gate enumeration and adapter-binding exclusivity — honored exactly; no new gate, no new binding.
- **Chapter 6**'s Gemini Flash contract — enforced, never altered.
- **Chapter 7**'s Prompt Builder mechanism, its structural/cross-cutting mapping, and its deterministic selection algorithm — extended by one category, never redesigned.
- **Chapter 10**'s conflict-resolution priority order and `proposeOwnershipChange` mechanism — an existing Tier 1 trigger is confirmed, never a new one added.
- **Chapter 11**'s Timing Engine and latency-budget table — treated as a binding constraint, never touched or revised (Chapter 21 owns eventual revision).
- **Chapter 12**'s Fairness/Silence/Ownership mechanisms — this chapter confirms, not redesigns, that personality never weakens their application, a rule that already governed Safety identically before this chapter existed.
- **Chapter 15**'s persona catalog and phrasing-variance boundary — unchanged; this chapter confirms no persona-specific exception exists.
- **Chapter 16**'s Configuration System mechanism — this chapter supplies a new parameter category (rule-set content) as a justified extension per §16.7's own explicit allowance; Chapter 16's loading/consumption mechanism is unchanged.
- **Chapter 22**'s adapter interfaces and binding-count design — reused exactly; adapter credential handling (§22.9's own hand-off) is named as a genuinely open question this chapter does not resolve, since credential security is a distinct concern from output validation and this chapter's own scope is precisely output checking, not vendor-connection security.

### 23.8 Advantages

Resolves the chapter's central design question — LLM-judge versus fast heuristic — via a real, decisive cross-reference (§11.6) rather than an assumed-obvious design choice, closing a genuine risk that a naively "safer-sounding" LLM-judge design would have silently contradicted already-frozen latency text. Draws the metadata-leakage/role-content distinction precisely, treating the more tractable mechanical check and the honestly-imperfect heuristic check as genuinely different problems rather than forcing both through one uniform mechanism. Designs detection and recovery together, making the heuristic's real imperfection the direct, stated justification for the retry-and-fallback path rather than an afterthought risk. Closes a real, previously-invisible gap in Chapter 7's own six-category Prompt Library list, following an already-established extension precedent rather than either silently assuming coverage or over-invoking the amendment procedure for a genuine extension.

### 23.9 Alternatives Considered

**(a) A second LLM call (an "judge" model) evaluating the first model's output for role/content violations.** Rejected outright (§23.3): would contradict §11.6's already-frozen ~30–50ms/no-vendor-call assumption by roughly doubling the turn's real latency cost — a genuine cross-chapter contradiction, not a design this chapter is free to choose.

**(b) One undifferentiated check mechanism for both metadata-leakage and role/content violations.** Rejected (§23.4): the two problems have genuinely different tractability (mechanical containment vs. semantic judgment); forcing both through one mechanism would either over-engineer the leakage check or under-serve the role/content check.

**(c) Treat the fallback utterance as fitting within an existing Prompt Library category (e.g., Silence-recovery) rather than adding a new one.** Rejected (§23.6): a rejection-triggered fallback is conceptually and causally distinct from a silence-triggered recovery — conflating their trigger conditions would blur two genuinely different Decision-Engine-versus-Safety-Layer-sourced events into one category, muddying §7.5's own clean structural/cross-cutting distinction rather than cleanly extending it.

**(d) Give the Safety Layer its own dedicated LLM adapter binding, reserved for potential future use, even though this chapter's current design makes no vendor call.** Rejected: would silently expand Chapter 22's binding count for a capability this chapter explicitly does not use, violating this document's consistent "extend only what's actually needed" discipline.

### 23.10 Recommended Approach

The non-vendor, text-analysis-only inspection mechanism (§23.3) per option (a)'s rejection; two distinctly-treated check categories (§23.4) per option (b)'s rejection; the bounded retry-and-fallback path reusing the pathway's existing binding (§23.5); and a new, explicitly-justified seventh Fallback Prompt Library category (§23.6) per option (c)'s rejection, with no speculative new adapter binding (§23.9's option (d) rejection).

### 23.11 Possible Risks

**The role/content heuristic check is a genuinely imperfect semantic approximation, named honestly rather than oversold.** A sufficiently subtly-phrased coaching remark or hidden hint could pass an keyword/pattern-based check that a human reviewer would catch instantly — this is not a defect to be engineered away within this chapter's own non-vendor-call constraint; it is an inherent limitation of the design chosen, and the retry-and-fallback path bounds its worst-case cost without eliminating the underlying detection gap.

**False positives from the heuristic check could reject legitimate, in-role output, consuming the bounded retry budget on turns that never actually needed correction.** Named honestly: a pattern-based check trades some false-positive rate for its speed; the real-world false-positive rate is unmeasured, since no real integration of this mechanism exists yet — the same "no real precedent" limitation named for other first-principles chapters in this range (12, 15, 20, 22).

**The metadata-leakage check's reliability depends entirely on Chapter 7 §7.8's own prevention discipline being followed correctly at every context-payload assembly site.** If a future implementation ever passed an internal signal to the model as unstructured prose rather than a demarcated field, this chapter's containment check would still catch a *literal* leak but could miss a paraphrased one — the backstop is real, but it is a backstop, not a substitute for §7.8's own prevention discipline holding.

### 23.12 Future Improvements

If real production experience ever shows the heuristic role/content check's false-negative rate is unacceptably high, a future revision could introduce a genuinely asynchronous, non-blocking secondary review (e.g., a post-delivery audit pass feeding Chapter 17's decision log and Chapter 18's alerting, never gating delivery itself) — explicitly not designed here, since it would be a new mechanism outside this chapter's own latency-bounded, pre-delivery scope, named as a real possibility rather than silently foreclosed. Once real usage data exists, the rule-set content (Chapter 16, via this chapter's extension) is the natural, low-cost tuning surface — a pure value change, never requiring this chapter's own mechanism to be revisited.

| **The role/content heuristic's imperfection was originally only named in Possible Risks**, after the mechanism was already presented as if fully adequate, risking an impression of overclaimed reliability | §23.4 — moved the honest limitation into the mechanism's own introduction, explicitly framing it as the direct justification for §23.5's retry-and-fallback design rather than a separately-discovered caveat |
| **The new Fallback Prompt Library category's first draft did not explicitly rule out reusing an existing category**, risking a reader wondering why this wasn't simply folded into Silence-recovery or Encouragement | §23.6 — added option (c) to Alternatives Considered, explicitly reasoning through and rejecting the reuse option |

### 23.14 Forward-Reference Index — Formal Validation Gauntlet

**Pass 1 — Adversarial.** Attempted rejection angle: "a fast, non-LLM heuristic check is fundamentally too weak for a *safety* mechanism — doesn't naming this limitation honestly amount to admitting the chapter doesn't actually solve its own charter?" Addressed: the chapter's charter (§1.5) is to check output and own a bounded fallback path, not to guarantee semantic perfection — §1.8's own bounded-retry-then-deterministic-fallback design already anticipates that detection is imperfect (an unbounded retry loop would only make sense if detection were expected to eventually succeed with certainty; a *bounded* one only makes sense against an imperfect detector) — this chapter's honesty about the heuristic's limits is consistent with, not a departure from, what §1.8 already implied. Second angle: "the new Fallback category could be seen as smuggled-in scope expansion of Chapter 7 without proper justification." Addressed: §23.6 traces the exact gap (no existing category fits both stage-independence and rejection-triggering), rejects the most tempting reuse alternative explicitly (§23.9(c)), and cites established precedent (Chapters 17/18's own justified-extension pattern) rather than asserting the extension is obviously fine.

**Pass 2 — Constitutional Compatibility.** Checked against all twenty-two frozen chapters' exact text: §1.3/§1.5/§1.8/§1.13 (charter, fallback path, role/content rules, personality-agnosticism — satisfied throughout), §2.7 (five-gate position, binding exclusivity — satisfied, §23.3/§23.5), §6.5/§6.7 (Gemini Flash contract — satisfied, §23.4), §7.5/§7.6/§7.7/§7.8 (mapping framework, content-vs-mechanism split, deterministic selection, leakage prevention — satisfied and precisely extended, §23.6), §10.4 (Tier 1 trigger — satisfied, §23.5), §11.6 (the decisive latency constraint — satisfied and central to the whole design, §23.2/§23.3), §12.8 (personality-agnosticism — satisfied, §23.4), §15's persona catalog (unchanged — satisfied, §23.7), §16.7/§16.8 (extension allowance, provisional retry value — satisfied and directly exercised, §23.5/§23.7), §22.4/§22.9 (binding design, credential hand-off — satisfied, §23.3/§23.7). No contradiction found; zero amendment procedures invoked.

**Pass 3 — Implementation.** Mentally built end-to-end: Gemini Flash returns text via the pathway's shared LLM binding → the Safety Layer, holding no binding of its own, runs its two check categories against the text and the context payload that produced it, completing in ~30–50ms → if both pass, approved text proceeds to Gradium (§1.14 step 6) → if either fails, the Prompt Builder is re-invoked with a corrective instruction, reusing the same binding, up to the Chapter 16 maximum (2) → if all retries are exhausted, the Fallback Prompt Library category's deterministic selection (§7.7's mechanism, unmodified) produces the neutral utterance, which proceeds to Gradium exactly as any other approved text would → separately, the rejection is a Tier 1 trigger already known to §10.4's conflict-resolution rule. No missing step found; no module invented beyond the already-counted ten, and no new adapter binding added to Chapter 22's count.

Convergence assessed as high.

**Pass 5 — Production-Readiness.** Read start-to-finish as new. Failure scenario: all retries exhausted on a genuinely difficult turn — resolves deterministically to the Fallback category, never silence, per §1.8's own already-frozen guarantee. Concurrency scenario: the Safety Layer's check runs entirely within one turn's own already-serialized processing (per-room, per Chapter 13's guarantees) — no new concurrency hazard, since it introduces no state shared across turns or rooms. Scale scenario: the check's ~30–50ms cost at high concurrent-room volume — a pure CPU-bound text operation, not a vendor-rate-limited or database-bound cost, and therefore not subject to the same scaling risks Chapter 20/21 already named for database-tier and vendor-spend concerns.

## Chapter 24 — Future Extensibility

### 24.0 Compatibility with Chapters 1–23

No point below required modifying Chapters 1–23. This chapter is different in kind from Chapters 15–23: it introduces almost no new mechanism, instead cataloging and cross-checking mechanisms every one of Chapters 2–23 already designed for itself, and closing exactly one substantive new question (§1.0/§1.10/§1.19/§1.24's future-scoring-module citation). Every citation below is either confirmed exactly as already frozen, or — for the one genuinely new finding (§24.4's randomness/idempotency tension) — stated as a constraint on an explicitly *unassigned* future chapter, never a change to any chapter that exists today.

- **§1.0/§1.10/§1.24 (frozen)** — the durable-transcript-feeds-future-scoring claim is verified in concrete detail (§24.5/§24.6), never redefined.
- **Every extension point named in Chapters 2–23's own text** — catalogued (§24.3), never redesigned.
- **§7.14/§13.3 (frozen, both independently, never previously cross-referenced)** — the randomness/idempotency finding (§24.4) states a new constraint on an *unassigned* future chapter; it modifies neither Chapter 7 nor Chapter 13's own frozen text.
- **§2.4's ten-module count, §10.15's fifth-sub-analyzer path (frozen)** — cross-checked and confirmed compatible (§24.4), neither redefined.
- **§14.12's fifth-Session-Object-field path, §20.8's capacity-budgeting methodology (frozen)** — cross-checked and confirmed compatible (§24.4), neither redefined.
- **§17's decision log, §20.9's retention policy (frozen)** — confirmed sufficient for a future scoring consumer (§24.5), with one honest, real dependency named rather than assumed away.

### 24.1 Purpose

To catalog, in one place, every extension point Chapters 2–23 have each already named for themselves; to cross-check a meaningful sample of them against each other — something no single chapter's own local self-review could do, since no chapter reads every other chapter's own forward-looking claims; and to close this document's one remaining substantive extensibility citation — future scoring-module compatibility — with concrete, verified detail rather than a restated claim.

### 24.2 Design Rationale

**This chapter's shape follows directly from an honest observation: the extensibility work is already mostly done.** Every chapter since 2 has scored its own "Extensibility" scorecard category and named concrete extension points in its own closing sections — §2.8's four-boundary adapter pattern, §4.5's exam-type-agnostic Stage Specification engine, §7.14's controlled-randomness seam, §9.12's fifth-record-type path, §10.15's fifth-sub-analyzer path, §11.13's configurable checkpoint list, §12.13's escalation-level list, §13.3's standing idempotency mandate, §14.12's fifth-field path, and more through §23.12. Re-deriving any of these here would duplicate work already done correctly; this chapter's real value is elsewhere — in synthesis and cross-checking.

**Why cross-checking, specifically, is genuine new work and not busywork.** Chapter 7's self-review checked its own claims against Chapters 1–6; Chapter 13's checked its own against Chapters 1–12. Neither ever checked its *own future-extension claim* against the *other's*, because neither had reason to — Chapter 7 was written before Chapter 13 existed, and Chapter 13's own self-review had no occasion to revisit Chapter 7's already-frozen text for a compatibility question specific to a hypothetical future feature neither chapter was designing. This is a structural blind spot every individually-scoped chapter necessarily has, and it is exactly what a dedicated extensibility-synthesis chapter, positioned after all the individual pieces are frozen, is positioned to close.
